1
Derek, Raph, and Lucas
WRS 101
Winter 2026 - 02/08/2026
Daniel Harvey
Learning From the Experts: Improving Personal Academic Writing Through the Analysis
of Professionals in the Field of Psychology
Introduction
Many new students going into university are faced with many challenges they have not
encountered before, one of which is the introduction of scholarly articles. When university
students are being introduced to the world of academic writing, it can be confusing and difficult
to understand specifically how to compose a proper academic article. In papers across different
academic fields, there is a great variety in the structure, purpose, and context that has been
curated for a target audience. This paper attempts to facilitate the writing process of formal
scholarly papers by demonstrating consistencies and deviations within the academic field of
psychology and its research articles. This analysis is necessary to shape the work of upcoming
scholars and pave the road of success for their future writings. In our research, we have analyzed
six peer-reviewed articles all in the psychology genre with a focus on mental health. Through our
analysis of these academic articles, we have concluded that psychology papers have strict
standards that are generally used, in learning from the structure of academic writing, personal
success in writing will improve.
2
Rhetorical Situation
In order to effectively convey the findings of their research, writers of academic articles
must first reach their target audience. An article is able to find its target audience through the
application of vocabulary and terms that is most often only relevant and meaningful to those
people. Our analysis indicates that psychology-focused papers are mainly trying to reach an
audience of other experts or researchers in their field. Furthermore, they are able to both appeal
to and designate their target audience through the use of knowledge that only their target
audience is likely to know. For papers relating to psychology and mental health, the knowledge
expected of the audience includes an understanding of mental health terms such as “problematic
internet use” (PIU) (Oka et al., 2021), its effects, a specific vocabulary, and a general idea of the
current basis of knowledge or context upon which modern research is conducted. Other
researchers would likely read these research articles to further their own knowledge on topics
presented. It is essential that these articles reach their intended audience because only the
audience is able to further the research presented in the article and / or use the knowledge gained
to make change in the current field (which in the case for our examined articles, may include
using video games in order to alleviate symptoms of mental illness). Overall, composing a
research article requires the careful consideration of the audience and their preexisting
knowledge.
Not only is an article targeting a specific audience, but it is also interacting as a part of a
discourse community. The articles we analyzed are most largely related to discourse
communities such as mental health advocates, psychology researchers, or even clinicians or
psychologists. Discourse communities like these would share a common goal of expanding
current knowledge on mental health and searching for possible treatments for mental illness. This
3
aligns with the purpose of every research article we reviewed, which was to fill a gap in
knowledge or research and impart the findings to the reader. Having a discourse community is
crucial to build an ever-growing foundation of knowledge that future researchers can build upon.
This foundation and community of experts allows for knowledge to advance more rapidly, as it
allows for others to further research without having to build background information and data; it
is already built up from years of research. The discourse community one is writing in also
influences the resulting quality of the work; the feedback and rebuttal that can come from
discourse communities ensures that writers will use proper evidence and provide reasonable
claims based on reliable data. In order to effectively write a psychology article and contribute to
the basis of knowledge, it is important to meet the standards of the discourse community.
Rhetorical Strategies
Once the target audience and discourse community has been determined, it is still
necessary to persuade them on the importance of the writer’s own article. Writers often employ
rhetorical strategies to do so. Ethos, the appeal to ethics and credibility, was very influential in
making an article persuasive during our analysis. One of the most important ways that articles
achieve ethos is through the in-depth vocabulary used. Specific word choice and correct
terminology demonstrates expertise in the subject matter, making the article both credible and
informative. This extensive vocabulary does, however, make the article hard to follow for
non-experts (this will be expanded on in the pathos section). Another crucial part of ethos is the
authors themselves. Throughout all of the articles we analyzed, all of the authors were experts in
their field, demonstrated by either having multiple articles published, or having necessary
credentials. Lastly, the presentation of data is also indicative of the article’s credibility. In some
4
of our articles, data was presented in a table made to easily digest the information given (Stevens
et al., 2020; Teng et al., 2021; Oka et al., 2021). Even if the content and ideas of an article are
impactful, without ethos, the readers will not believe or trust the information.
The next important method of persuasion is logos, the appeal to logic. The articles we
analyzed all made logical conclusions and had a clear thought process, which is primarily seen in
the methods sections of the articles. The ways in which the researchers conducted their research
followed a clear logic, this simple logic makes parts of the article easy to follow (relating to
pathos as well) and it makes the information of the articles easier to accept and digest. It is
important for an article to have strong logos in order to have it align with current knowledge and
have the findings be believable. Logos is essential to have opinions and points rooted in fact
when trying to persuade a reader. Articles also achieved logical validity through the consistency
of their beliefs, arguments, and data. This consistency is demonstrated as having no
contradictions in their arguments and not changing interpretations of data depending on what
suits an argument most. Consistency is important to maintain both the strength of the arguments
presented in the article as well as the believability of the claims. Logos is essential to
communicate ideas in a way that is understandable and appealing to the reader’s beliefs.
The final persuasive technique is pathos. In many academic articles, an appeal to pathos
often takes the shape of how captivating or understandable the article is, and not directly an
appeal to emotion. While this is also mostly true for psychology articles, the subject of some
articles can result in persuasion through genuine emotion. Many of our articles touched on topics
like mental health, which can evoke a sense of sympathy. We found that this sympathy can result
in a desire to read further in order to understand solutions to mental health problems. Another
positive force of pathos was when other persuasive methods such as logos were at play. When
5
arguments followed a clear logic, it was much easier to follow along, this made the article more
understandable and encouraged further reading. Opposite to this, when an article contained
high-end vocabulary that could be attributed to ethos, the article became much harder to
comprehend and it was discouraging to read further. However, the difficulty we experienced in
understanding some articles is also simply because we are a secondary audience to them. The
authors do not need to concern themselves with breaking down complicated words because they
are standard to their audience. Generally, pathos is important in realizing the purpose of the
article by making the information they are trying to convey easy to understand.
Macro-Organization
In order to successfully write an article that is accepted by your discourse community, it
is important to align with the expected formatting. Based on the articles we have revised the
general organization of the article often follows the IMRD model. Most articles began with an
introduction, one of our articles had a “background” section instead of an introduction, but the
function of the section was very similar. The introduction is an essential part of an article, it is
used to give context on the current state of research, provide the article’s purpose (which was
consistently a research gap they are attempting to fill), and some articles introduced their
methods of research. All of our articles also contained the method section, which described how
the data was collected. The methods section, as mentioned earlier, was appealing to logic,
making it much better at conveying information. Articles most often did not expand on the
implications of research findings until the discussion section (Teng et al., 2021). The discussion
section involved exploring the implications of their research but also a larger part was providing
ideas on where to take future research. Organizing an article in the IMRD structure is important
6
to easily access information so the reader does not have to go through the entire article to assess
its relevance / importance to their own research.
Most of our articles contained multiple subsections designed to further organize the
article’s information. The amount of subsections per major section varied heavily per article, but
the one thing that stayed relatively consistent was the methods section including the most
subsections. This organizational method makes sense, since there are many factors one must
consider when conducting research and it is therefore necessary to outline the entire procedure to
ensure it has as few flaws as possible. The methods section often included subsections for how
they gathered subjects, how they measured their dependent variables, and the procedure for
conducting their research. Another section with many subsections was the discussion section,
where authors would have specific subsections to direct further research, discuss the implications
of their findings, and outline any limitations or potential flaws in their study. Having many
subsections to describe the study’s findings is important to be able to do an in-depth analysis of
the research findings, as it is the part that is most essential to fulfilling the purpose of the article
by filling the research gap. For the articles that conducted research via interviews, there were
subsections for “bins” that the responses fell into, such as positive or negative responses (Colder
et al. 2018). Subsections are a very useful tool for organizing information to make your article
accessible to a reader.
All articles contain an argument, and the placement of that argument is important. The
arguments in our papers are placed in two different regions with different reasons. Some are at
the end of the article in the discussion (Colder et al., 2018) or conclusion (Stevens et al., 2020),
while others present their findings in the abstract (Teng et al., 2021; Oka et al., 2021). Arguments
placed in the abstract state a position and use the rest of the article to explain how it came about,
7
while other papers that place their argument after the results in an attempt to reduce early bias for
readers of the article by not revealing the results and implications until after all the methodology
and data is shown. Another trend noticed for the arguments was that they were very simple and
very agreeable. The arguments outlined their findings and gave a small suggestion on how their
discourse community should use the findings. One article simply argues that college campuses
should “consider how to integrate this information” in an attempt to “support undergraduate
student success” (Stevens et al., 2020, p.1134). Arguments are an essential part of an academic
article that directs further action by the reader and attempts to make change.
Despite all articles containing IMRD structures, there were also a lot of extra sections not
part of the IMRD model. One article contained a “highlights” section, which seemed to be a
shorter abstract (this article still included a full-length abstract) as well (Colder et al., 2018). This
highlights section most likely serves as a compressed abstract that allows a reader to swiftly
identify how relevant the article is to their own research. It is also possible that the highlights
section is used to provide keywords that can direct a reader to further research in similar topics.
As mentioned earlier there was an article that contained a “background” section that still had
incredibly similar content and structure to an introduction section. Generally, the articles we
studied had very little deviation from the IMRD model save for the minor deviations mentioned
above.
Micro-Organization
Along with a general guideline based around the larger structure of an article, there are
also specific moves that seem to form the basis of many sections in a paper. Firstly in the
introduction, a necessary move was to present the topic. This move had very similar formatting
8
across the articles, being generally: “the present study examines… to assess…” (Stevens et al.,
2020, p.1128). Other important moves important to the introduction included: presenting a gap in
modern research and presenting how their research will fill that gap (Stevens et al., 2020; Colder
et al., 2018; Teng et al., 2021; Oka et al., 2021). All of these moves are important to achieve the
purpose of the introduction and also align with Swales’ 3-move model: establishing a territory,
establishing a niche, and occupying the niche.
The method section of the article also contained many essential moves. In the method
section of the articles, they would mainly restate the research gap and how they will fill the
research gap. Other moves in the methods section expanded on the specific ways that research
will be conducted, such as: “the present study focused on investigating… . Based on the
assumptions of …, the present longitudinal study examines the role of…” (Teng et al., p. 171).
These moves are essential to effectively communicate with other members of the discourse
community, they allow for the experiment to not only be reproduced, but scrutinized for potential
confounding factors that could contribute to unrealistic data. These standards are necessary
components of the communicative process of a discourse community and ensure good quality
and maintain honesty.
Overall, the results section of the different articles did not have many consistencies
between them. Since each article conducted different research with different methods, there was
a large variance in the results sections. Broadly speaking, all articles present their data in similar
ways, some articles presented data in data tables (Teng et al., 2021), whereas others simply
discussed the results of their research verbally and provided the collected data as a part of the
citations / resources section at the end of the article. The presentation of data was consistently
done in a digestible format and allowed for a more efficient communicative process.
9
Finally, the discussion section provided multiple important moves. The main purpose of
the discussion section is to expand on the implications of the research findings, and direct future
research. This purpose is achieved through common moves like “Another area of potential is…
.” (Colder et al., 2018, p. 129), of which was used in multiple articles with slight variations.
Other moves included stating limitations of the study: “There are several limitations to this study.
First, … .” (Oka et al., 2021, p. 224) and exploring potential biases and uncertainties and thus the
implications of the data obtained. These moves seem to be standard, if not essential, to
discussion sections across psychology articles. This section is also where the argument is most
likely to be found. Overall, the discussion section is critical and efficient in elaborating upon the
research and communicating its results.
Conclusion
In this paper my group has analyzed the general structure and methods used in academic
writing in the field of psychology. In our analysis, we have concluded that there is a standard for
how information is presented and conveyed through the use of subsections, persuasion methods,
and rhetorical moves. All of these techniques illustrated throughout this paper demonstrates the
importance of following the standards set by experts in the field and the strength it can bring to
both your argument and structure when presenting your findings in psychology. The same skills
used in these papers can also be translated to personal writing through intentional usage of
structure (macro and micro), appeals, and awareness of rhetorical situations.
10
References

Mini Lessons: Genre as Social Action: Based on Miller (1984), remember that genres are not just static templates or 'scripts.' They are 'typified rhetorical actions' that respond to recurring social situations. When you analyze a genre, look for how the structure solves a specific communication problem for the community.

The Function of Metaphor in Science: As seen in the analysis of Masten's 'Ordinary Magic,' metaphors in academic writing are not just decorative. They serve as 'rhetorical moves' that can bridge the gap between complex data and conceptual understanding, making new theories feel intuitive to the audience.

Academic Gatekeeping: Diction and citation density often serve a 'boundary-maintenance' function. By using specialized jargon and assuming prior knowledge, authors signal their membership in a 'discourse community' (Swales, 1990), which builds ethos but also intentionally limits the audience to experts.

1
A Rhetorical and Genre Analysis of Conceptual Research Summaries in Psychology
Violet Chen, Zhiqi Cai, and Ximing Yu
Department of English and Film Studies, University of Alberta
WRS 101: Exploring Writing
Daniel Harvey
February 8, 2026
2
A Rhetorical and Genre Analysis of Conceptual Research Summaries in Psychology
Academic research writing relies on recognizable genres, which determine how
knowledge is constructed and communicated in the discipline group. The function of these
genres is a repetitive rhetorical response to shared communication situations. Miller (1984)
believes that genres represent a social behavior, and the text uses a predictable structure to serve
the common purpose of a specific audience. In psychology, research summaries play a vital role
in clarifying concepts, forming theories and guiding future research.
The six texts investigated in this report all focus on psychology. The definition of
resilience in psychology is conceptually complex and ambiguous. Because of this conceptual
confusion, the research summary acts as more than just a list of facts; it is a strategic tool that
authors use to draw lines and define the boundaries of the field. The selected articles include
Bonanno (2004), Luthar, Cicchetti and Becker (2000), Masten (2001), Rutter (1987), Southwick
et al. (2014) and Ungar (2011). Although these authors study resilience from developmental,
clinical, ecological and interdisciplinary perspectives, all six articles are of the same genre: the
conceptual psychology research summary.
Different from empirical research articles, conceptual research summarizes the existing
theoretical achievements, evaluates theoretical assumptions, and puts forward an explanatory
framework. The purpose of this report is to analyze the common rhetorical and genre
characteristics of these texts, and to examine how variations reflect different academic aims. The
analysis shows that although the articles show strong similarity in rhetorical situation,
arrangement, argument construction and academic style, there are meaningful differences in their
scope and author status, which illustrates how this genre balances stability with flexibility
3
Rhetorical Situation
The rhetorical situation includes the shaping of text by author, audience, purpose, genre
and context (Bitzer, 1968). In these six articles, these components show a lot of overlap, which
helps to explain the rhetorical patterns they share.
All six texts are published by famous scholars in major research institutions, and in
peer-reviewed psychology journals, such as American Psychologist and Child Development.
This publication choice proves that the authors aren't just writing for anyone; they are writing for
a very specific discourse community. By using dense jargon and heavy citations, they effectively
build disciplinary boundaries that keep non-experts out, allowing them to jump straight into
complex theoretical fights.
The historical background of the articles further influenced their rhetorical goals. Earlier
articles, such as Rutter (1987), reflect the formative research on resilience. At that time, the main
rhetorical strategies focused on the research on the resilience of the protection mechanism. Later
articles respond to the rapid growth of the field by trying to clarify unclear definitions, while
more recent studies focus on combining ideas from different disciplines.
The target audience is mainly composed of members of the psychological research
community, including psychological researchers, graduate students, clinicians and policy
scholars. The use of formal reference practices, limited explanation of foundational concepts,
and frequent specialized terminology clearly indicate the intended target audience. As Swales
(1990) pointed out, discourse communities share conventions and communication goals,
allowing authors to participate in advanced theoretical discussions without re-expounding basic
knowledge.
4
The main purpose of summarizing genres in conceptual research is to provide
information and persuasiveness. In six texts, the authors try to clarify concepts, criticize the
shortcomings of previous studies, and guide future studies, which determines the rhetoric and
structural choice of genres.
Rhetorical Strategies: Ethos, Pathos, and Logos
Across the six articles, ethos, pathos, and logos function in distinct but complementary
ways.
Ethos is mainly established through academic authority. Through intensive reference to
practice, contact with basic theories, publication in famous journals and recognition of the
limitations of methods, credibility has been improved. Rutter’s early work established theoretical
authority, and later authors put their arguments within established scholarly conversations.
Pathos plays a limited and controlled role, and emotional appeal appears in the form of
professional concern rather than personal emotion. The mention of trauma or social
consequences highlights the relevance of resilience research, but still maintains academic
objectivity, which is consistent with the expectation of discipline neutrality.
Logos is the main rhetorical appeal. The author uses concept differentiation and synthesis
of previous findings rather than providing new empirical data. Bonanno (2004) uses the result
trajectory as a rhetorical organization method to distinguish resilience from recovery. Masten
(2001) organized the literature into an adaptive system and used macro-organization to explain
the complexity. Luthar et al. (2000) relied on systematic criticism and response to solve the
definition differences, and Ungar (2011) adopted the principle of taxonomic ecology to guide the
5
interpretation. Southwick et al. (2014) adopted the question-and-response form to facilitate
interdisciplinary comparison.
Together, these strategies show how conceptual research summaries rely on rhetorical
organization and logical sequencing, rather than empirical data, to produce convincing scholarly
arguments for academic audiences.
Macro-organization of the research articles
We can very directly understand the writing style of psychology by focusing on the
macro-organization of writing. While this report examines six foundational texts, the following
analysis focuses on the distinct macro-organizational patterns of three primary articles to
illustrate different communicative purposes. Bonanno (2004) deviates from standard conventions
by using a point-based structure instead of the traditional IMRD format. Instead of following the
usual academic script, he uses sub-points to systematically disassemble old myths about grief,
making his argument function as a critique on old theories. There are a lot of small sub-points
besides the three obvious sub-points in Bonanno (2004). The author used a large amount of text
to raise an argument and refute this argument, so the purpose of Bonanno (2004) is more likely
to correct some academic mistakes by specific cases. That is why there are a lot of small
sub-points in Bonanno (2004), because sub-points can be effective in refining and elaborating the
main claim (Toulmin, 1958). We can find a similar structure in Masten (2001), which has an
obvious introduction and conclusion and uses very clear sub-points to organize the body of the
article. These sub-points replace the part of the methods and results in the normal IMRD
structure. They also allow people to understand the argument in a step-by-step way because they
can effectively explain a specific aspect of resilience. In this way, readers can not only follow the
author's pace to gradually understand the complicated concept, but people also don't have to try
6
to understand massive amounts of information at once. Masten (2001) relied on a large number
of models and categories to define and differentiate resilience. In the normal IMRD structure,
the methods mean how data is produced, and the results mean what data shows. However, in
Masten (2001), models mean how resilience works, and the categories help people to distinguish
different situations. Therefore, the clear sub-points can help people to quickly locate the concept
and compare different models.
Furthermore, we can find the pattern of the article in the psychology discipline that it is
more important for psychology research to provide a clear definition of a concept; otherwise,
research can't be explained and compared (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955). Luthar et al. (2000) sticks
to a more traditional, problem-response-guideline structure. While it’s complex, it feels like a
safe bet for the field—systematic but maybe a bit predictable compared to the more aggressive
moves we see in Bonanno’s work. By organizing the body around the existing shortages in
research, the author raises guidelines that feel systematic but perhaps a bit predictable. In the
body of this article, each section is organized around analyzing the shortage of the existing
research. Then, the author raised guidelines for future research, which form a whole
problem-response-guideline-based structure. Such a structure is not only effective for the reader
to quickly find specific arguments by each different section, but the reader can also understand
the critical logic and accept guidelines raised by the author.
Micro-organization and language/style features of the research articles
Moving from macro-structure to micro-organization, the use of rhetorical moves—as
defined by Swales (1990)—further distinguishes how each author achieves their specific
communicative purpose. The rhetorical purpose of Bonanno (2004) is to redefine resilience and
refute those traditional, popular assumptions. Then, the pattern in the move structure used by the
7
author is that they first raise an argument, identify the problem of this argument, introduce a
large number of research studies, and finally explain how those research studies work. The
diction here serves a specific rhetorical function. The heavy use of restrictive words and
references is a calculated move to build academic gatekeeping, ensuring that the argument is
only taken seriously by other insiders in the discourse community. For instance, a large number
of restrictive words and references are used by the author to increase accuracy and credibility.
Finally, the micro-organization of Bonanno (2004) is effective because the author firstly
challenges dominant assumptions with enough reliable evidence and redefines the assumption in
order to make the reader believe that resilience is common.
However, the rhetorical purpose of Masten (2001) is to systematically build a framework
of resilience. Masten (2001) uses a teaching-oriented strategy. She isn't just giving facts; she’s
using the 'Ordinary Magic' metaphor as a rhetorical move to make a difficult concept feel like
common sense. It’s a smart way to claim authority without sounding too aggressive and lastly
indicates the meaning of models in developing psychology. Furthermore, the teaching-oriented
diction and clear move structure in Masten (2001) effectively achieve the communicative
purpose, which is to help the reader understand complicated concepts.
Interestingly, Luthar et al. (2000) focus on criticizing existing research on resilience and
proposing research guidelines and suggestions. Luthar et al. (2000) applied a special pattern in
the move structure, in which they first indicate the problem or confusion in existing research,
explain why there is a problem, analyze what the outcome of this problem is, and propose
guidelines or suggestions. The author uses critical diction and style to write this article; that is
why the reader can be effective in identifying where the problems are and how to correct them.
8
Although there are very obvious differences between all three articles, each author applies a
special pattern in the move structure to achieve their own special communication purpose.
Although all three articles research resilience, they apply distinct argument organization,
which means different communicational goals. Bonanno (2004) focused on changing the
dominant argument of resilience, Masten (2001) paid attention to clarifying the concept of
resilience, and Luthar et al. (2000) used a large number of texts to critique the problem of
existing research on resilience. The distinct main claims trigger different evidence selection. For
example, Bonanno (2004) applied abundant empirical studies to emphasize the trend and
quantity; in contrast, Masten (2001) used a lot of models and illustrative evidence to clarify the
concept. Across all articles, the evidence is highly aligned with the authors' main claim. In other
words, it is clear that none of this is random. Every piece of evidence is a strategic move
designed to make the author's theory the new standard. As a result, the evidence selection is
highly effective because it directly supports the main claim rather than being an unintentional
citation (Toulmin, 1958). As a result, the argument organization of these articles is highly
effective because it helps to increase the authority of the authors, understand complicated
concepts, and provide guidelines.
Conclusion
It is quite clear that these articles are more than just "papers." They function as a
"strategic social response" to all the confusion in the resilience field (Miller, 1984). Instead of
just listing data, these authors use the literature review as a flexible tool to systematically
disassemble the core assumptions of old models. While they say the goal is defining resilience,
they are actually using rhetorical moves to fill specific gaps. This flexibility isn't just about
9
science; it's a way to protect the "professional boundaries" of the psychology discipline. They
employ this strategy. By using Swales’ (1990) idea of discourse communities, we can see these
texts are for "insiders" only. The heavy use of jargon and intertextuality shows they only care
about expert audience. This is clearly a strategy. By assuming everyone already knows the
basics, they can bypass foundational concepts and jump into the hard theories. It makes the text
less accessible for general audiences, but it definitely builds their own authority.
This is where the difference between authors becomes very obvious. Bonanno (2004) is
really the one who stands out here. He doesn't just show new data; he systematically
disassembles the core assumptions of the old "grief work" idea, making the previous models look
completely outdated. This represents a significant theoretical departure. Then we have Masten
(2001), whose use of the "Ordinary Magic" metaphor is a significant rhetorical achievement. By
calling it "magic," she changes resilience from something rare to a normal part of growing up.
This metaphorical move effectively bridges the gap between complex psychological processes
and normative human development. In contrast, Luthar et al. (2000) adhere to a more
conventional structure. Their work just follows the basic problem-solution structure we always
see. While it is clear and does the job, it lacks the persuasive impact that Bonanno and Masten
have. Luthar just reports what everyone agrees on, while the other two are busy reshaping the
whole field.
It is acknowledged that this report has some limitations. This report focuses mainly on
introductions, so we may have overlooked rhetorical nuances in the methods sections. However,
the main point is still there: a good research summary does more than just "summarizing." It
pushes the theory forward. Additionally, the lesson is that "academic authority" isn't just about
10
having big numbers or data. Ultimately, academic authority is constructed through strategic
rhetorical moves that guard disciplinary knowledge and dictate the direction of future research.
11

The Rhetoric of Objectivity: In scientific writing, 'objectivity' is itself a rhetorical performance. By using passive voice, technical jargon, and hedging, authors build 'ethos' by appearing to step back and let the data speak for itself.

Move Analysis (CARS Model): The paper effectively uses John Swales' 'Create a Research Space' (CARS) model to show how researchers justify their work by first establishing a territory, then finding a 'gap' in that territory, and finally 'occupying' that gap with their own study.
data.essay_text:
Rhetorical and Generic Conventions in Longitudinal Mental Health
Research on University Students
Mahin Rahman
WRS 101- Winter 2026 - Exploring Writing
Prof. Dan Harvey
Introduction
Over the past decade, university student mental health has become a central
concern within psychology, psychiatry, and public health research. Rising rates of
anxiety, depression, and psychological distress among first-year students have generated
an expanding body of longitudinal empirical studies aimed at identifying symptom
trajectories, risk factors, and protective variables. Although these studies differ in
institutional context, statistical modeling strategies, and disciplinary emphasis, they
adhere to recognizable structural and rhetorical conventions that define the empirical
research article genre within psychology and health sciences.
This report analyzes three longitudinal mental health studies published in BMJ
Open, Psychological Reports, and the Journal of Affective Disorders. While each article
reflects subtle differences in methodological focus and journal positioning, they
consistently employ the IMRaD structure, prioritize logos-driven argumentation through
statistical modeling, and follow standardized rhetorical move patterns in their
introductions. These shared conventions demonstrate that longitudinal mental health
research in psychology functions as a highly codified academic genre designed to
construct methodological transparency, reinforce disciplinary credibility, and
communicate findings efficiently within specialized discourse communities.
Rhetorical Situation
The three longitudinal studies analyzed here are situated within a broader
disciplinary concern regarding the prevalence and progression of mental health problems
among university students. Each article frames the transition to university as a critical
developmental period associated with heightened psychological vulnerability. For
example, Adams et al. (2021) explicitly state that “the transition to university coincides
with the peak period for the onset of mental illnesses” (p. 1). Similarly, Farrer et al.
(2024) note that “young people commencing university study for the first time may be
especially vulnerable” (p. 2). Porru et al. (2022) begin by emphasizing that “mental
health problems are highly prevalent among university students” (p. 250). These opening
moves establish a shared rhetorical situation: the need to systematically investigate
student mental health during a period of transition.
The intended audience across all three articles consists primarily of researchers,
public health scholars, and mental health professionals. This is evident through the
consistent use of technical language and statistical terminology without simplification.
Adams et al. (2021) describe using “binary logistic regression” to analyze predictors (p.
3). Farrer et al. (2024) report employing “latent growth curve models” to estimate
symptom change over time (p. 7). Porru et al. (2022) explain that a “between-within
linear regression model was used” to distinguish differences between individuals and
changes within individuals (pp. 250–251). The absence of lay explanations for these
methods signals an audience already familiar with advanced statistical modeling.
The communicative purpose of these articles is primarily to inform and contribute
empirically grounded evidence to ongoing scholarly discussions. Adams et al. (2021)
clearly articulate their research questions regarding predictors of “recovery” and
“emergence” of symptoms during first year (p. 2). Farrer et al. (2024) state that their
study aimed to “estimate initial levels of mental health symptoms… and identify factors
associated with change over time” (p. 4). Porru et al. (2022) similarly aim to assess “to
what extent the exposure to student life challenges is associated with mental health” (p.
251). Across journals, the shared purpose is to produce evidence capable of informing
institutional policy and intervention strategies.
The longitudinal design itself significantly shapes the rhetorical situation. Each
study emphasizes temporal measurement and change. Adams et al. distinguish between
“persistence and new onset” of clinically significant symptoms over the first academic
year (p. 2). Farrer et al. conduct a “four-wave online longitudinal study” (p. 1). Porru et
al. describe a “longitudinal study with 6 months follow-up” (p. 250). By foregrounding
repeated measurement over time, these articles position themselves as methodologically
rigorous contributions to understanding dynamic mental health trajectories rather than
static prevalence rates.
In line with genre theory, these research articles function as structured responses to
a recurring communicative problem: how to measure, model, and interpret student mental
health trends in a credible and reproducible way. The use of formal sectioning, statistical
modeling, and standardized instruments reflects alignment with the expectations of
psychology and health sciences discourse communities. Through these rhetorical choices,
the authors construct authority not through personal voice but through methodological
precision and empirical transparency.
Rhetorical Strategies: Ethos, Logos, and Pathos
Across the three longitudinal mental health studies, rhetorical appeals are
structured according to the epistemological priorities of psychology and health sciences,
where empirical validation takes precedence over emotional persuasion. As a result,
logos functions not simply as one persuasive strategy among others, but as the dominant
organizing principle of the genre.
Logos is most visible in the systematic presentation of quantitative data and
statistical modeling. For instance, Adams et al. (2021) report adjusted odds ratios such as
“AOR=1.14, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.20” when modeling recovery trajectories (p. 4),
foregrounding statistical precision as the basis of persuasion. Rather than asserting that
university connectedness improves outcomes, the authors rely on numerical probability
statements to establish credibility. Similarly, the Psychological Reports study employs
latent growth modeling to examine symptom trajectories across multiple time points,
emphasizing model fit and statistical significance rather than narrative explanation. In the
Journal of Affective Disorders article, regression analyses are presented through detailed
tables that quantify associations between risk factors and depressive symptoms. In all
three cases, persuasion occurs through measurable, replicable evidence. Even the visual
presentation of data—trajectory graphs and regression tables—functions rhetorically by
allowing readers to independently verify the strength of statistical relationships.
Ethos is constructed primarily through methodological transparency and adherence
to disciplinary protocols rather than through overt authorial authority. Adams et al. (2021)
explicitly report that “ethical approval was granted by the Queen’s University Health
Sciences and Affiliated Teaching Hospitals Research Ethics Board” (p. 4), signaling
compliance with institutional research standards. The consistent use of validated
instruments such as the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 further strengthens credibility; Adams et al.
describe these measures as having “demonstrated both construct and criterion validity”
(p. 3), reinforcing methodological rigor. Across the three articles, extensive detail is
devoted to participant recruitment, statistical assumptions, and analytical procedures.
Credibility in this genre therefore emerges not from rhetorical self-assertion, but from
procedural clarity and alignment with scientific norms of reproducibility and ethical
responsibility.
Pathos, by contrast, plays a limited but strategic role. Emotional appeals are
largely absent from Methods and Results sections, where objectivity is carefully
maintained. However, the introductions subtly frame student mental health as urgent and
socially significant. Adams et al. (2021) note that “the transition to university coincides
with the peak period for the onset of mental illnesses” (p. 1), establishing seriousness
without compromising academic tone. Similarly, references to academic attrition,
vulnerability, and increasing prevalence rates create contextual urgency. These restrained
emotional cues function to justify the relevance of the research while remaining
subordinate to statistical reasoning. In this genre, excessive emotional appeal could
undermine perceived objectivity; therefore, pathos is carefully controlled and embedded
within empirical framing.
Together, the distribution of rhetorical appeals across these studies reflects the
disciplinary values of psychology and health sciences. Logos provides argumentative
force through data-driven reasoning, ethos ensures credibility through methodological
rigor, and pathos establishes contextual importance without dominating the analysis. This
hierarchy of appeals demonstrates how longitudinal mental health research achieves
persuasion primarily through alignment with the expectations of a specialized academic
discourse community.
Macro-Organization of the Research Articles
All three articles follow the conventional IMRaD structure (Introduction,
Methods, Results, and Discussion), which functions as the dominant
macro-organizational framework for empirical research in psycholoigy and health
sciences. This predictable structure is not merely stylistic but rhetorical: it enables readers
within the discourse community to efficiently locate specific types of information and
evaluate methodological validity before accepting interpretive claims.
Despite this shared framework, each journal implements the structure with subtle
variations that reflect disciplinary emphasis and publication requirements. The BMJ Open
article demonstrates the most formally segmented organization. In addition to the
traditional IMRaD sequence, it includes structured abstracts, clearly labeled subsections
within Methods (Participants, Procedure, Measures, Statistical Analysis), and
supplementary transparency statements such as ethical approval and data availability.
This layered organization reflects the journal’s strong emphasis on public health reporting
standards and methodological transparency.
In contrast, the Psychological Reports article present a slightly more condensed
macro-structure, while still maintaining clear divisions between Introduction, Method,
Results, and Discussion. Its organizational focus centers heavily on statistical modeling
and trajectory analysis, and its Results section occupies proportionally more space than
other sections. This structural weight given to Results reflects the rhetorical priority of
empirical evidence within psychological research, where argument strength is measured
primarily through data presentation.
Similarly, the Journal of Affective Disorders article follows IMRaD conventions
but integrates clinical framing more prominently in both the Introduction and Discussion
sections. The Introduction often separates background context fro clearly stated research
aims, while the Discussion extends into implications for clinical understanding and
intervention. This variation highlights how journal scope influences macro-organization
without altering the foundational genre structure.
Across all three articles, the Methods sections are the most subdivided, commonly
including headings for sample characteristics, measurement instruments, and statistical
procedures. This detailed subdivision serves a crucial rhetorical function: it foregrounds
reproducibility and methodological clarity. By isolating analytical procedures into clearly
labeled subsections, the authors invite scrutiny and demonstrate compliance with
disciplinary standards of rigor.
The central argumentative force of each article is located primarily in the
Discussion sections. While the Introduction establishes the research gap and the Results
present statistical findings, the Discussion is where authors interpret data, assert
significance, and connect findings to broader disciplinary conversations. In longitudinal
studies, this section often emphasizes predictive implications, trajectory stability, and
potential intervention strategies. Thus, the macro-structure strategically separates
evidence presentation from interpretation, reinforcing the genre’s commitment to
analytical objectivity before advancing argumentative claims.
Visual elements further contribute to macro-level persuasion. All three articles
incorporate tables and, in some cases, trajectory graphs that visually represent statistical
associations and symptom changes over time. These visual forms of argument enhance
navigability and allow readers to verify relationships between variables independently.
The integration of tables immediately following relevant textual explanation reflects a
design principle common in scientific publishing: evidence is displayed in close
proximity to interpretive commentary to maintain logical coherence.
Ultimately, the macro-organization of these articles reflects a highly standardized
genre that balances accessibility for expert readers with methodological thoroughness.
The IMRaD framework, subdivided Methods sections, visually suppoted Results, and
interpretive Discussions collectively function to align the research with the expectations
of psychology and health sciences communities. The consistency of this organizational
pattern across journals demonstrates how empirical longitudinal research operates within
a codified structure designed to facilitate credibility, reproducibility, and efficient
scholarly communication.
Micro-Organization and Language/Style Features
At the micro level, all three longitudinal studies follow a recognizable move
structure, particularly in their Introduction and Discussion sections. The introduction
sections of all three articles follow a recognizable move structure that progresses from
establishing a research territory to identifying a gap and finally articulating a specific
research purpose. For example, the Psychological Reports article begins by establishing
territory with the statement, “University students are at heightened risk of experiencing
mental health problems” (Farrer et al., 2024, p. 2). This opening positions student mental
health as an already recognized disciplinary concern. The authors then narrow the focus
by identifying a gap in existing research, noting that “very few longitudinal studies” have
assessed mental health symptoms before and during entry to university (Farrer et al.,
2024, p. 3). Finally, the introduction concludes by occupying the niche through a clear
purpose statement: “The current study reports the results of a longitudinal cohort
study…” (Farrer et al., 2024, p. 4). This movement from general concern to research
limitation and then to explicit aim reflects the conventional introduction pattern of
empirical health research, where establishing necessity precedes methodological
justification.. Each introduction begins by establishing the broader issue of rising mental
health concerns among university students. The authors then narrow the focus by
identifying gaps in existing research—such as limited longitudinal data or insufficient
modeling of symptom trajectories—before concluding with a clearly stated research
objective. This move sequence (territory → gap → purpose) guides readers logically
from disciplinary concern to specific empirical contribution.
Because all three studies are longitudinal, their language consistently emphasizes
change over time. Terms such as “baseline,” “trajectory,” “emergence,” “recovery,” and
“odds ratios” frame mental health as a dynamic and measurable process. This repeated
temporal vocabulary reinforces the analytical focus on prediction and progression rather
than static description.
The Methods sections rely heavily on passive voice and technical phrasing (e.g.,
“logistic regression was used,” “participants were recruited”), foregrounding procedures
rather than researchers. This impersonal style aligns with scientific norms that prioritize
objectivity and reproducibility. Frequent nominalizations such as “analysis,”
“measurement,” and “validation” further contribute to a formal and abstract tone.
Hedging is especially prominent in the Discussion sections. Phrases like “may
suggest,” “appears to indicate,” and “is associated with” temper claims and signal
statistical caution. Rather than asserting definitive causation, the authors present findings
as probabilistic and context-dependent. In psychology and health sciences, such restraint
enhances credibility because it reflects awareness of methodological limitations.
Disciplinary terminology is used without definition, assuming an expert readership
familiar with instruments such as the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 and with modeling techniques
like latent growth analysis. This lexical density promotes efficiency within the discourse
community while reinforcing the specialized nature of the genre.
Overall, these micro-level features—standardized move structure, temporal
vocabulary, passive constructions, hedging, and technical diction—demonstrate how
longitudinal mental health research conforms to codified rhetorical norms. Through these
stylistic choices, the articles construct authority and precision while maintaining
alignment with disciplinary expectations.
Conclusion
This genre analysis examined three longitudinal empirical studies on university
student mental health, focusin on their rhetorical situations, persuasive strategies,
macro-organization, and micro-level language features. Although published in different
journals and reflecting slightly varied disciplinary emphases, all three articles adhere to a
highly standardized research article structure rooted in the IMRaD framework. Their
shared reliance on quantitative modeling, methodological transparency, and technical
precision demonstrates how longitudinal mental health research operates within a
codified academic genre.
Across the articles, logos functions as the dominant persuasive appeal, with
statistical analysis serving as the primary means of argumntation. Ethos is constructed
through detailed reporting of methods, validated measurement instruments, and ethical
compliance, while pathos remains limited and strategically restrained. At both macro and
micro levels, the organizational patterns and stylistic features reinforce disciplinary
values of objectivity, reproducibility, and analytical caution. The consistent use of
hedging, passive constructions, and specialized vocabulary reflects an audience trained to
evaluate credibility through methodological rigor rather than emotional appeal.
These findings support the understanding of genre as a socially recognized
response to recurring rhetorical situations. In the context of rising concern about student
mental health, longitudinal empirical research articles function as structured mechanisms
for producing credible, generalizable knowledge. Their effectiveness lies not only in the
data they present but in their alignment with the expectations of psychology and health
sciences discourse communities.
A limitation of this analysis is its focus on three closely related longitudinal
studies within overlapping subfields. Broader cross-disciplinary comparison might reveal
greater variation in genre conventions. Nevertheless, this analysis demonstrates how
recognizing macro- and micro-level rhetorical patterns enhances awareness of how
academic writing functions as both communication and social action within specialized
communities.

longitudinal cohort study. BMJ Open, 11(10), e047393.
https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2020-047393

data.essay_text:
Patterns Found in Six Kinesiology Research Articles
Alex Patrickson, Tiyana Freer, Olivia Beaver-Whyte
WRS 101 SEM X50 - Winter 2026 - EXPLORING WRITING
Dan Harvey
Introduction
Research papers, especially academic ones, typically follow patterns that help writers
communicate their findings in a manner that is clear and organized. This genre analysis compares
six research articles written in the discipline of Kinesiology to identify the patterns in four
different categories; these categories are rhetorical situation, rhetorical strategies, macrostructure,
as well as the microstructures within each of the articles. By analyzing these differences and
similarities, this analysis will highlight the choices different researchers make in order to obtain
credibility. The paper illustrates how different structures and other verbal approaches can both be
used as persuasive and organizational tools within kinesiology.
Rhetorical Situation
Though all six articles have more formal and serious tones, The articles by Merlin et al.,
2024 and Shirahata et al., 2025 are written more towards the coaches and athletes who would
find this information useful. All of these research articles are written by professionals in their
field, and have appropriate jargon. They all have substantial evidence for their studies except for
the article by Merlin et al., 2024, which had an experimental group but no control group in their
trials. All of the articles effectively fulfilled their purposes, that is that their articles were written
well enough that those not within the field could still understand. However, some articles
(Paravlic et al., 2024; Vacher et al., 2023; Merlin et al., 2024) may take non-professionals more
effort to understand due to extensive jargon.
Rhetorical Strategies
Rhetorical strategies are the techniques authors use to influence their audience, and
strengthen their argument. Ethos pertains to the credibility of an author and their work. Pathos
refers to the author's way of appealing to emotion, or keeping a reader engaged in the text. Logos
means logic, it applies to the statistics, data and information that the readers must consider when
reading.
All six articles have high author credibility, the authors are prominent in their fields of
study and provide appropriate statistics and jargon for their fields However only the articles by
Paravlic et al., 2024 and Shirahata et al., 2025 have large sample sizes which calls into question
the research credibility of the other articles. The experiment done by Merlin et al., 2024 did not
include a control group in their trials so the credibility of their statistics may also be
questionable. Despite this, all six articles provide sufficient data and statistics for research in the
form of tables and other figures, meaning a great appeal to logos. They provide background
information as well as explanations for their statistics and other results. A few of these articles
appeal to pathos, however this is achieved mainly through clear language in the background
information This is mainly seen in articles the articles by Shirahata et al., 2025 and Crown et al.,
2016, with the article by Vacher et al., 2023 also having a slight appeal to pathos. The main
rhetorical strategy used between the articles is logos. The articles provide copious information on
the statistics and background for the studies, however, some articles also appeal greatly to ethos
(Paravlic et al., 2024) focusing on extensive background knowledge and past studies as well as
the credibility of the publisher and the application of the study.
Macrostructure
The main macrostructure model is the IMRD model, this stands for Introduction,
Methods, Results, and Discussion. This model uses the 4 terms as headings throughout the paper,
sometimes adding more or less headings depending on whether the heading is needed or can be
tied in with another. The model has evolved over the 19th and the 20th centuries beginning with
a scientist named Louis Pasteur, and around the 1940s becoming the leading format for research
papers (Subject Guides: Writing Guides: Writing Research Articles: The IMRaD Model, 2026).
The research articles being compared here use this method with varying extents, for example the
essay by Vacher et al., 2023 conforms quite well to this model using each heading to keep the
text neat and organized though it is slightly less structured.
In each of the 6 articles the argument is made clear in the conclusion, which means the
reader will have a good idea what the article was written to explain by the time the author(s)
actually tell the reader. One article, Merlin et al., 2024, shows its evidence with very detailed
tables, and the remainder use both tables and figures. These figures vary between photos (Khaki
et al., 2025; Chown et al., 2016), a graph (Khaki et al., 2025) and diagrams (Vacher et al., 2023;
Khaki et al., 2025; Shirahata et al., 2025; Chown et al., 2016) These tables and figures help to
establish credibility and have the readers believe in the research more.
There is little difference again in the articles when talking about the amount of sections
within the texts, the articles each have 5 headings. These headings correlate with the IMRD
organization method, the Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, as well as having a
conclusion. The length of these sections however do vary quite a bit, with only 2 articles (Vacher
et al., 2023; Shirahata et al., 2025) not having the most paragraphs under the methods heading.
The introductions have between 4 and 6 paragraphs and 5 of the 6 conclusions have a single
paragraph with only one outlier (Chown et al., 2016), the other shortest sections are the results
sections with a normal range of 3 to 6 paragraphs. The discussion area is often the second largest
section with 2 of the articles having 13 paragraphs in order to fully investigate the findings
within the study. It stands to reason that in research papers the longest section would be the
method area, being that this is the place that the experiments in the paper are introduced and
explained. These articles are no exception, meaning that of the 6 texts only one has a method
section that is the second largest and not the largest, that being the article by Shirahata et al.,
2025
After the main headings and their, typically, short introduction there are often
sub-headings, these can appear once or multiple times during their respective sections, even not
at all just as it so often does in the introduction and conclusion. Like so often with the amount of
paragraphs, the method section largely has the most amount of sub-headings followed by
discussion. This can vary however because the discussion just as often does not have any
subheadings, this is most common when the section is being used to discuss a single thing like
questions that came about while conducting an experiment. The subheadings are often a way to
explain the following test, in turn they are often clear and descriptive though the few words
chosen can cause confusion.(Vacher et al., 2023) The length of these sections change due to the
authors of the paper and the amount of information that needs to be conveyed, though they tend
to stay in the range of 1 to 5 and often the paragraphs remain only a few sentences long.
Microstructure
John Swales (1990) developed a widely used model for research articles called the Create
a Research Space (CaRS) model. Swales examined the microstructure of articles from hundreds
of disciplines, and concluded that most follow the same three ‘moves’; establishing a territory,
establishing a niche, and occupying a niche.
Typically, the first two or even three paragraphs of a Kinesiology introduction are
dedicated to introducing the general topics, providing background information, citing and
reviewing previous work, and attributing importance or value. Most of the articles describe the
problem and its importance at the end of the first paragraph in a very structured ‘x causes y’
(Paravlic et al., 2024; Khaki et al., 2025; Chown et al., 2016) or ‘w is important for z’ (Merlin et
al., 2024). Others introduce the value earlier on and tie it into new areas for investigation (Vacher
et al., 2023), or an issue with current methods (Shirahata et al., 2025). After the first paragraph,
the papers introduce the background information and general topic, including extensive citations.
Every article—with the exception of the paper by Merlin et al., 2024—includes a statement such
as ‘however, x does not y because z’, stating a lack in the current knowledge on the topic.
The purpose of the next two or three paragraphs is to challenge previous works, identify
gaps in the knowledge, and give insight on the area of the current study. Many of the articles use
moves like ‘despite x knowledge, y has not been explored’ indicating that previous work is not
sufficient, and there is a gap in the knowledge (Paravlic et al., 2024; Khaki et al., 2025; Shirahata
et al., 2025). Others indicate discrepancies in current research, stating evidence is not sufficient
(Chown et al., 2016). While articles by Vacher et al., 2023 and Merlin et al., 2024 extend the
current knowledge using moves like ‘considering w, it is a necessity to explore z’.
The last paragraph, or paragraphs, compose a short section that outlines the purpose of
the article. Common phrases to introduce the purpose include ‘the aim of this study…’ (Paravlic
et al., 2024; Khaki et al., 2025; ), ‘the primary goal…’ (Merlin et al., 2024), ‘the present study
was designed to…’ (Vacher et al., 2023), or ‘the purpose of this study…’ (Shirahata et al., 2025;
Chown et al., 2016). Each article—aside from the article by Khaki et al., 2025—also introduced
their hypotheses, with the article by Chown et al., 2016 going as far as to include the null and
alternative hypotheses. Only the articles by Vacher et al., 2023 and Merlin et al., 2024 include a
brief description of the proposed structure.
Overall, the introductions of six articles showed similarities to Swales’ CaRS model, but
more in depth papers by Vacher et al., 2023 and Merlin et al., 2024 seemed to stray in terms of
the structure and location of these moves, focusing more significantly on the background
knowledge and literature.
Conclusion
The purpose of this genre analysis was to explore the classic research article structure in
the discipline of Kinesiology. By using models learned in this course so far like the CaRS model
and IMRD model, as well as classic rhetorical concepts, we compared and contrasted six articles.
While the articles were similar in areas like rhetorical strategies, classic IMRD structure, and
general context, structures and content differed depending on the depth and importance of the
research presented. Comparing these articles was both straightforward and challenging. Research
articles already have a very defined structure to them, and easy models to compare them too, but
understanding the extent of the content behind them was challenging. Though this work may not
necessarily be considered important to everyone, it helps build important analytical skills that
will continue to be used through our educational careers.
References

criteria.name: Comparative Analysis of Rhetorical Situation
criteria.feedback: Good identification of audience and rhetor. The analysis of jargon and evidence levels across the six sources provides a solid comparative foundation.

criteria.name: Comparative Analysis of Rhetorical Strategies (Ethos, Pathos, Logos)
criteria.feedback: The authors correctly identify and apply the three appeals. The critique of sample sizes as a factor of ethos/logos is a particularly insightful comparative point.

criteria.name: Comparative Analysis of Macro-organization
criteria.feedback: Excellent detail here. The use of paragraph counts to compare the weight given to different IMRD sections across the six articles is highly effective and data-driven.

criteria.name: Comparative Analysis of Micro-organization (Moves/Style)
criteria.feedback: The application of Swales’ CaRS model is the highlight of the paper. The authors provide specific 'move' examples and linguistic markers (e.g., 'the aim of this study') from the primary texts.

criteria.name: Paragraph Organization and Cohesion
criteria.feedback: Paragraphs are generally well-structured, but some transitions between the analysis of different articles feel repetitive. Some sentences are overly long, affecting flow.

criteria.name: Conclusion and Implications

criteria.feedback: The tone is appropriate, but there are several mechanical issues including comma splices, missing commas after introductory phrases, and occasional repetitive phrasing.

criteria.feedback: The paper shows a high level of polish and adherence to the specific models (IMRD, CaRS) taught in the course, suggesting careful revision.

John Swales' CaRS (Create a Research Space) model is essential for understanding how academics justify their work. By identifying 'gaps' in existing knowledge (Move 2), researchers create a logical necessity for their own study (Move 3).

Patterns Found in Six Kinesiology Research Articles
Alex Patrickson, Tiyana Freer, Olivia Beaver-Whyte
WRS 101 SEM X50 - Winter 2026 - EXPLORING WRITING
Dan Harvey
Introduction
Research papers, especially academic ones, typically follow patterns that help writers
communicate their findings in a manner that is clear and organized. This genre analysis compares
six research articles written in the discipline of Kinesiology to identify the patterns in four
different categories; these categories are rhetorical situation, rhetorical strategies, macrostructure,
as well as the microstructures within each of the articles. By analyzing these differences and
similarities, this analysis will highlight the choices different researchers make in order to obtain
credibility. The paper illustrates how different structures and other verbal approaches can both be
used as persuasive and organizational tools within kinesiology.
Rhetorical Situation
Though all six articles have more formal and serious tones, The articles by Merlin et al.,
2024 and Shirahata et al., 2025 are written more towards the coaches and athletes who would
find this information useful. All of these research articles are written by professionals in their
field, and have appropriate jargon. They all have substantial evidence for their studies except for
the article by Merlin et al., 2024, which had an experimental group but no control group in their
trials. All of the articles effectively fulfilled their purposes, that is that their articles were written
well enough that those not within the field could still understand. However, some articles
(Paravlic et al., 2024; Vacher et al., 2023; Merlin et al., 2024) may take non-professionals more
effort to understand due to extensive jargon.
Rhetorical Strategies
Rhetorical strategies are the techniques authors use to influence their audience, and
strengthen their argument. Ethos pertains to the credibility of an author and their work. Pathos
refers to the author's way of appealing to emotion, or keeping a reader engaged in the text. Logos
means logic, it applies to the statistics, data and information that the readers must consider when
reading.
All six articles have high author credibility, the authors are prominent in their fields of
study and provide appropriate statistics and jargon for their fields However only the articles by
Paravlic et al., 2024 and Shirahata et al., 2025 have large sample sizes which calls into question
the research credibility of the other articles. The experiment done by Merlin et al., 2024 did not
include a control group in their trials so the credibility of their statistics may also be
questionable. Despite this, all six articles provide sufficient data and statistics for research in the
form of tables and other figures, meaning a great appeal to logos. They provide background
information as well as explanations for their statistics and other results. A few of these articles
appeal to pathos, however this is achieved mainly through clear language in the background
information This is mainly seen in articles the articles by Shirahata et al., 2025 and Crown et al.,
2016, with the article by Vacher et al., 2023 also having a slight appeal to pathos. The main
rhetorical strategy used between the articles is logos. The articles provide copious information on
the statistics and background for the studies, however, some articles also appeal greatly to ethos
(Paravlic et al., 2024) focusing on extensive background knowledge and past studies as well as
the credibility of the publisher and the application of the study.
Macrostructure
The main macrostructure model is the IMRD model, this stands for Introduction,
Methods, Results, and Discussion. This model uses the 4 terms as headings throughout the paper,
sometimes adding more or less headings depending on whether the heading is needed or can be
tied in with another. The model has evolved over the 19th and the 20th centuries beginning with
a scientist named Louis Pasteur, and around the 1940s becoming the leading format for research
papers (Subject Guides: Writing Guides: Writing Research Articles: The IMRaD Model, 2026).
The research articles being compared here use this method with varying extents, for example the
essay by Vacher et al., 2023 conforms quite well to this model using each heading to keep the
text neat and organized though it is slightly less structured.
In each of the 6 articles the argument is made clear in the conclusion, which means the
reader will have a good idea what the article was written to explain by the time the author(s)
actually tell the reader. One article, Merlin et al., 2024, shows its evidence with very detailed
tables, and the remainder use both tables and figures. These figures vary between photos (Khaki
et al., 2025; Chown et al., 2016), a graph (Khaki et al., 2025) and diagrams (Vacher et al., 2023;
Khaki et al., 2025; Shirahata et al., 2025; Chown et al., 2016) These tables and figures help to
establish credibility and have the readers believe in the research more.
There is little difference again in the articles when talking about the amount of sections
within the texts, the articles each have 5 headings. These headings correlate with the IMRD
organization method, the Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, as well as having a
conclusion. The length of these sections however do vary quite a bit, with only 2 articles (Vacher
et al., 2023; Shirahata et al., 2025) not having the most paragraphs under the methods heading.
The introductions have between 4 and 6 paragraphs and 5 of the 6 conclusions have a single
paragraph with only one outlier (Chown et al., 2016), the other shortest sections are the results
sections with a normal range of 3 to 6 paragraphs. The discussion area is often the second largest
section with 2 of the articles having 13 paragraphs in order to fully investigate the findings
within the study. It stands to reason that in research papers the longest section would be the
method area, being that this is the place that the experiments in the paper are introduced and
explained. These articles are no exception, meaning that of the 6 texts only one has a method
section that is the second largest and not the largest, that being the article by Shirahata et al.,
2025
After the main headings and their, typically, short introduction there are often
sub-headings, these can appear once or multiple times during their respective sections, even not
at all just as it so often does in the introduction and conclusion. Like so often with the amount of
paragraphs, the method section largely has the most amount of sub-headings followed by
discussion. This can vary however because the discussion just as often does not have any
subheadings, this is most common when the section is being used to discuss a single thing like
questions that came about while conducting an experiment. The subheadings are often a way to
explain the following test, in turn they are often clear and descriptive though the few words
chosen can cause confusion.(Vacher et al., 2023) The length of these sections change due to the
authors of the paper and the amount of information that needs to be conveyed, though they tend
to stay in the range of 1 to 5 and often the paragraphs remain only a few sentences long.
Microstructure
John Swales (1990) developed a widely used model for research articles called the Create
a Research Space (CaRS) model. Swales examined the microstructure of articles from hundreds
of disciplines, and concluded that most follow the same three ‘moves’; establishing a territory,
establishing a niche, and occupying a niche.
Typically, the first two or even three paragraphs of a Kinesiology introduction are
dedicated to introducing the general topics, providing background information, citing and
reviewing previous work, and attributing importance or value. Most of the articles describe the
problem and its importance at the end of the first paragraph in a very structured ‘x causes y’
(Paravlic et al., 2024; Khaki et al., 2025; Chown et al., 2016) or ‘w is important for z’ (Merlin et
al., 2024). Others introduce the value earlier on and tie it into new areas for investigation (Vacher
et al., 2023), or an issue with current methods (Shirahata et al., 2025). After the first paragraph,
the papers introduce the background information and general topic, including extensive citations.
Every article—with the exception of the paper by Merlin et al., 2024—includes a statement such
as ‘however, x does not y because z’, stating a lack in the current knowledge on the topic.
The purpose of the next two or three paragraphs is to challenge previous works, identify
gaps in the knowledge, and give insight on the area of the current study. Many of the articles use
moves like ‘despite x knowledge, y has not been explored’ indicating that previous work is not
sufficient, and there is a gap in the knowledge (Paravlic et al., 2024; Khaki et al., 2025; Shirahata
et al., 2025). Others indicate discrepancies in current research, stating evidence is not sufficient
(Chown et al., 2016). While articles by Vacher et al., 2023 and Merlin et al., 2024 extend the
current knowledge using moves like ‘considering w, it is a necessity to explore z’.
The last paragraph, or paragraphs, compose a short section that outlines the purpose of
the article. Common phrases to introduce the purpose include ‘the aim of this study…’ (Paravlic
et al., 2024; Khaki et al., 2025; ), ‘the primary goal…’ (Merlin et al., 2024), ‘the present study
was designed to…’ (Vacher et al., 2023), or ‘the purpose of this study…’ (Shirahata et al., 2025;
Chown et al., 2016). Each article—aside from the article by Khaki et al., 2025—also introduced
their hypotheses, with the article by Chown et al., 2016 going as far as to include the null and
alternative hypotheses. Only the articles by Vacher et al., 2023 and Merlin et al., 2024 include a
brief description of the proposed structure.
Overall, the introductions of six articles showed similarities to Swales’ CaRS model, but
more in depth papers by Vacher et al., 2023 and Merlin et al., 2024 seemed to stray in terms of
the structure and location of these moves, focusing more significantly on the background
knowledge and literature.
Conclusion
The purpose of this genre analysis was to explore the classic research article structure in
the discipline of Kinesiology. By using models learned in this course so far like the CaRS model
and IMRD model, as well as classic rhetorical concepts, we compared and contrasted six articles.
While the articles were similar in areas like rhetorical strategies, classic IMRD structure, and
general context, structures and content differed depending on the depth and importance of the
research presented. Comparing these articles was both straightforward and challenging. Research
articles already have a very defined structure to them, and easy models to compare them too, but
understanding the extent of the content behind them was challenging. Though this work may not
necessarily be considered important to everyone, it helps build important analytical skills that
will continue to be used through our educational careers.
References

Morphology and Kinesiology, 9(1), 23. https://doi.org/10.3390/jfmk9010023
