data.essay_text:
1
A Rhetorical and Genre Analysis of Conceptual Research Summaries in Psychology
Violet Chen, Zhiqi Cai, and Ximing Yu
Department of English and Film Studies, University of Alberta
WRS 101: Exploring Writing
Daniel Harvey
February 8, 2026
2
A Rhetorical and Genre Analysis of Conceptual Research Summaries in Psychology
Academic research writing relies on recognizable genres, which determine how
knowledge is constructed and communicated in the discipline group. The function of these
genres is a repetitive rhetorical response to shared communication situations. Miller (1984)
believes that genres represent a social behavior, and the text uses a predictable structure to serve
the common purpose of a specific audience. In psychology, research summaries play a vital role
in clarifying concepts, forming theories and guiding future research.
The six texts investigated in this report all focus on psychology. The definition of
resilience in psychology is conceptually complex and ambiguous. Because of this conceptual
confusion, the research summary acts as more than just a list of facts; it is a strategic tool that
authors use to draw lines and define the boundaries of the field. The selected articles include
Bonanno (2004), Luthar, Cicchetti and Becker (2000), Masten (2001), Rutter (1987), Southwick
et al. (2014) and Ungar (2011). Although these authors study resilience from developmental,
clinical, ecological and interdisciplinary perspectives, all six articles are of the same genre: the
conceptual psychology research summary.
Different from empirical research articles, conceptual research summarizes the existing
theoretical achievements, evaluates theoretical assumptions, and puts forward an explanatory
framework. The purpose of this report is to analyze the common rhetorical and genre
characteristics of these texts, and to examine how variations reflect different academic aims. The
analysis shows that although the articles show strong similarity in rhetorical situation,
arrangement, argument construction and academic style, there are meaningful differences in their
scope and author status, which illustrates how this genre balances stability with flexibility
3
Rhetorical Situation
The rhetorical situation includes the shaping of text by author, audience, purpose, genre
and context (Bitzer, 1968). In these six articles, these components show a lot of overlap, which
helps to explain the rhetorical patterns they share.
All six texts are published by famous scholars in major research institutions, and in
peer-reviewed psychology journals, such as American Psychologist and Child Development.
This publication choice proves that the authors aren't just writing for anyone; they are writing for
a very specific discourse community. By using dense jargon and heavy citations, they effectively
build disciplinary boundaries that keep non-experts out, allowing them to jump straight into
complex theoretical fights.
The historical background of the articles further influenced their rhetorical goals. Earlier
articles, such as Rutter (1987), reflect the formative research on resilience. At that time, the main
rhetorical strategies focused on the research on the resilience of the protection mechanism. Later
articles respond to the rapid growth of the field by trying to clarify unclear definitions, while
more recent studies focus on combining ideas from different disciplines.
The target audience is mainly composed of members of the psychological research
community, including psychological researchers, graduate students, clinicians and policy
scholars. The use of formal reference practices, limited explanation of foundational concepts,
and frequent specialized terminology clearly indicate the intended target audience. As Swales
(1990) pointed out, discourse communities share conventions and communication goals,
allowing authors to participate in advanced theoretical discussions without re-expounding basic
knowledge.
4
The main purpose of summarizing genres in conceptual research is to provide
information and persuasiveness. In six texts, the authors try to clarify concepts, criticize the
shortcomings of previous studies, and guide future studies, which determines the rhetoric and
structural choice of genres.
Rhetorical Strategies: Ethos, Pathos, and Logos
Across the six articles, ethos, pathos, and logos function in distinct but complementary
ways.
Ethos is mainly established through academic authority. Through intensive reference to
practice, contact with basic theories, publication in famous journals and recognition of the
limitations of methods, credibility has been improved. Rutter’s early work established theoretical
authority, and later authors put their arguments within established scholarly conversations.
Pathos plays a limited and controlled role, and emotional appeal appears in the form of
professional concern rather than personal emotion. The mention of trauma or social
consequences highlights the relevance of resilience research, but still maintains academic
objectivity, which is consistent with the expectation of discipline neutrality.
Logos is the main rhetorical appeal. The author uses concept differentiation and synthesis
of previous findings rather than providing new empirical data. Bonanno (2004) uses the result
trajectory as a rhetorical organization method to distinguish resilience from recovery. Masten
(2001) organized the literature into an adaptive system and used macro-organization to explain
the complexity. Luthar et al. (2000) relied on systematic criticism and response to solve the
definition differences, and Ungar (2011) adopted the principle of taxonomic ecology to guide the
5
interpretation. Southwick et al. (2014) adopted the question-and-response form to facilitate
interdisciplinary comparison.
Together, these strategies show how conceptual research summaries rely on rhetorical
organization and logical sequencing, rather than empirical data, to produce convincing scholarly
arguments for academic audiences.
Macro-organization of the research articles
We can very directly understand the writing style of psychology by focusing on the
macro-organization of writing. While this report examines six foundational texts, the following
analysis focuses on the distinct macro-organizational patterns of three primary articles to
illustrate different communicative purposes. Bonanno (2004) deviates from standard conventions
by using a point-based structure instead of the traditional IMRD format. Instead of following the
usual academic script, he uses sub-points to systematically disassemble old myths about grief,
making his argument function as a critique on old theories. There are a lot of small sub-points
besides the three obvious sub-points in Bonanno (2004). The author used a large amount of text
to raise an argument and refute this argument, so the purpose of Bonanno (2004) is more likely
to correct some academic mistakes by specific cases. That is why there are a lot of small
sub-points in Bonanno (2004), because sub-points can be effective in refining and elaborating the
main claim (Toulmin, 1958). We can find a similar structure in Masten (2001), which has an
obvious introduction and conclusion and uses very clear sub-points to organize the body of the
article. These sub-points replace the part of the methods and results in the normal IMRD
structure. They also allow people to understand the argument in a step-by-step way because they
can effectively explain a specific aspect of resilience. In this way, readers can not only follow the
author's pace to gradually understand the complicated concept, but people also don't have to try
6
to understand massive amounts of information at once. Masten (2001) relied on a large number
of models and categories to define and differentiate resilience. In the normal IMRD structure,
the methods mean how data is produced, and the results mean what data shows. However, in
Masten (2001), models mean how resilience works, and the categories help people to distinguish
different situations. Therefore, the clear sub-points can help people to quickly locate the concept
and compare different models.
Furthermore, we can find the pattern of the article in the psychology discipline that it is
more important for psychology research to provide a clear definition of a concept; otherwise,
research can't be explained and compared (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955). Luthar et al. (2000) sticks
to a more traditional, problem-response-guideline structure. While it’s complex, it feels like a
safe bet for the field—systematic but maybe a bit predictable compared to the more aggressive
moves we see in Bonanno’s work. By organizing the body around the existing shortages in
research, the author raises guidelines that feel systematic but perhaps a bit predictable. In the
body of this article, each section is organized around analyzing the shortage of the existing
research. Then, the author raised guidelines for future research, which form a whole
problem-response-guideline-based structure. Such a structure is not only effective for the reader
to quickly find specific arguments by each different section, but the reader can also understand
the critical logic and accept guidelines raised by the author.
Micro-organization and language/style features of the research articles
Moving from macro-structure to micro-organization, the use of rhetorical moves—as
defined by Swales (1990)—further distinguishes how each author achieves their specific
communicative purpose. The rhetorical purpose of Bonanno (2004) is to redefine resilience and
refute those traditional, popular assumptions. Then, the pattern in the move structure used by the
7
author is that they first raise an argument, identify the problem of this argument, introduce a
large number of research studies, and finally explain how those research studies work. The
diction here serves a specific rhetorical function. The heavy use of restrictive words and
references is a calculated move to build academic gatekeeping, ensuring that the argument is
only taken seriously by other insiders in the discourse community. For instance, a large number
of restrictive words and references are used by the author to increase accuracy and credibility.
Finally, the micro-organization of Bonanno (2004) is effective because the author firstly
challenges dominant assumptions with enough reliable evidence and redefines the assumption in
order to make the reader believe that resilience is common.
However, the rhetorical purpose of Masten (2001) is to systematically build a framework
of resilience. Masten (2001) uses a teaching-oriented strategy. She isn't just giving facts; she’s
using the 'Ordinary Magic' metaphor as a rhetorical move to make a difficult concept feel like
common sense. It’s a smart way to claim authority without sounding too aggressive and lastly
indicates the meaning of models in developing psychology. Furthermore, the teaching-oriented
diction and clear move structure in Masten (2001) effectively achieve the communicative
purpose, which is to help the reader understand complicated concepts.
Interestingly, Luthar et al. (2000) focus on criticizing existing research on resilience and
proposing research guidelines and suggestions. Luthar et al. (2000) applied a special pattern in
the move structure, in which they first indicate the problem or confusion in existing research,
explain why there is a problem, analyze what the outcome of this problem is, and propose
guidelines or suggestions. The author uses critical diction and style to write this article; that is
why the reader can be effective in identifying where the problems are and how to correct them.
8
Although there are very obvious differences between all three articles, each author applies a
special pattern in the move structure to achieve their own special communication purpose.
Although all three articles research resilience, they apply distinct argument organization,
which means different communicational goals. Bonanno (2004) focused on changing the
dominant argument of resilience, Masten (2001) paid attention to clarifying the concept of
resilience, and Luthar et al. (2000) used a large number of texts to critique the problem of
existing research on resilience. The distinct main claims trigger different evidence selection. For
example, Bonanno (2004) applied abundant empirical studies to emphasize the trend and
quantity; in contrast, Masten (2001) used a lot of models and illustrative evidence to clarify the
concept. Across all articles, the evidence is highly aligned with the authors' main claim. In other
words, it is clear that none of this is random. Every piece of evidence is a strategic move
designed to make the author's theory the new standard. As a result, the evidence selection is
highly effective because it directly supports the main claim rather than being an unintentional
citation (Toulmin, 1958). As a result, the argument organization of these articles is highly
effective because it helps to increase the authority of the authors, understand complicated
concepts, and provide guidelines.
Conclusion
It is quite clear that these articles are more than just "papers." They function as a
"strategic social response" to all the confusion in the resilience field (Miller, 1984). Instead of
just listing data, these authors use the literature review as a flexible tool to systematically
disassemble the core assumptions of old models. While they say the goal is defining resilience,
they are actually using rhetorical moves to fill specific gaps. This flexibility isn't just about
9
science; it's a way to protect the "professional boundaries" of the psychology discipline. They
employ this strategy. By using Swales’ (1990) idea of discourse communities, we can see these
texts are for "insiders" only. The heavy use of jargon and intertextuality shows they only care
about expert audience. This is clearly a strategy. By assuming everyone already knows the
basics, they can bypass foundational concepts and jump into the hard theories. It makes the text
less accessible for general audiences, but it definitely builds their own authority.
This is where the difference between authors becomes very obvious. Bonanno (2004) is
really the one who stands out here. He doesn't just show new data; he systematically
disassembles the core assumptions of the old "grief work" idea, making the previous models look
completely outdated. This represents a significant theoretical departure. Then we have Masten
(2001), whose use of the "Ordinary Magic" metaphor is a significant rhetorical achievement. By
calling it "magic," she changes resilience from something rare to a normal part of growing up.
This metaphorical move effectively bridges the gap between complex psychological processes
and normative human development. In contrast, Luthar et al. (2000) adhere to a more
conventional structure. Their work just follows the basic problem-solution structure we always
see. While it is clear and does the job, it lacks the persuasive impact that Bonanno and Masten
have. Luthar just reports what everyone agrees on, while the other two are busy reshaping the
whole field.
It is acknowledged that this report has some limitations. This report focuses mainly on
introductions, so we may have overlooked rhetorical nuances in the methods sections. However,
the main point is still there: a good research summary does more than just "summarizing." It
pushes the theory forward. Additionally, the lesson is that "academic authority" isn't just about
10
having big numbers or data. Ultimately, academic authority is constructed through strategic
rhetorical moves that guard disciplinary knowledge and dictate the direction of future research.
11
References

Bonanno, G. A. (2004). Loss, trauma, and human resilience: Have we underestimated the human
capacity to thrive after extremely aversive events? American Psychologist, 59(1), 20–28.
https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.59.1.20
Devitt, A. J. (1993). Generalizing about genre: New conceptions of an old concept. College
Composition and Communication. https://doi.org/10.2307/358391

evaluation and guidelines for future work. Child Development, 71(3), 543–562.
https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-8624.00164
Masten, A. S. (2001). Ordinary magic: Resilience processes in development. American
Psychologist, 56(3), 227–238. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.3.227

criteria.name: Introduction states topic and purpose; includes a clear argumentative thesis or a research question; briefly outlines report content
criteria.feedback: The introduction clearly identifies the topic (psychology research articles) and the purpose of the analysis. The thesis is present, though it leans more toward a functional benefit ('personal success in writing will improve') rather than a complex rhetorical argument.

criteria.name: Comparative analysis of the rhetorical situation (rhetor, audience, genre, purpose, context), backed up with compelling evidence from the primary sources
criteria.feedback: The analysis of audience and discourse communities is strong. The authors correctly identify the 'expert' nature of the audience and use specific examples like 'PIU' to illustrate how vocabulary defines the rhetorical situation.

criteria.name: Comparative analysis and discussion of rhetorical strategies (ethos, pathos, logos) employed, backed up with compelling evidence from the primary sources
criteria.feedback: Good coverage of the rhetorical triad. The discussion of how pathos manifests as 'understandability' rather than just emotion in a scientific context is a sophisticated observation.

criteria.name: Comparative analysis of macro-organization; assesses how this contributes to the rhetorical purpose, backed up with compelling evidence from the primary sources
criteria.feedback: Excellent breakdown of the IMRD model and its variations. The observation regarding the placement of arguments (abstract vs. discussion) to manage reader bias is insightful.

criteria.name: Comparative analysis of the micro-organization (rhetorical move structure), as well as patterns of word choice, syntax, style, and their functions
criteria.feedback: The application of Swales’ 3-move model is a highlight of the paper. The authors provide specific sentence stems as evidence of these moves across different texts.

criteria.name: Paragraphs are well-organized; topic sentences state the main idea of each paragraph; sentence-to-sentence and paragraph-to-paragraph movement is cohesive; appropriate transitions are used; writing is concise.
criteria.feedback: The paper is logically structured. Transitions between sections are clear, though some internal paragraph transitions could be more varied to avoid repetitive phrasing.

criteria.name: Conclusion wraps up the results of the rhetorical genre analysis; articulates a clear argumentative thesis statement regarding the persuasiveness of the argument made in the genre texts; proposes implications/significance of the findings
criteria.feedback: The conclusion is functional but somewhat brief. It restates the findings well but could further emphasize the 'persuasiveness' aspect required by the rubric.

criteria.name: Correct citational practices are used throughout
criteria.feedback: APA citations are handled correctly both in-text and in the reference list. Minor formatting issues in the reference list (hanging indents) are the only slight detraction.

criteria.name: The report uses proper academic tone and style, polished English and is free of grammar, spelling, and punctuation mistakes.
criteria.feedback: The tone is appropriately academic. There are a few minor grammatical slips (comma splices and subject-verb agreement) that do not significantly impede meaning.

criteria.name: Revised based on formative feedback
criteria.feedback: The paper shows a high level of polish and structural integrity, suggesting significant attention to the drafting process.

suggestions: Strengthen the thesis statement by making a more specific claim about *why* the IMRD structure is the most persuasive choice for the psychology discourse community.
Review the 'Rhetorical Strategies' section for comma splices, particularly where 'this' is used to start a new independent clause.
Ensure consistency in authorial voice; the paper shifts between 'we' and 'my group' in the conclusion.
Expand the discussion of 'Pathos' to include how the visual rhetoric of tables and figures might also influence the reader's emotional trust in the data.

highlighted_passages.text: The same skills used in these papers can also be translated to personal writing through intentional usage of structure (macro and micro), appeals, and awareness of rhetorical situations.
highlighted_passages.suggestion: This effectively answers the 'so what?' question.

Mini Lessons: Swales' CARS Model: The paper effectively uses John Swales' 'Create a Research Space' (CARS) model. This is a standard framework in applied linguistics for understanding how academic introductions function by establishing a territory, identifying a gap (niche), and then filling that gap.

The Rhetoric of the IMRD: The authors correctly identify that the IMRD (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion) structure is not just a template, but a rhetorical strategy. By placing the argument in the abstract or the discussion, writers control the flow of information to manage reader expectations and potential bias.

Pathos in Science: While often thought of as 'emotional,' pathos in academic writing frequently relates to the 'accessibility' and 'relevance' of the text to the reader. If a text is too jargon-heavy for its audience, it fails rhetorically because it creates a negative 'pathos' response (frustration), regardless of the logic (logos) of the data.

1
Derek, Raph, and Lucas
WRS 101
Winter 2026 - 02/08/2026
Daniel Harvey
Learning From the Experts: Improving Personal Academic Writing Through the Analysis
of Professionals in the Field of Psychology
Introduction
Many new students going into university are faced with many challenges they have not
encountered before, one of which is the introduction of scholarly articles. When university
students are being introduced to the world of academic writing, it can be confusing and difficult
to understand specifically how to compose a proper academic article. In papers across different
academic fields, there is a great variety in the structure, purpose, and context that has been
curated for a target audience. This paper attempts to facilitate the writing process of formal
scholarly papers by demonstrating consistencies and deviations within the academic field of
psychology and its research articles. This analysis is necessary to shape the work of upcoming
scholars and pave the road of success for their future writings. In our research, we have analyzed
six peer-reviewed articles all in the psychology genre with a focus on mental health. Through our
analysis of these academic articles, we have concluded that psychology papers have strict
standards that are generally used, in learning from the structure of academic writing, personal
success in writing will improve.
2
Rhetorical Situation
In order to effectively convey the findings of their research, writers of academic articles
must first reach their target audience. An article is able to find its target audience through the
application of vocabulary and terms that is most often only relevant and meaningful to those
people. Our analysis indicates that psychology-focused papers are mainly trying to reach an
audience of other experts or researchers in their field. Furthermore, they are able to both appeal
to and designate their target audience through the use of knowledge that only their target
audience is likely to know. For papers relating to psychology and mental health, the knowledge
expected of the audience includes an understanding of mental health terms such as “problematic
internet use” (PIU) (Oka et al., 2021), its effects, a specific vocabulary, and a general idea of the
current basis of knowledge or context upon which modern research is conducted. Other
researchers would likely read these research articles to further their own knowledge on topics
presented. It is essential that these articles reach their intended audience because only the
audience is able to further the research presented in the article and / or use the knowledge gained
to make change in the current field (which in the case for our examined articles, may include
using video games in order to alleviate symptoms of mental illness). Overall, composing a
research article requires the careful consideration of the audience and their preexisting
knowledge.
Not only is an article targeting a specific audience, but it is also interacting as a part of a
discourse community. The articles we analyzed are most largely related to discourse
communities such as mental health advocates, psychology researchers, or even clinicians or
psychologists. Discourse communities like these would share a common goal of expanding
current knowledge on mental health and searching for possible treatments for mental illness. This
3
aligns with the purpose of every research article we reviewed, which was to fill a gap in
knowledge or research and impart the findings to the reader. Having a discourse community is
crucial to build an ever-growing foundation of knowledge that future researchers can build upon.
This foundation and community of experts allows for knowledge to advance more rapidly, as it
allows for others to further research without having to build background information and data; it
is already built up from years of research. The discourse community one is writing in also
influences the resulting quality of the work; the feedback and rebuttal that can come from
discourse communities ensures that writers will use proper evidence and provide reasonable
claims based on reliable data. In order to effectively write a psychology article and contribute to
the basis of knowledge, it is important to meet the standards of the discourse community.
Rhetorical Strategies
Once the target audience and discourse community has been determined, it is still
necessary to persuade them on the importance of the writer’s own article. Writers often employ
rhetorical strategies to do so. Ethos, the appeal to ethics and credibility, was very influential in
making an article persuasive during our analysis. One of the most important ways that articles
achieve ethos is through the in-depth vocabulary used. Specific word choice and correct
terminology demonstrates expertise in the subject matter, making the article both credible and
informative. This extensive vocabulary does, however, make the article hard to follow for
non-experts (this will be expanded on in the pathos section). Another crucial part of ethos is the
authors themselves. Throughout all of the articles we analyzed, all of the authors were experts in
their field, demonstrated by either having multiple articles published, or having necessary
credentials. Lastly, the presentation of data is also indicative of the article’s credibility. In some
4
of our articles, data was presented in a table made to easily digest the information given (Stevens
et al., 2020; Teng et al., 2021; Oka et al., 2021). Even if the content and ideas of an article are
impactful, without ethos, the readers will not believe or trust the information.
The next important method of persuasion is logos, the appeal to logic. The articles we
analyzed all made logical conclusions and had a clear thought process, which is primarily seen in
the methods sections of the articles. The ways in which the researchers conducted their research
followed a clear logic, this simple logic makes parts of the article easy to follow (relating to
pathos as well) and it makes the information of the articles easier to accept and digest. It is
important for an article to have strong logos in order to have it align with current knowledge and
have the findings be believable. Logos is essential to have opinions and points rooted in fact
when trying to persuade a reader. Articles also achieved logical validity through the consistency
of their beliefs, arguments, and data. This consistency is demonstrated as having no
contradictions in their arguments and not changing interpretations of data depending on what
suits an argument most. Consistency is important to maintain both the strength of the arguments
presented in the article as well as the believability of the claims. Logos is essential to
communicate ideas in a way that is understandable and appealing to the reader’s beliefs.
The final persuasive technique is pathos. In many academic articles, an appeal to pathos
often takes the shape of how captivating or understandable the article is, and not directly an
appeal to emotion. While this is also mostly true for psychology articles, the subject of some
articles can result in persuasion through genuine emotion. Many of our articles touched on topics
like mental health, which can evoke a sense of sympathy. We found that this sympathy can result
in a desire to read further in order to understand solutions to mental health problems. Another
positive force of pathos was when other persuasive methods such as logos were at play. When
5
arguments followed a clear logic, it was much easier to follow along, this made the article more
understandable and encouraged further reading. Opposite to this, when an article contained
high-end vocabulary that could be attributed to ethos, the article became much harder to
comprehend and it was discouraging to read further. However, the difficulty we experienced in
understanding some articles is also simply because we are a secondary audience to them. The
authors do not need to concern themselves with breaking down complicated words because they
are standard to their audience. Generally, pathos is important in realizing the purpose of the
article by making the information they are trying to convey easy to understand.
Macro-Organization
In order to successfully write an article that is accepted by your discourse community, it
is important to align with the expected formatting. Based on the articles we have revised the
general organization of the article often follows the IMRD model. Most articles began with an
introduction, one of our articles had a “background” section instead of an introduction, but the
function of the section was very similar. The introduction is an essential part of an article, it is
used to give context on the current state of research, provide the article’s purpose (which was
consistently a research gap they are attempting to fill), and some articles introduced their
methods of research. All of our articles also contained the method section, which described how
the data was collected. The methods section, as mentioned earlier, was appealing to logic,
making it much better at conveying information. Articles most often did not expand on the
implications of research findings until the discussion section (Teng et al., 2021). The discussion
section involved exploring the implications of their research but also a larger part was providing
ideas on where to take future research. Organizing an article in the IMRD structure is important
6
to easily access information so the reader does not have to go through the entire article to assess
its relevance / importance to their own research.
Most of our articles contained multiple subsections designed to further organize the
article’s information. The amount of subsections per major section varied heavily per article, but
the one thing that stayed relatively consistent was the methods section including the most
subsections. This organizational method makes sense, since there are many factors one must
consider when conducting research and it is therefore necessary to outline the entire procedure to
ensure it has as few flaws as possible. The methods section often included subsections for how
they gathered subjects, how they measured their dependent variables, and the procedure for
conducting their research. Another section with many subsections was the discussion section,
where authors would have specific subsections to direct further research, discuss the implications
of their findings, and outline any limitations or potential flaws in their study. Having many
subsections to describe the study’s findings is important to be able to do an in-depth analysis of
the research findings, as it is the part that is most essential to fulfilling the purpose of the article
by filling the research gap. For the articles that conducted research via interviews, there were
subsections for “bins” that the responses fell into, such as positive or negative responses (Colder
et al. 2018). Subsections are a very useful tool for organizing information to make your article
accessible to a reader.
All articles contain an argument, and the placement of that argument is important. The
arguments in our papers are placed in two different regions with different reasons. Some are at
the end of the article in the discussion (Colder et al., 2018) or conclusion (Stevens et al., 2020),
while others present their findings in the abstract (Teng et al., 2021; Oka et al., 2021). Arguments
placed in the abstract state a position and use the rest of the article to explain how it came about,
7
while other papers that place their argument after the results in an attempt to reduce early bias for
readers of the article by not revealing the results and implications until after all the methodology
and data is shown. Another trend noticed for the arguments was that they were very simple and
very agreeable. The arguments outlined their findings and gave a small suggestion on how their
discourse community should use the findings. One article simply argues that college campuses
should “consider how to integrate this information” in an attempt to “support undergraduate
student success” (Stevens et al., 2020, p.1134). Arguments are an essential part of an academic
article that directs further action by the reader and attempts to make change.
Despite all articles containing IMRD structures, there were also a lot of extra sections not
part of the IMRD model. One article contained a “highlights” section, which seemed to be a
shorter abstract (this article still included a full-length abstract) as well (Colder et al., 2018). This
highlights section most likely serves as a compressed abstract that allows a reader to swiftly
identify how relevant the article is to their own research. It is also possible that the highlights
section is used to provide keywords that can direct a reader to further research in similar topics.
As mentioned earlier there was an article that contained a “background” section that still had
incredibly similar content and structure to an introduction section. Generally, the articles we
studied had very little deviation from the IMRD model save for the minor deviations mentioned
above.
Micro-Organization
Along with a general guideline based around the larger structure of an article, there are
also specific moves that seem to form the basis of many sections in a paper. Firstly in the
introduction, a necessary move was to present the topic. This move had very similar formatting
8
across the articles, being generally: “the present study examines… to assess…” (Stevens et al.,
2020, p.1128). Other important moves important to the introduction included: presenting a gap in
modern research and presenting how their research will fill that gap (Stevens et al., 2020; Colder
et al., 2018; Teng et al., 2021; Oka et al., 2021). All of these moves are important to achieve the
purpose of the introduction and also align with Swales’ 3-move model: establishing a territory,
establishing a niche, and occupying the niche.
The method section of the article also contained many essential moves. In the method
section of the articles, they would mainly restate the research gap and how they will fill the
research gap. Other moves in the methods section expanded on the specific ways that research
will be conducted, such as: “the present study focused on investigating… . Based on the
assumptions of …, the present longitudinal study examines the role of…” (Teng et al., p. 171).
These moves are essential to effectively communicate with other members of the discourse
community, they allow for the experiment to not only be reproduced, but scrutinized for potential
confounding factors that could contribute to unrealistic data. These standards are necessary
components of the communicative process of a discourse community and ensure good quality
and maintain honesty.
Overall, the results section of the different articles did not have many consistencies
between them. Since each article conducted different research with different methods, there was
a large variance in the results sections. Broadly speaking, all articles present their data in similar
ways, some articles presented data in data tables (Teng et al., 2021), whereas others simply
discussed the results of their research verbally and provided the collected data as a part of the
citations / resources section at the end of the article. The presentation of data was consistently
done in a digestible format and allowed for a more efficient communicative process.
9
Finally, the discussion section provided multiple important moves. The main purpose of
the discussion section is to expand on the implications of the research findings, and direct future
research. This purpose is achieved through common moves like “Another area of potential is…
.” (Colder et al., 2018, p. 129), of which was used in multiple articles with slight variations.
Other moves included stating limitations of the study: “There are several limitations to this study.
First, … .” (Oka et al., 2021, p. 224) and exploring potential biases and uncertainties and thus the
implications of the data obtained. These moves seem to be standard, if not essential, to
discussion sections across psychology articles. This section is also where the argument is most
likely to be found. Overall, the discussion section is critical and efficient in elaborating upon the
research and communicating its results.
Conclusion
In this paper my group has analyzed the general structure and methods used in academic
writing in the field of psychology. In our analysis, we have concluded that there is a standard for
how information is presented and conveyed through the use of subsections, persuasion methods,
and rhetorical moves. All of these techniques illustrated throughout this paper demonstrates the
importance of following the standards set by experts in the field and the strength it can bring to
both your argument and structure when presenting your findings in psychology. The same skills
used in these papers can also be translated to personal writing through intentional usage of
structure (macro and micro), appeals, and awareness of rhetorical situations.
10

Mini Lessons: The CARS Model: This paper effectively uses John Swales' 'Creating a Research Space' (CARS) model to analyze introductions. Understanding the three moves—Establishing a Territory, Establishing a Niche (the gap), and Occupying the Niche—is essential for both analyzing and writing academic introductions.

The Rhetoric of Objectivity: While science is often viewed as 'just facts,' this analysis shows that objectivity is a rhetorical choice. Using the passive voice and avoiding first-person pronouns are strategies used to shift focus from the researcher to the data, thereby increasing the perceived validity of the findings.

Hedging as a Scientific Value: In academic writing, 'hedging' (using words like 'suggests' or 'might') is not a sign of weakness. Instead, it is a rhetorical necessity that demonstrates the author's understanding of the limits of their data and the iterative nature of scientific discovery.

Patterns in Mental Health Research: A Genre Analysis of Five Empirical Articles
Zachariah Isaac
WRS 101- Winter 2026 - Exploring Writing
Prof. Dan Harvey
Introduction
Mental health among university students has become a pressing concern in higher
education, with research showing that first-year students experience significant psychological
challenges dung the transition to university. This report analyzes five empirical research articles
from the field of psychology that examine mental health outcomes among first-year university
students: Wyatt et al (2017), King et al. (2020), Adams et al. (2021), King et al (2023), and Duffy
et al. (2020). All five articles belong to the genre of empirical research and were published in peer-
reviewed journals within health sciences and psychology.
The purpose of this analysis is to examine how these articles function as examples of the
research article genre, comparing their rhetorical situations, rhetorical strategies, and
organizational structures. This analysis argues that while the five articles share fundamental genre
conventions typical of empirical research in health sciences, including the IMRD structure,
objective tone, and reliance on quantitative evidence, they also demonstrate meaningful variations
that reflect both disciplinary conventions and journal-specific requirements. These shared
conventions make the articles highly persuasive to their intended audience of researchers and
clinicians because they align with the expectations of the health sciences community.
This report is organized into four main sections: rhetorical situation, rhetorical strategies
(ethos, pathos, and logos), macro-organization, and micro-organization and language features.
Finally, I conclude with an assessment of how these genre conventions contribute to the
persuasiveness of the articles.
Rhetorical Situation
All five articles share similar rhetorical situations, which shapes their form and content.
The authors are academic researchers affiliated with universities and research institutions,
establishing them as credible members of the academic discourse community. Wyatt et al. (2017)
are affiliated with American higher education institutions, while King et al. (2020, 2023), Adams
et al. (2021), and Duffy et al. (2020) include researchers from Canadian and British universities.
As Dirk (2010) explains, genres develop because they respond appropriately to situations that
writers encounter repeatedly within their communities, and these authors clearly write as insiders
within health sciences research. For example, Adams et al. (2021) explicitly identify their
institutional affiliations as Psychology and Psychiatry departments, University of Oxford and
Queens University, signaling their expertise in the field.
The intended audience for all five articles is other researchers, clinicians, and policymakers
interested in student mental health. This audience belongs to the health sciences and psychology
communities and possesses specialized knowledge about mental health assessment and statistical
methods. Evidence of this specialized audience appears in the articles' use of technical terminology
without extensive explanation. For instance, King et al. (2020) refer to "log-binomial regression"
(p. 600) without defining the term, and Adams et al. (2021) mention "Cronbach's alpha" (p. 4)
assuming reader familiarity. This technical language signals that the articles are written for expert
readers who share disciplinary knowledge. This audience wants to know which risk factors predict
poor mental health outcomes and which interventions are most effective, because such evidence
directly informs clinical practice and campus policy decisions.
The primary purpose of these articles is to inform by presenting new empirical findings
about student mental health. However, as Duffy (2022) argues, rhetoric is fundamentally about
persuasion, and academic writing is no exception because researchers must convince readers that
their methods are sound and their conclusions valid. This persuasive dimension is evident in how
the articles frame their contributions. For example, Duffy et al. (2020) state that “there are little
reliable data to inform the extent of mental health need in the transition to and over the course of
university study” (p.1) thereby explicitly positioning their work as a valuable contribution. The
context for all five articles is peer-reviewed academic publishing, which imposes specific genre
conventions and quality standards. The research article genre, as Dirk (2010) explains, functions
as a social action that enables effective communication within academic communities.
Rhetorical Strategies: Ethos, Pathos, and Logos
The five articles rely heavily on logos, appealing to logic and evidence as their primary
rhetorical strategy, which is consistent with the conventions of scientific writing that prioritize
objectivity and empirical evidence. All five articles present quantitative data, statistical analyses,
and logical arguments based on their findings. Wyatt et al. (2017) use "adjusted odds ratios" with
"99.5% confidence intervals" (p. 180) to demonstrate relationships between mental health and
academic performance. The extensive use of tables and figures in all articles further supports logos
by presenting data in accessible visual formats that allow readers to evaluate the evidence directly.
Ethos is established through several mechanisms across the articles. First, author
credentials and institutional affiliations signal expertise. Second, the use of validated measurement
instruments demonstrates methodological rigor. King et al. (2020) describe using the seven-item
Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-7) and the nine-item Patient Health Questionnaire
(PHQ-9) (p. 598), both of which are established clinical tools. Third, extensive citation of previous
research shows that the authors are knowledgeable about their field. King et al. (2020) cite over
40 sources, establishing their work within a broader scholarly conversation. Additionally, the BMJ
Open articles include detailed ethics statements such as "ethical approval was granted by the
Queen's University Health Sciences and Affiliated Teaching Hospitals Research Ethics Board”
(Adams et al., 2021, p. 9), which enhance credibility by demonstrating adherence to research ethics
standards.
Pathos plays a limited but strategic role in these articles. While scientific writing typically
avoids overt emotional appeals, the introductions establish the importance of the research by
highlighting consequences of poor student mental health. King et al. (2023) note that mental health
difficulties are associated with "lower academic performance and greater attrition" (p. 1123).
Wyatt et al. (2017) open by stating that "students enter institutions of higher education with a
variety of physical and mental health concerns" (p. 178), creating concern about student wellbeing.
This framing creates urgency without compromising the objective tone expected in scientific
writing. The limited use of pathos is appropriate for this genre because excessive emotional appeals
could undermine the perceived objectivity of the research and thus reduce its persuasiveness for
the target audience. As Dirk (2010) argues, knowing what is appropriate in a given rhetorical
situation requires an understanding of how the genre’s conventions shape what the audience will
find credible.
Macro-Organization of the Research Articles
All five articles follow the IMRD (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion) structure
that is standard for empirical research in the sciences and social sciences. However, each article
modifies this basic structure in ways that reflect journal requirements and disciplinary conventions.
Wyatt et al. (2017) organize their paper into five main sections: Introduction, Subjects and
Methods, Results, Discussion and Recommendations, and Limitations and Future Research. This
structure merges Discussion with Recommendations and separates Limitations into its own
section. King et al. (2020) use a more traditional structure with Introduction, Methods, Results,
Discussion, and a separate Conclusion section.
The Adams et al. (2021) article published in BMJ Open and Duffy et al. (2020) published
in BJPsych Open (British Journal of Psychiatry Open) include additional sections required by the
journal, such as "Patient and Public Involvement" statements, "Ethics" declarations, "Author
Contributions," and "Data Availability" statements. These sections reflect the journal's emphasis
on research transparency and ethics. Duffy et al. (2020) notably splits the traditional Introduction
into separate "Background" and "Aims" sections, which allows for clear separation between the
literature review and the specific research objectives. This macro-level organization serves the
rhetorical purpose of enabling readers to quickly locate specific types of information, which is
essential given that genre conventions help readers navigate texts efficiently by establishing
predictable structures (Dirk, 2010).
The Methods sections are consistently the most subdivided across all articles, with common
subsections including participants/sample description, measures/instruments, and statistical
analysis procedures. This detailed subdivision serves the crucial rhetorical purpose of establishing
reproducibility—a core value in scientific research. For example, King et al. (2020) include
subsections for "Overview," "Key Variables," and "Statistical Analysis" (pp. 598-600), allowing
readers to evaluate each aspect of the methodology separately. The Results sections tend to be the
longest, particularly in articles with complex analyses, reflecting the genre's emphasis on
presenting evidence. Regarding headings, Wyatt et al. (2017) use numeric headings (1., 2., 2.1),
while the other four articles use bold descriptive text headings. Despite this stylistic difference, all
heading systems serve the same organizational purpose of enhancing navigability. In terms of
where the argument is located, the authors present their central claims primarily in the Discussion
sections, where they interpret findings and argue for their significance. For example, Adams et al.
(2021) argue that certain mental health trajectories predict university dropout, while King et al.
(2023) claim that international students face distinct challenges. The Introduction sections also
contain argumentative elements through gap statements that justify each study, but the Discussion
is where the authors most explicitly advocate for their work’s implications. Additionally, all five
articles employ visual forms of argument through tables and figures. Wyatt et al. (2017) include
tables displaying odds ratios that demonstrate the strength of associations between variables, while
Adams et al. (2021) use trajectory graphs to illustrate distinct patterns of mental health change
over time. These visual elements function as persuasive tools because they allow readers to
independently verify the authors’ claims and grasp complex statistical relationships at a glance.
Micro-Organization and Language/Style Features
The introductions of all five articles follow a similar move structure that reflects what Dirk
(2010) describes as the rhetorical conventions that develop when writers repeatedly encounter
similar situations. Each introduction begins by establishing the research territory, identifying
mental health among university students as an important topic. Wyatt et al. (2017) open by stating
that "mental health issues in college students have consistently increased over time" (p. 178). King
et al. (2020) similarly begin by noting “high prevalence of mental health problems in
postsecondary students” (p. 2). These opening statements function to establish the significance of
the research area and capture reader interest.
Following the territory establishment, all articles execute Move 2: establishing a niche by
identifying a gap in existing research. Common gap-indicating phrases such as “scope of need may
be underrepresented," (King et al., 2023, p. 1), "most research in university students has been
limited by small, unrepresentative samples, driven by low participation rates and participation
biases" (Adams et al., 2021, p. 2), and "research to date has been limited" (Duffy et al., 2020, p.
1). These gap statements serve the rhetorical function of justifying the research by demonstrating
that it addresses an unresolved question. Finally, each introduction concludes with Move 3:
occupying the niche by stating the purpose or research questions. Wyatt et al. (2017) state: "The
primary purpose of the study is to examine" (p. 179), while Adams et al. (2021) write: "this study
examined the" (p. 2). This three-move pattern creates a logical flow from broad context to specific
research focus, effectively persuading readers of the study's importance.
Stylistically, all five articles use formal academic language with passive voice
constructions and hedging. Passive voice is particularly common in Methods sections, such as
"students were emailed the link to participate" (Adams et al., 2021, p. 2) and "academic data
abstracted from" (King et al., 2020, p. 600). This passive construction serves the function of
creating objectivity and focusing attention on procedures rather than researchers, which aligns with
scientific conventions of impersonality. Hedging language appears throughout the Discussion
sections, with phrases like "may suggest," "could indicate," and "appears to be." For example,
Adams et al. (2021) write that findings "may indicate" a relationship (p. 8). This hedging serves
the important function of reflecting the tentative nature of scientific claims and demonstrates what
Duffy (2022) describes as the adaptation of rhetoric to the demands of specific contexts and
audiences.
Vocabulary from the discipline is used extensively without definition, indicating that the
authors expect readers to be familiar with specialized terms. The articles refer to "multivariate
analysis," "effect size," "confidence interval," and specific scales like "PHQ-9" and "GAD-7"
without explanation. This word choice functions to signal membership in the discourse community
and communicate efficiently with expert readers. The sentence structure tends toward complexity,
with embedded clauses and precise qualifications. For example, Adams et al. (2021) write: "Binary
logistic regression was used for analysis” (p. 5). This complex syntax serves the function of
conveying precise methodological information but assumes a sophisticated reader capable of
understanding such constructions.
Conclusion
This genre analysis examined five empirical research articles on student mental health,
comparing their rhetorical situations, rhetorical strategies, and organizational structures. The
analysis reveals that these articles share fundamental genre conventions: they are written by
academic researchers for specialized audiences, rely primarily on logos while establishing ethos
through methodological rigor, follow the IMRD structure with modifications, and employ formal
academic language with passive constructions and hedging. The variations observed—such as
different heading styles, the separation or combination of certain sections, and the inclusion of
journal-specific elements—reflect the influence of different publishing venues rather than
fundamental differences in genre conventions.
The rhetorical choices made by these authors are highly effective for persuading their target
audience. The heavy reliance on logos through quantitative evidence and statistical analysis
appeals to readers who value empirical proof. The establishment of ethos through validated
instruments, ethical approvals, and extensive citations builds trust in the researchers' competence.
The consistent use of the IMRD structure allows readers to efficiently locate information and
evaluate the research. The hedging and passive voice constructions signal adherence to scientific
norms of objectivity and tentativeness. Together, these genre conventions make the articles
persuasive because they align perfectly with the expectations and values of the health sciences
discourse community. This finding supports Dirk’s (2010) view that genres function as social
actions that help people accomplish goals, and their effectiveness depends on embodying the
conventions that audiences expect and trust.
This analysis has practical implications for students learning to write within academic
disciplines. Understanding genre conventions such as the move structure for introductions,
methodological detail, and hedging can help novice writers produce texts that meet disciplinary
expectations. By recognizing that genre conventions serve specific rhetorical purposes, students
can make more intentional choices in their own writing. A limitation of this analysis is that it
examined only five articles from closely related fields within health sciences; a broader sample
across disciplines would reveal greater variation in genre conventions. Nevertheless, this analysis
demonstrates how genre analysis can illuminate the rhetorical patterns that make academic writing
effective within its discourse community.
