This actually makes a big difference when we’re reading. With the traditional structure, we could easily jump to the Results section if we just wanted to know what they found. But with the thematic headings, we have to read more carefully to figure out which parts were observations and which parts were the authors' interpretations. We also noticed that where the main argument shows up depends on the paper. Usually it's in the Discussion or Conclusion, but the Velorum paper (Filippenko et al. 1999) kind of makes its argument throughout the Analysis section instead. So the claim and evidence are mixed together more, which made it harder for me to separate them.

Evidence:

The types of evidence used in these papers really depend on what question they're trying to answer. The observational papers, Velorum (Filippenko et al. 1999) and Gliese 12 b (Dholakia et al. 2024), use a lot of different types of physics data, including tables and some calculations. The disk structure papers (UX Tauri, AB Aurigae, and the protoplanetary disk one) are totally different because they're basically built around images (Ménard et al. 2020; Boccaletti et al. 2020; Speedie et al. 2024). They have interesting pictures from ALMA and other telescopes showing spiral structures, gaps, and weird asymmetries in the disks. What's cool is that these images aren't just there to look nice, they're actually the main evidence for the whole argument. Like, the AB Aurigae paper's whole point about planet formation comes from this "twist" they spotted in the disk images (Boccaletti et al. 2020). The newest paper does something really clever, where they compare images from different years to show that the spirals are actually moving over time (Speedie et al. 2024). It's almost like a before-and-after photo, and it helps them argue that gravitational instability is happening. Making the argument more clear for us to understand.

All of these papers use theoretical models, but in different amounts. I'd guess Velorum is like 70% actual data and 30% compared to models (Filippenko et al. 1999), while the disk papers are closer to half and half. The disk papers need simulations to help explain what their images are showing, which makes sense because we can't just look at a spiral and immediately know what's causing it.

Micro-organization and language/style features of the research articles
Looking at these papers in detail we found some patterns in Introductions. They all do the same thing: start with the big picture, point out something we don't know yet, and then say what their study adds. They move from general stuff like "we don't really understand how planets form" to specific things like "AB Aurigae is perfect for studying this because..." (Boccaletti et al. 2020). The language shows that they have a lot of weak claims instead of strong claims, for example using “this suggests that..” instead of saying “this claims”.
The Methods or Observations sections sound really different. They use a lot of passive voice, like "Data was obtained using..." or "The images were reduced following standard procedures." It sounds kind of robotic, but we think the point is to focus on what was done rather than who did it, which makes it seem more objective. One thing we noticed is that newer papers have way more detail about their methods. The Velorum paper explains its spectroscopic analysis in like three sentences (Filippenko et al. 1999), but Gliese 12 b has entire subsections breaking down different techniques allocated to that topic (Dholakia et al. 2024).


The Results and Discussion sections were the most different from paper to paper and showed me how each author was trying to convince their readers. Results sections use really precise language with numbers and error bars, like "we measure a mass of 3.2 ± 0.3 solar masses" (Filippenko et al. 1999). They present things in a logical order, usually starting with what they actually saw and then moving to what they calculated from that.
The Discussion sections are where you can actually hear the authors' voices more. This is where they interpret what everything means, make guesses about what's going on, and connect their findings to other research. The language shifts from "we observed" to "this suggests" or "one possible explanation is." The disk papers are especially interesting here because they compare different possibilities like, could this be planet formation, or gravitational instability, or maybe a stellar companion? before picking the one they think is most likely (Ménard et al. 2020; Boccaletti et al. 2020; Speedie et al. 2024) and this also helps us to think rather than just reading the paper.
We also realized that how they format everything matters a lot. When they put a figure right next to the paragraph talking about it, it really helps you follow along, especially with complicated arguments. Tables do something different—they cram a bunch of information into one place so you can check facts quickly. The Velorum paper puts all its spectroscopic measurements in a single table (Filippenko et al. 1999), which we found helpful when we were trying to understand how they calculated the black hole mass. 


Conclusion:
In this genre analysis, we examined five astronomy articles published between 1999 and 2025 to understand how rhetorical strategies and different structure and format have evolved over time. We found a pattern where discipline is moving from rigid, methodological reporting to more fluid, thematic structures. This shift suggests that with modern times the writing style has also changed. The rhetorical choices we observed are highly effective for this community. By combining the objectivity of  passive voice in methods with careful claims in the discussions, the authors have successfully built credibility without overstating their findings.

	The analysis is important because it proves that the scientific writing is not static, it changes based on the tools and evidence available. For us the main benefit of this work is realizing that to write effectively in astronomy as well as any other scientific topic is more than just following a template, it depends on the small details of rhetorical devices, different ways of supporting our claims and many more. However, there are limitations to our analysis, Since we only looked at the 5 papers on a specific topic and genre, there might be more variations and nuances that we might have missed and can be learnt through different papers. Despite this, analyzing this gives us a clearer roadmap for how to communicate with this specific audience and understand the basics of writing a scientific paper.

As this paper demonstrates, modern scientific articles often hybridize these sections into thematic narratives to better integrate complex visual data like ALMA imagery.

data.essay_text:
Introduction
It is not an understatement to say that humanity has looked to the sky and stars in wonder for millennia before the current day. This can be seen in our mythologies which describe the constellations and scribe tales of how they came to be; such as the constellations ursa major and orion. It is only in recent history that humanity has had the ability to observe the universe much more closely with the invention of the telescope and our relatively new technology allowing us to send probes into space for deeper study. Astronomy, the study of anything outside earth’s atmosphere, was born from our fascination with space. The selection articles chosen return to the base of astronomy and focus on the analysis of observations of celestial phenomena. By analyzing 5 unique astronomical articles published between 1999 to 2025, this paper argues that as astronomical observation has shifted from raw data to more imagining data, moreover it has also evolved from using rigid IMRAD structure to hybridized, thematic narratives that blend with the Aristotle's three modes to guide reader through the paper. This paper moves from analyzing rhetorical situations and moves to how different organization techniques have evolved with the time.


Rhetorical situation
Selected articles are primarily focused on analyzing the data and observations made of astronomical objects and the primary audience of these scientific articles are most likely written for fellow astronomers as the language they use: filled with unexplained acronyms such as ALMA (Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array) or TESS, referring to the instruments used for the observations and analysis along with being published by astronomy and astrophysics based journals which is unlikely to attract the attention of those not in their field. A secondary audience for these papers are the undergraduate/graduate students pursuing their subjects involving astronomy. They would have to read these articles for their research work and to develop their knowledge across these subjects. The intended audience is most likely aware of basic astronomy concepts such as binary systems and their different classifications. 
Given that the intended audience of this paper, it is most likely composed of fellow peers of the authors who are interested in the details of astronomical objects such as their weight, behavior and classification. The primary purpose of these articles is to formally record observational data and persuade the academic community of the authors’ interpretations of the specific claim. The earlier Nova Velorum paper (1999/2001) has two authors from UC Berkeley, a relatively compact team using a single telescope. The four more recent papers all feature large international author lists: Ménard et al. draw from France, the Netherlands, and Chile; Dholakia et al. involve TESS, CHEOPS, MINERVA-Australis, SPECULOOS, and Purple Mountain Observatory as named collaborating facilities. This shows a shift in the field that modern astrophysics papers require multi-institutional, multi-instrument collaborations to draw conclusions for deep research papers, and more institutions signal more robustly validated data. Different papers prove their claim through different approaches, some support it with numerical raw data while others support it with visual images, more details on this as we move on.
Rhetorical strategies: ethos, pathos, logos: 
As scientific articles the most obvious rhetorical strategy used would be their appeal to Logos, logic and reasoning. These papers establish their arguments using the observations made using scientific tools and hard numbers obtained using different frameworks.  This can be observed in the figures 1 and 2 in Ménard et al. in Ongoing Flyby in the Young Multiple System UX Tauri, which present multi-wavelength disk images alongside hydrodynamical simulations, it allows us to compare predicted and observed disk morphology, this move alone carries the logical argument that an unbound stellar flyby best explains the asymmetric disk structure. Similarly in the paper Filippenko & Chornock in A Black Hole in the X-Ray Nova Velorum 1993 derive a mass function of M₁ ≥ 3.9 M☉ from spectroscopic radial velocity measurements, a numerical data supporting the main argument of the paper. Hence we can see how these different approaches for establishing logos within paper support the argument and build up the paper.
The Ethos or credibility of these articles is established from their status as peer reviewed works which indicates their accuracy and validity. The credentials of the authors of the papers build more credibility for these papers, contributors like Stéphane Guilloteau, listed among the authors of the UX Tauri paper, hold institutional affiliations at major research laboratories and They also published numerous papers which adds more reliability. But this also differs around different papers, such as the Nova Velorum paper, authored by only two researchers at UC Berkeley, relies almost entirely on the prestige of their Keck Observatory spectroscopy and the reputation of the journal while the recent papers are supported by collective ethos through large, multi-institutional author lists: Ménard et al. draw collaborators from France, the Netherlands, and Chile, while Dholakia et al. involve five separate observing facilities across three continents. This shift shows the evolution of how astrophysics papers build reliability.
The Pathos is by far the most difficult to spot in these scientific articles as it is the least prominent strategy used by the authors. Emotion is one of the things that is often absent from scientific research; The closest thing to an appeal to Pathos or emotion comes in the form of their article titles which could grab the volume reader’s attention towards the actual article however the delivery of information within is often to the point leaving those with no deep interest in the subject lacking in response to the content. 

Macro-organization of the research articles
After looking at these five papers, it reveals that the structures of these papers evolve with the time. Since they were published between 1999 and 2025. The oldest one, the Velorum paper from 1999 (Filippenko et al. 1999), sticks to the methodological approach while the new papers follow the thematic approach, in addition to that newer papers all follow IMRD structure but not strictly, with a bit of nuances, For example, the UX Tauri (Ménard et al. 2020) and AB Aurigae (Boccaletti et al. 2020) papers use "Introduction," "Observations," "Analysis," and "Discussion/Conclusion" instead. The Gliese 12 b paper (Dholakia et al. 2024) is even more different—it uses headings like "Planetary system overview" and "Atmospheric characterization" 
This modern labeling of types rather than its scientific significance allows an expert reader to navigate directly to the data they need. Although this format is more convenient, the clever move from Ménard et al. (2020) paper, they use "Observations and Results" as their title for second section, which is a thematic turn forcing more active reading, rather than skipping to the results, the reader have to engage with the argumentative logic threaded through the section. This format is further followed by one of the latest papers about the protoplanetary disk (Speedie et al. 2024) where the sections blend results with interpretation, like "Evidence of spirals winding with time." With the similar approach as Ménard et al. (2020) article.

It can also be noticed that the location of the main argument varies from paper to paper. In the majority of papers it's in the Discussion or Conclusion, which follow IMRaD convention of presenting the data before presenting interpretation. Ménard et al. (2020) follows this clearly, the key question of whether UX Tau C is a bound companion or an unbound flyby is only addressed as a titled subsection within Section 4 (Discussion), so the reader knows where description ends and judgment begins. The Velorum paper (Filippenko & Chornock 1999), however, makes its argument throughout the Results and "Mass of the Compact Primary" sections instead. So the claim and evidence are mixed together more, which made it harder for me to separate them. This pattern suggests that argument placement is not random but it follows the nature of evidence.

Evidence:

The types of evidence used in these papers depend on the question they're trying to answer. The observational papers, Velorum (Filippenko et al. 1999) and Gliese 12 b (Dholakia et al. 2024), use a variety of different types of physics data, including tables and some calculations. The disk structure papers (UX Tauri, AB Aurigae, and the protoplanetary disk one) are totally different because they're grounded around images (Ménard et al. 2020; Boccaletti et al. 2020; Speedie et al. 2024). They have interesting pictures from ALMA and other telescopes showing spiral structures, gaps, and weird asymmetries in the disks. The presence of these images is not to enhance the look of the paper, instead they're actually the main evidence for the whole argument. Like the AB Aurigae paper's main argument about planet formation comes from this "twist" they spotted in the disk images (Boccaletti et al. 2020). The newest paper does something really unique, where they compare images from different years to show that the spirals are actually moving over time (Speedie et al. 2024). It helps them argue that gravitational instability is happening and to successfully support their claim . Making the argument more clear for us to understand and develop Ethos.

All of these papers use theoretical models, but in different amounts. Approximately Velorum paper is 70% actual data and 30% compared to models (Filippenko et al. 1999), while the disk papers are closer to half and half. The disk papers need simulations to help explain what images are describing and its connection to the argument, which makes sense as it is not obvious for a reader to look at a spiral and immediately know what's causing it.

Micro-organization and language/style features of the research articles
Examining these papers at micro level reveals some patterns in how sections are written and organized. All Five Introductions follow the same moves: start with the big picture (Give context),Identify a gap in current knowledge, and provide their proposition to fill the gap. Boccaletti et al. (2020) demonstrate this clearly, opening with the general problem of planet formation before narrowing to why AB Aurigae is an ideal case study. This structure is replicated across all five papers. The introductions are more written in a professional tone, such that it fulfills all the genre’s requirements, using language like “this suggests” and “may indicate” rather than assertive tone.
The Methods and Observations section are more uniform across the chosen articles. They use a lot of passive voice, like "Data was obtained using..." or "The images were reduced following standard procedures." It is an artistic choice that grounds the process over the individual, projecting objectivity by removing the human agent from the methodology section. As we evolve the depth of methodological reporting expands significantly. The Velorum paper explains its spectroscopic analysis briefly in three sentences (Filippenko et al. 1999), but Gliese 12 b has entire subsections breaking down different techniques allocated to that topic (Dholakia et al. 2024).
The Results and Discussion sections show the greatest variation from paper to paper and exhibits how each author is trying to persuade their readers. Results sections consistently use precise language with numbers and error bars, like "we measure a mass of 3.2 ± 0.3 solar masses" (Filippenko et al. 1999). They present things in a logical order, usually starting with what they actually saw and then moving to what they calculated from that. The Discussion sections portray more about the author's voices. This is where they interpret what everything means, make guesses about what's going on, and draw connections to other research. The language shifts from "we observed" to "this suggests" or "one possible explanation is." The disk papers (Ménard et al. (2020), Boccaletti et al. (2020), and Speedie et al. (2025)) make particularly unique use of this section by enumerating competing hypotheses (gravitational instability, stellar companion perturbation, planet formation) before ruling out alternatives and stating their claim. This structure models scientific reasoning for the reader rather than simply delivering a verdict, which helps the reader to think rather than just absorb the information.


It is observable that the format of everything plays a crucial role. Placing a figure next to the connecting paragraph helps the reader follow along, especially with complicated arguments. Tables do something different, they cram a bunch of information into one place so the reader can check facts quickly. The Velorum paper puts all its spectroscopic measurements in a single table (Filippenko et al. 1999), which can be found helpful when the reader is trying to understand how the mass of black hole is calculated. 

Conclusion:
This genre analysis examined five astronomy articles published between 1999 and 2025 to understand how rhetorical strategies and different structure and format have evolved over time. A clear pattern emerged where discipline is moving from rigid, methodological reporting to more fluid, thematic structures. This shift suggests that with modern times the writing style has also changed. The rhetorical choices observed across these papers prove highly effective for their intended discourse community: by combining the objectivity of  passive voice in methods sections with careful claims in the discussions, the authors have successfully built credibility without overstating their findings.

	This analysis also demonstrates that scientific writing is not static, it changes based on the tools and evidence available. data.essay_text:
Introduction
It is not an understatement to say that humanity has looked to the sky and stars in wonder for millennia before the current day. This can be seen in our mythologies, which describe the constellations and scribe tales of how they came to be, such as the constellations Ursa Major and Orion. It is only in recent history that humanity has had the ability to observe the universe much more closely with the invention of the telescope and our relatively new technology allowing us to send probes into space for deeper study. Astronomy, the study of anything outside Earth's atmosphere, was born from our fascination with space. The selection of articles chosen returns to the base of astronomy and focuses on the analysis of observations of celestial phenomena. By analyzing 5 unique astronomical articles published between 1999 and 2025, this paper argues that as astronomical observation has shifted from raw data to more imaging data, it has also evolved from using a rigid IMRAD structure to hybridized, thematic narratives that blend with Aristotle's three modes to guide the reader through the paper. This paper moves from analyzing rhetorical situations and moves to how different organization techniques have evolved with time.
Rhetorical situation
Selected articles are primarily focused on analyzing the data and observations made of astronomical objects, and the primary audience of these scientific articles are most likely fellow astronomers, as the language they use is filled with unexplained acronyms such as ALMA (Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array) or TESS, referring to the instruments used for the observations and analysis, along with being published by astronomy and astrophysics-based journals, which is unlikely to attract the attention of those not in their field. A secondary audience for these papers are the undergraduate/graduate students pursuing their subjects involving astronomy. They would have to read these articles for their research work and to develop their knowledge across these subjects. The intended audience is most likely aware of basic astronomy concepts such as binary systems and their different classifications. 
Given the intended audience of this paper, it is most likely composed of fellow peers of the authors who are interested in the details of astronomical objects, such as their weight, behavior, and classification. The primary purpose of these articles is to formally record observational data and persuade the academic community of the authors’ interpretations of the specific claim. The earlier Nova Velorum paper (1999/2001) has two authors from UC Berkeley, a relatively compact team using a single telescope. The four more recent papers all feature large international author lists: Ménard et al. draw from France, the Netherlands, and Chile; Dholakia et al. involve TESS, CHEOPS, MINERVA-Australis, SPECULOOS, and Purple Mountain Observatory as named collaborating facilities. This shows a shift in the field: modern astrophysics papers require multi-institutional, multi-instrument collaborations to draw conclusions for deep research papers, and more institutions signal more robustly validated data. Different papers prove their claim through different approaches; some support it with numerical raw data, while others support it with visual images. More details on this as we move on.
Rhetorical strategies: ethos, pathos, and logos:
As scientific articles, the most obvious rhetorical strategy used would be their appeal to logos, logic, and reasoning. These papers establish their arguments using the observations made using scientific tools and hard numbers obtained using different frameworks. This can be observed in figures 1 and 2 in Ménard et al.'s Ongoing Flyby in the Young Multiple System UX Tauri, which present multi-wavelength disk images alongside hydrodynamical simulations; it allows us to compare predicted and observed disk morphology. This move alone carries the logical argument that an unbound stellar flyby best explains the asymmetric disk structure. Similarly, in the paper Filippenko & Chornock in A Black Hole in the X-Ray Nova Velorum 1993 derive a mass function of M₁ ≥ 3.9 M☉ from spectroscopic radial velocity measurements, a numerical data point supporting the main argument of the paper. Hence, we can see how these different approaches for establishing logos within the paper support the argument and build up the paper.
The ethos, or credibility, of these articles is established from their status as peer-reviewed works, which indicates their accuracy and validity. The credentials of the authors of the papers build more credibility for these papers; contributors like Stéphane Guilloteau, listed among the authors of the UX Tauri paper, hold institutional affiliations at major research laboratories, and they have also published numerous papers, which adds more reliability. But this also differs among different papers; for example, the Nova Velorum paper, authored by only two researchers at UC Berkeley, relies almost entirely on the prestige of their Keck Observatory spectroscopy and the reputation of the journal, while the recent papers are supported by collective ethos through large, multi-institutional author lists: Ménard et al. draw collaborators from France, the Netherlands, and Chile, while Dholakia et al. involve five separate observing facilities across three continents. This shift shows the evolution of how astrophysics papers build reliability.
Pathos is by far the most difficult to spot in these scientific articles, as it is the least prominent strategy used by the authors. Emotion is one of the things that is often absent from scientific research; the closest thing to an appeal to pathos, or emotion, comes in the form of their article titles, which could grab the volume reader’s attention towards the actual article. However, the delivery of information within is often to the point, leaving those with no deep interest in the subject lacking in response to the content.

 Macro-organization of the research articles
After looking at these five papers, it reveals that the structures of these papers evolve with the time. Since they were published between 1999 and 2025. The oldest one, the Velorum paper from 1999 (Filippenko et al. 1999), sticks to the methodological approach, while the new papers follow the thematic approach. In addition to that, the newer papers all follow the IMRD structure, but not strictly, with a bit of nuance. For example, the UX Tauri (Ménard et al. 2020) and AB Aurigae (Boccaletti et al. 2020) papers use "Introduction," "Observations," "Analysis," and "Discussion/Conclusion" instead. The Gliese 12 b paper (Dholakia et al. 2024) is even more different—it uses headings like "Planetary system overview" and "Atmospheric characterization." 
This modern labeling of types rather than its scientific significance allows an expert reader to navigate directly to the data they need. Although this format is more convenient, the clever move from the Ménard et al. (2020) paper is that they use "Observations and Results" as their title for the second section, which is a thematic turn forcing more active reading. Rather than skipping to the results, the reader has to engage with the argumentative logic threaded through the section. This format is further followed by one of the latest papers about the protoplanetary disk (Speedie et al. 2024), where the sections blend results with interpretation, like "Evidence of spirals winding with time." With a similar approach as the Ménard et al. (2020) article.
It can also be noticed that the location of the main argument varies from paper to paper. In the majority of papers it's in the discussion or conclusion, which follows the IMRaD convention of presenting the data before presenting interpretation. Ménard et al. (2020) follows this clearly; the key question of whether UX Tau C is a bound companion or an unbound flyby is only addressed as a titled subsection within Section 4 (Discussion), so the reader knows where description ends and judgment begins. The Velorum paper (Filippenko & Chornock 1999), however, makes its argument throughout the Results and "Mass of the Compact Primary" sections instead. So the claim and evidence are mixed together more, which made it harder for me to separate them. This pattern suggests that argument placement is not random, but it follows the nature of evidence.
Evidence:
The types of evidence used in these papers depend on the question they're trying to answer. The observational papers, Velorum (Filippenko et al. 1999) and Gliese 12 b (Dholakia et al. 2024), use a variety of different types of physics data, including tables and some calculations. The disk structure papers (UX Tauri, AB Aurigae, and the protoplanetary disk one) are totally different because they're grounded around images (Ménard et al. 2020; Boccaletti et al. 2020; Speedie et al. 2024). They have interesting pictures from ALMA and other telescopes showing spiral structures, gaps, and weird asymmetries in the disks. The presence of these images is not to enhance the look of the paper; instead, they're actually the main evidence for the whole argument. Like the AB Aurigae paper's main argument about planet formation comes from this "twist" they spotted in the disk images (Boccaletti et al. 2020). The newest paper does something really unique, where they compare images from different years to show that the spirals are actually moving over time (Speedie et al. 2024). It helps them argue that gravitational instability is happening and successfully support their claim. Making the argument more clear for us to understand and develop ethos.
All of these papers use theoretical models, but in different amounts. Approximately 70% of the Velorum paper is actual data and 30% is compared to models (Filippenko et al. 1999), while the disk papers are closer to half and half. The disk papers need simulations to help explain what images are describing and its connection to the argument, which makes sense as it is not obvious for a reader to look at a spiral and immediately know what's causing it.
Micro-organization and language/style features of the research articles
Examining these papers at the micro level reveals some patterns in how sections are written and organized. All five introductions follow the same moves: start with the big picture (give context), Identify a gap in current knowledge, and provide their proposition to fill the gap. Boccaletti et al. (2020) demonstrate this clearly, opening with the general problem of planet formation before narrowing to why AB Aurigae is an ideal case study. This structure is replicated across all five papers. The introductions are more written in a professional tone, such that they fulfill all the genre’s requirements, using language like “this suggests” and “may indicate” rather than an assertive tone.
The Methods and Observations section is more uniform across the chosen articles. They use a lot of passive voice, like "Data was obtained using..." or "The images were reduced following standard procedures." It is an artistic choice that grounds the process over the individual, projecting objectivity by removing the human agent from the methodology section. As we evolve, the depth of methodological reporting expands significantly. The Velorum paper explains its spectroscopic analysis briefly in three sentences (Filippenko et al. 1999), but Gliese 12 b has entire subsections breaking down different techniques allocated to that topic (Dholakia et al. 2024).
The Results and Discussion sections show the greatest variation from paper to paper and exhibit how each author is trying to persuade their readers. Results sections consistently use precise language with numbers and error bars, like "we measure a mass of 3.2 ± 0.3 solar masses" (Filippenko et al. 1999). They present things in a logical order, usually starting with what they actually saw and then moving to what they calculated from that. The Discussion sections portray more about the author's voices. This is where they interpret what everything means, make guesses about what's going on, and draw connections to other research. The language shifts from "we observed" to "this suggests" or "one possible explanation is." The disk papers (Ménard et al. (2020), Boccaletti et al. (2020), and Speedie et al. (2025)) make particularly unique use of this section by enumerating competing hypotheses (gravitational instability, stellar companion perturbation, and planet formation) before ruling out alternatives and stating their claim. This structure models scientific reasoning for the reader rather than simply delivering a verdict, which helps the reader to think rather than just absorb the information.
It is observable that the format of everything plays a crucial role. Placing a figure next to the connecting paragraph helps the reader follow along, especially with complicated arguments. Tables do something different; they cram a bunch of information into one place so the reader can check facts quickly. The Velorum paper puts all its spectroscopic measurements in a single table (Filippenko et al. 1999), which can be found helpful when the reader is trying to understand how the mass of a black hole is calculated.

 Conclusion:
This genre analysis examined five astronomy articles published between 1999 and 2025 to understand how rhetorical strategies and different structures and formats have evolved over time. A clear pattern emerged where discipline is moving from rigid, methodological reporting to more fluid, thematic structures. This shift suggests that with modern times the writing style has also changed. The rhetorical choices observed across these papers prove highly effective for their intended discourse community: by combining the objectivity of passive voice in methods sections with careful claims in the discussions, the authors have successfully built credibility without overstating their findings.

This analysis also demonstrates that scientific writing is not static; it changes based on the tools and evidence available. For students in university, the main benefit of this work is realizing that to write effectively in astronomy as well as any other scientific topic is more than just following a template; it depends on the small details of rhetorical devices, different ways of supporting the claims, and many more. However, there are limitations to the analysis. Since this analysis is only on the 5 papers and on a specific topic and genre, there might be more variations and nuances that might have been missed and can be learned through different papers. Despite this, analyzing these papers provides a clearer roadmap to how to communicate with this specific audience and understand the basics of writing a scientific paper.

Mini Lessons: The 'IMRAD' (Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion) structure is the 'default' for scientific writing, but as fields become more complex and data becomes more visual, authors often move toward 'Thematic' structures. This allows them to group evidence and interpretation together, making a more persuasive narrative for the reader.

In scientific rhetoric, 'Ethos' is often 'distributed' rather than individual. In older papers, a single famous name might provide the credibility. In modern 'Big Science,' ethos is built through the sheer number of collaborating institutions and the variety of instruments (like ALMA or TESS) used to verify the data.

The use of the passive voice in scientific 'Methods' sections isn't just a grammar rule; it's a rhetorical choice. By saying 'The data was collected' instead of 'I collected the data,' the author removes human bias and makes the process seem objective and replicable by anyone.

After looking at these five papers, it reveals that the structures of these papers evolve with the time. Since they were published between 1999 and 2025. The oldest one, the Velorum paper from 1999 (Filippenko et al. 1999), sticks to the methodological approach, while the new papers follow the thematic approach. In addition to that, the newer papers all follow the IMRaD structure, but not strictly, with a bit of nuance. For example, the UX Tauri (Ménard et al. 2020) and AB Aurigae (Boccaletti et al. 2020) papers use "Introduction," "Observations," "Analysis," and "Discussion/Conclusion" instead. The Gliese 12 b paper (Dholakia et al. 2024) is even more different—it uses headings like "Planetary system overview" and "Atmospheric characterization." 
This modern labeling of types rather than its scientific significance allows an expert reader to navigate directly to the data they need. Although this format is more convenient, the clever move from the Ménard et al. (2020) paper is that they use "Observations and Results" as their title for the second section, which is a thematic turn forcing more active reading. Rather than skipping to the results, the reader has to engage with the argumentative logic threaded through the section. This format is further followed by one of the latest papers about the protoplanetary disk (Speedie et al. 2024), where the sections blend results with interpretation, like "Evidence of spirals winding with time." With a similar approach as the Ménard et al. (2020) article.
It can also be noticed that the location of the main argument varies from paper to paper. In the majority of papers it's in the discussion or conclusion, which follows the IMRAD convention of presenting the data before presenting interpretation. Ménard et al. (2020) follows this clearly; the key question of whether UX Tau C is a bound companion or an unbound flyby is only addressed as a titled subsection within Section 4 (Discussion), so the reader knows where description ends and judgment begins. The Velorum paper (Filippenko & Chornock 1999), however, makes its argument throughout the Results and "Mass of the Compact Primary" sections instead. So the claim and evidence are mixed together more, which made it harder for me to separate them. This pattern suggests that argument placement is not random, but it follows the nature of evidence.
Evidence:
The types of evidence used in these papers depend on the question they're trying to answer. The observational papers, Velorum (Filippenko et al. 1999) and Gliese 12 b (Dholakia et al. 2024), use a variety of different types of physics data, including tables and some calculations. The disk structure papers (UX Tauri, AB Aurigae, and the protoplanetary disk one) are totally different because they're grounded around images (Ménard et al. 2020; Boccaletti et al. 2020; Speedie et al. 2024). They have interesting pictures from ALMA and other telescopes showing spiral structures, gaps, and irregular asymmetries in the disks. The presence of these images is not to enhance the look of the paper; instead, they're actually the main evidence for the whole argument. Like the AB Aurigae paper's main argument about planet formation comes from this "twist" they spotted in the disk images (Boccaletti et al. 2020). The newest paper does something really unique, where they compare images from different years to show that the spirals are actually moving over time (Speedie et al. 2024). It helps them argue that gravitational instability is happening and successfully support their claim. Making the argument more clear for us to understand and develop ethos.
All of these papers use theoretical models, but in different amounts. Approximately 70% of the Velorum paper is actual data and 30% is compared to models (Filippenko et al. 1999), while the disk papers are closer to half and half. The disk papers need simulations to help explain what images are describing and its connection to the argument, which makes sense as it is not obvious for a reader to look at a spiral and immediately know what's causing it.
Micro-organization and language/style features of the research articles
Examining these papers at the micro level reveals some patterns in how sections are written and organized. All five introductions follow the same moves: start with the big picture (give context), Identify a gap in current knowledge, and provide their proposition to fill the gap. Boccaletti et al. (2020) demonstrate this clearly, opening with the general problem of planet formation before narrowing to why AB Aurigae is an ideal case study. This structure is replicated across all five papers. The introductions are more written in a professional tone, such that they fulfill all the genre’s requirements, using language like “this suggests” and “may indicate” rather than an assertive tone.
The Methods and Observations section is more uniform across the chosen articles. They use a lot of passive voice, like "Data was obtained using..." or "The images were reduced following standard procedures." It is an artistic choice that foregrounds the process over the individual, projecting objectivity by removing the human agent from the methodology section. As we evolve, the depth of methodological reporting expands significantly. The Velorum paper explains its spectroscopic analysis briefly in three sentences (Filippenko et al. 1999), but Gliese 12 b has entire subsections breaking down different techniques allocated to that topic (Dholakia et al. 2024).
The Results and Discussion sections show the greatest variation from paper to paper and exhibit how each author is trying to persuade their readers. Results sections consistently use precise language with numbers and error bars, like "we measure a mass of 3.2 ± 0.3 solar masses" (Filippenko et al. 1999). They present things in a logical order, usually starting with what they actually saw and then moving to what they calculated from that. The Discussion sections portray more about the author's voices. This is where they interpret what everything means, make guesses about what's going on, and draw connections to other research. The language shifts from "we observed" to "this suggests" or "one possible explanation is." The disk papers (Ménard et al. (2020), Boccaletti et al. (2020), and Speedie et al. (2025)) make particularly unique use of this section by enumerating competing hypotheses (gravitational instability, stellar companion perturbation, and planet formation) before ruling out alternatives and stating their claim. This structure models scientific reasoning for the reader rather than simply delivering a verdict, which helps the reader to think rather than just absorb the information.
It is observable that the format of everything plays a crucial role. Placing a figure next to the connecting paragraph helps the reader follow along, especially with complicated arguments. Tables do something different; they contain a significant amount of information into one place so the reader can check facts quickly. The Velorum paper puts all its spectroscopic measurements in a single table (Filippenko et al. 1999), which can be found helpful when the reader is trying to understand how the mass of a black hole is calculated.

 Conclusion:
This genre analysis examined five astronomy articles published between 1999 and 2025 to understand how rhetorical strategies and different structures and formats have evolved over time. A clear pattern emerged where discipline is moving from rigid, methodological reporting to more fluid, thematic structures. This shift suggests that as astronomical tools have evolved, the writing style has shifted to accommodate complex visual data. The rhetorical choices observed across these papers prove highly effective for their intended discourse community: by combining the objectivity of passive voice in methods sections with careful claims in the discussions, the authors have successfully built credibility without overstating their findings.

This analysis also demonstrates that scientific writing is not static; it changes based on the tools and evidence available. For students in university, the main benefit of this work is realizing that to write effectively in astronomy as well as any other scientific topic is more than just following a template; it depends on the small details of rhetorical devices, different ways of supporting the claims, and many more. However, there are limitations to the analysis. Since this analysis is only on the 5 papers and on a specific topic and genre, there might be more variations and nuances that might have been missed and can be learned through different papers. Despite this, analyzing these papers provides a clearer roadmap to how to communicate with this specific audience and understand the basics of writing a scientific paper.

Mini Lessons: **Hedging in Scientific Writing**: In your essay, you mentioned 'weak claims' like 'this suggests'. In academic writing, this is called 'hedging'. It is not a weakness; it is a vital tool. Scientists use hedging to account for the fact that new data might change our understanding. It protects the author's credibility by not overstating the certainty of a finding. When you analyze this, use terms like 'hedging' or 'qualifying statements' to sound more professional.

**Maintaining Academic Voice**: Think of an academic report like a formal interview. Using words like 'cool', 'thing', or 'I'd guess' is like wearing a t-shirt to that interview. You want your language to be precise and objective. Instead of saying something is 'cool', explain *why* it is effective (e.g., 'The integration of images and text enhances the reader's spatial understanding'). Avoid 'I guess'—if you aren't sure of a percentage, use 'approximately' or 'appears to be'.

Subject: astronomy
Genre: astrological observations 
Introduction
It is not an understatement to say that humanity has looked to the sky and stars in wonder for millennia before the current day. This can be seen in our mythologies which describe the constellations and scribe tales of how they came to be; such as the constellations ursa major and orion. It is only in recent history that humanity has had the ability to observe the universe much more closely with the invention of the telescope and our relatively new technology allowing us to send probes into space for deeper study. Astronomy, the study of anything outside earth’s atmosphere, was born from our fascination with space. The selection articles chosen return to the base of astronomy and focus on the analysis of observations of celestial phenomena. Looking across these 5 astronomical articles, the authors relied on a combination of both the structure and an appeal to Logos and Ethos to effectively lead readers into believing in the conclusion arrived at by the authors themselves.
Rhetorical situation
The 5 articles are primarily focused on analyzing the data and observations made of astronomical objects. The primary audience of these scientific articles are most likely written for fellow astronomers as the language they use, which is filled with unexplained acronyms referring to the instruments used for the observations and analysis along with being published by astronomy and astrophysics based journals which is unlikely to attract the attention of those not in their field. A secondary audience for these papers would likely be university students in classes involving astronomy who would have to read these articles for their essays. The intended audience is most likely aware of basic astronomy concepts such as binary systems and their different classifications. 
Given that the intended audience of this paper is most likely composed of fellow peers of the authors who are interested in the details of astronomical objects such as their weight, behavior and classification. They receive reading these articles whose purpose is to inform others and record information on details gained from observations of astronomical objects. 
Rhetorical strategies: ethos, pathos, logos: 
As scientific articles the most obvious rhetorical strategy used would be their appeal to Logos, logic and reasoning, as they primarily use observations made using scientific tools and hard numbers obtained using those observations such as the figures 1 and 2 in the article Ongoing flyby in the young multiple system UX Tauri. 
The credibility or Ethos of these articles come from their status as peer reviewed works which indicates their accuracy and validity. Additionally authors involved in these articles have written numerous other additional peer reviewed articles such as stephane guilloteau who has written many other articles and is currently employed at an astrophysics laboratory. (ORCID. 2026).
The Pathos is by far the most difficult to spot in these articles. Emotion is one of the things that is often absent from scientific research; The closest thing to an appeal to Pathos or emotion comes in the form of their article titles which could grab the volume reader’s attention towards the actual article however the delivery of information within is often to the point leaving those with no deep interest in the subject lacking in response to the content. 
Macro-organization of the research articles
After looking at these five papers, we noticed that the structures of these papers evolve with the time. Since they were published between 1999 and 2025. The oldest one, the Velorum paper from 1999 (Filippenko et al. 1999), sticks to the methodological approach while the new papers follow the thematic approach, in addition to that newer papers all follow IMRD structure but not strictly, with a bit of nuances, For example, the UX Tauri (Ménard et al. 2020) and AB Aurigae (Boccaletti et al. 2020) papers use "Introduction," "Observations," "Analysis," and "Discussion/Conclusion" instead. The Gliese 12 b paper (Dholakia et al. 2024) is even more different—it uses headings like "Planetary system overview" and "Atmospheric characterization" that describe what we’re reading about rather than just labeling the section type.

The newest paper about the protoplanetary disk (Speedie et al. 2024) does this cool hybrid thing where the sections blend results with interpretation, like "Evidence of spirals winding with time." This actually makes a big difference when we’re reading. With the traditional structure, we could easily jump to the Results section if we just wanted to know what they found. But with the thematic headings, we have to read more carefully to figure out which parts were observations and which parts were the authors' interpretations. We also noticed that where the main argument shows up depends on the paper. Usually it's in the Discussion or Conclusion, but the Velorum paper (Filippenko et al. 1999) kind of makes its argument throughout the Analysis section instead. So the claim and evidence are mixed together more, which made it harder for me to separate them.

Evidence:

The types of evidence used in these papers really depend on what question they're trying to answer. The observational papers, Velorum (Filippenko et al. 1999) and Gliese 12 b (Dholakia et al. 2024), use a lot of different types of physics data, including tables and some calculations. The disk structure papers (UX Tauri, AB Aurigae, and the protoplanetary disk one) are totally different because they're basically built around images (Ménard et al. 2020; Boccaletti et al. 2020; Speedie et al. 2024). They have interesting pictures from ALMA and other telescopes showing spiral structures, gaps, and weird asymmetries in the disks. What's cool is that these images aren't just there to look nice, they're actually the main evidence for the whole argument. Like, the AB Aurigae paper's whole point about planet formation comes from this "twist" they spotted in the disk images (Boccaletti et al. 2020). The newest paper does something really clever, where they compare images from different years to show that the spirals are actually moving over time (Speedie et al. 2024). It's almost like a before-and-after photo, and it helps them argue that gravitational instability is happening. Making the argument more clear for us to understand.

All of these papers use theoretical models, but in different amounts. I'd guess Velorum is like 70% actual data and 30% compared to models (Filippenko et al. 1999), while the disk papers are closer to half and half. The disk papers need simulations to help explain what their images are showing, which makes sense because we can't just look at a spiral and immediately know what's causing it.

Micro-organization and language/style features of the research articles
Looking at these papers in detail we found some patterns in Introductions. They all do the same thing: start with the big picture, point out something we don't know yet, and then say what their study adds. They move from general stuff like "we don't really understand how planets form" to specific things like "AB Aurigae is perfect for studying this because..." (Boccaletti et al. 2020). The language shows that they have a lot of weak claims instead of strong claims, for example using “this suggests that..” instead of saying “this claims”.
The Methods or Observations sections sound really different. They use a lot of passive voice, like "Data was obtained using..." or "The images were reduced following standard procedures." It sounds kind of robotic, but we think the point is to focus on what was done rather than who did it, which makes it seem more objective. One thing we noticed is that newer papers have way more detail about their methods. The Velorum paper explains its spectroscopic analysis in like three sentences (Filippenko et al. 1999), but Gliese 12 b has entire subsections breaking down different techniques allocated to that topic (Dholakia et al. 2024).


The Results and Discussion sections were the most different from paper to paper and showed me how each author was trying to convince their readers. Results sections use really precise language with numbers and error bars, like "we measure a mass of 3.2 ± 0.3 solar masses" (Filippenko et al. 1999). They present things in a logical order, usually starting with what they actually saw and then moving to what they calculated from that.
The Discussion sections are where you can actually hear the authors' voices more. This is where they interpret what everything means, make guesses about what's going on, and connect their findings to other research. The language shifts from "we observed" to "this suggests" or "one possible explanation is." The disk papers are especially interesting here because they compare different possibilities like, could this be planet formation, or gravitational instability, or maybe a stellar companion? before picking the one they think is most likely (Ménard et al. 2020; Boccaletti et al. 2020; Speedie et al. 2024) and this also helps us to think rather than just reading the paper.
We also realized that how they format everything matters a lot. When they put a figure right next to the paragraph talking about it, it really helps you follow along, especially with complicated arguments. Tables do something different—they cram a bunch of information into one place so you can check facts quickly. The Velorum paper puts all its spectroscopic measurements in a single table (Filippenko et al. 1999), which we found helpful when we were trying to understand how they calculated the black hole mass. 


Conclusion:
In this genre analysis, we examined five astronomy articles published between 1999 and 2025 to understand how rhetorical strategies and different structure and format have evolved over time. We found a pattern where discipline is moving from rigid, methodological reporting to more fluid, thematic structures. This shift suggests that with modern times the writing style has also changed. The rhetorical choices we observed are highly effective for this community. By combining the objectivity of  passive voice in methods with careful claims in the discussions, the authors have successfully built credibility without overstating their findings.

	The analysis is important because it proves that the scientific writing is not static, it changes based on the tools and evidence available. For us the main benefit of this work is realizing that to write effectively in astronomy as well as any other scientific topic is more than just following a template, it depends on the small details of rhetorical devices, different ways of supporting our claims and many more. However, there are limitations to our analysis, Since we only looked at the 5 papers on a specific topic and genre, there might be more variations and nuances that we might have missed and can be learnt through different papers. Despite this, analyzing this gives us a clearer roadmap for how to communicate with this specific audience and understand the basics of writing a scientific paper.

Mini Lessons: The Difference Between a Bibliography and an Essay: A bibliography is a list of sources used for research, whereas an essay is a structured argument that uses those sources to prove a point. Think of the bibliography as the 'ingredients list' and the essay as the 'finished meal.' To satisfy the rubric, you must provide the analysis (the meal), not just the list of sources.

Consistency in Citation Styles: Academic writing requires a single, consistent citation style (like APA, MLA, or Chicago). Switching between 'First Name Last Name' and 'Last Name, First Initial' within the same document is confusing for readers. Choose one style and apply it to every entry to maintain professional standards and credibility (ethos).

Cleaning Digital Links: When citing online journals, always use the DOI (Digital Object Identifier) or a stable URL. Avoid copying links directly from your browser if you are logged into a university library, as these 'proxy' links (containing 'ezproxy') will not work for people outside your institution. A clean link ensures your evidence is verifiable by any reader.

Mini Lessons: The 'CARS' Model (Create a Research Space): This paper correctly identifies how scientific introductions move from a broad context to a specific gap and then to a proposed solution. Understanding this 'funnel' structure is essential for effective academic writing.

Rhetorical Function of Passive Voice: While often discouraged in creative writing, the passive voice in scientific 'Methods' sections serves a specific rhetorical purpose: it emphasizes the replicability of the experiment and the objectivity of the process by removing the subjective 'human' element.

Ethos in Modern Science: Credibility in contemporary research is increasingly built through 'distributed ethos'—the collaboration of multiple institutions and the use of shared, high-prestige facilities (like ALMA or TESS), rather than relying solely on the reputation of a single author.

Name: Prem Bhatia and William Li 
Introduction
It is not an understatement to say that humanity has looked to the sky and stars in wonder for millennia before the current day. This can be seen in our mythologies which describe the constellations and scribe tales of how they came to be; such as the constellations ursa major and orion. It is only in recent history that humanity has had the ability to observe the universe much more closely with the invention of the telescope and our relatively new technology allowing us to send probes into space for deeper study. Astronomy, the study of anything outside earth’s atmosphere, was born from our fascination with space. The selection articles chosen return to the base of astronomy and focus on the analysis of observations of celestial phenomena. By analyzing 5 unique astronomical articles published between 1999 to 2025, this paper argues that as astronomical observation has shifted from raw data to more imagining data, moreover it has also evolved from using rigid IMRAD structure to hybridized, thematic narratives that blend with the Aristotle's three modes to guide reader through the paper. This paper moves from analyzing rhetorical situations and moves to how different organization techniques have evolved with the time.


Rhetorical situation
Selected articles are primarily focused on analyzing the data and observations made of astronomical objects and the primary audience of these scientific articles are most likely written for fellow astronomers as the language they use: filled with unexplained acronyms such as ALMA (Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array) or TESS, referring to the instruments used for the observations and analysis along with being published by astronomy and astrophysics based journals which is unlikely to attract the attention of those not in their field. A secondary audience for these papers are the undergraduate/graduate students pursuing their subjects involving astronomy. They would have to read these articles for their research work and to develop their knowledge across these subjects. The intended audience is most likely aware of basic astronomy concepts such as binary systems and their different classifications. 
Given that the intended audience of this paper, it is most likely composed of fellow peers of the authors who are interested in the details of astronomical objects such as their weight, behavior and classification. The primary purpose of these articles is to formally record observational data and persuade the academic community of the authors’ interpretations of the specific claim. The earlier Nova Velorum paper (1999/2001) has two authors from UC Berkeley, a relatively compact team using a single telescope. The four more recent papers all feature large international author lists: Ménard et al. draw from France, the Netherlands, and Chile; Dholakia et al. involve TESS, CHEOPS, MINERVA-Australis, SPECULOOS, and Purple Mountain Observatory as named collaborating facilities. This shows a shift in the field that modern astrophysics papers require multi-institutional, multi-instrument collaborations to draw conclusions for deep research papers, and more institutions signal more robustly validated data. Different papers prove their claim through different approaches, some support it with numerical raw data while others support it with visual images, more details on this as we move on.
Rhetorical strategies: ethos, pathos, logos: 
As scientific articles the most obvious rhetorical strategy used would be their appeal to Logos, logic and reasoning. These papers establish their arguments using the observations made using scientific tools and hard numbers obtained using different frameworks.  This can be observed in the figures 1 and 2 in Ménard et al. in Ongoing Flyby in the Young Multiple System UX Tauri, which present multi-wavelength disk images alongside hydrodynamical simulations, it allows us to compare predicted and observed disk morphology, this move alone carries the logical argument that an unbound stellar flyby best explains the asymmetric disk structure. Similarly in the paper Filippenko & Chornock in A Black Hole in the X-Ray Nova Velorum 1993 derive a mass function of M₁ ≥ 3.9 M☉ from spectroscopic radial velocity measurements, a numerical data supporting the main argument of the paper. Hence we can see how these different approaches for establishing logos within paper support the argument and build up the paper.
The Ethos or credibility of these articles is established from their status as peer reviewed works which indicates their accuracy and validity. The credentials of the authors of the papers build more credibility for these papers, contributors like Stéphane Guilloteau, listed among the authors of the UX Tauri paper, hold institutional affiliations at major research laboratories and They also published numerous papers which adds more reliability. But this also differs around different papers, such as the Nova Velorum paper, authored by only two researchers at UC Berkeley, relies almost entirely on the prestige of their Keck Observatory spectroscopy and the reputation of the journal while the recent papers are supported by collective ethos through large, multi-institutional author lists: Ménard et al. draw collaborators from France, the Netherlands, and Chile, while Dholakia et al. involve five separate observing facilities across three continents. This shift shows the evolution of how astrophysics papers build reliability.
The Pathos is by far the most difficult to spot in these scientific articles as it is the least prominent strategy used by the authors. Emotion is one of the things that is often absent from scientific research; The closest thing to an appeal to Pathos or emotion comes in the form of their article titles which could grab the volume reader’s attention towards the actual article however the delivery of information within is often to the point leaving those with no deep interest in the subject lacking in response to the content. 

Macro-organization of the research articles
After looking at these five papers, it reveals that the structures of these papers evolve with the time. Since they were published between 1999 and 2025. The oldest one, the Velorum paper from 1999 (Filippenko et al. 1999), sticks to the methodological approach while the new papers follow the thematic approach, in addition to that newer papers all follow IMRAD structure but not strictly, with a bit of nuances, For example, the UX Tauri (Ménard et al. 2020) and AB Aurigae (Boccaletti et al. 2020) papers use "Introduction," "Observations," "Analysis," and "Discussion/Conclusion" instead. The Gliese 12 b paper (Dholakia et al. 2024) is even more different—it uses headings like "Planetary system overview" and "Atmospheric characterization" 
This modern labeling of types rather than its scientific significance allows an expert reader to navigate directly to the data they need. Although this format is more convenient, the clever move from Ménard et al. (2020) paper, they use "Observations and Results" as their title for second section, which is a thematic turn forcing more active reading, rather than skipping to the results, the reader have to engage with the argumentative logic threaded through the section. This format is further followed by one of the latest papers about the protoplanetary disk (Speedie et al. 2024) where the sections blend results with interpretation, like "Evidence of spirals winding with time." With the similar approach as Ménard et al. (2020) article.

It can also be noticed that the location of the main argument varies from paper to paper. In the majority of papers it's in the Discussion or Conclusion, which follow IMRaD convention of presenting the data before presenting interpretation. Ménard et al. (2020) follows this clearly, the key question of whether UX Tau C is a bound companion or an unbound flyby is only addressed as a titled subsection within Section 4 (Discussion), so the reader knows where description ends and judgment begins. The Velorum paper (Filippenko & Chornock 1999), however, makes its argument throughout the Results and "Mass of the Compact Primary" sections instead. So the claim and evidence are mixed together more, which made it harder for me to separate them. This pattern suggests that argument placement is not random but it follows the nature of evidence.

Evidence:

The types of evidence used in these papers depend on the question they're trying to answer. The observational papers, Velorum (Filippenko et al. 1999) and Gliese 12 b (Dholakia et al. 2024), use a variety of different types of physics data, including tables and some calculations. The disk structure papers (UX Tauri, AB Aurigae, and the protoplanetary disk one) are totally different because they're grounded around images (Ménard et al. 2020; Boccaletti et al. 2020; Speedie et al. 2024). They have interesting pictures from ALMA and other telescopes showing spiral structures, gaps, and weird asymmetries in the disks. The presence of these images is not to enhance the look of the paper, instead they're actually the main evidence for the whole argument. Like the AB Aurigae paper's main argument about planet formation comes from this "twist" they spotted in the disk images (Boccaletti et al. 2020). The newest paper does something really unique, where they compare images from different years to show that the spirals are actually moving over time (Speedie et al. 2024). It helps them argue that gravitational instability is happening and to successfully support their claim . Making the argument more clear for us to understand and develop Ethos.

All of these papers use theoretical models, but in different amounts. Approximately Velorum paper is 70% actual data and 30% compared to models (Filippenko et al. 1999), while the disk papers are closer to half and half. The disk papers need simulations to help explain what images are describing and its connection to the argument, which makes sense as it is not obvious for a reader to look at a spiral and immediately know what's causing it.

Micro-organization and language/style features of the research articles
Examining these papers at micro level reveals some patterns in how sections are written and organized. All Five Introductions follow the same moves: start with the big picture (Give context),Identify a gap in current knowledge, and provide their proposition to fill the gap. Boccaletti et al. (2020) demonstrate this clearly, opening with the general problem of planet formation before narrowing to why AB Aurigae is an ideal case study. This structure is replicated across all five papers. The introductions are more written in a professional tone, such that it fulfills all the genre’s requirements, using language like “this suggests” and “may indicate” rather than assertive tone.
The Methods and Observations section are more uniform across the chosen articles. They use a lot of passive voice, like "Data was obtained using..." or "The images were reduced following standard procedures." It is an artistic choice that grounds the process over the individual, projecting objectivity by removing the human agent from the methodology section. As we evolve the depth of methodological reporting expands significantly. The Velorum paper explains its spectroscopic analysis briefly in three sentences (Filippenko et al. 1999), but Gliese 12 b has entire subsections breaking down different techniques allocated to that topic (Dholakia et al. 2024).
The Results and Discussion sections show the greatest variation from paper to paper and exhibits how each author is trying to persuade their readers. Results sections consistently use precise language with numbers and error bars, like "we measure a mass of 3.2 ± 0.3 solar masses" (Filippenko et al. 1999). They present things in a logical order, usually starting with what they actually saw and then moving to what they calculated from that. The Discussion sections portray more about the author's voices. This is where they interpret what everything means, make guesses about what's going on, and draw connections to other research. The language shifts from "we observed" to "this suggests" or "one possible explanation is." The disk papers (Ménard et al. (2020), Boccaletti et al. (2020), and Speedie et al. (2025)) make particularly unique use of this section by enumerating competing hypotheses (gravitational instability, stellar companion perturbation, planet formation) before ruling out alternatives and stating their claim. This structure models scientific reasoning for the reader rather than simply delivering a verdict, which helps the reader to think rather than just absorb the information.


It is observable that the format of everything plays a crucial role. Placing a figure next to the connecting paragraph helps the reader follow along, especially with complicated arguments. Tables do something different, they cram a bunch of information into one place so the reader can check facts quickly. The Velorum paper puts all its spectroscopic measurements in a single table (Filippenko et al. 1999), which can be found helpful when the reader is trying to understand how the mass of black hole is calculated. 

Conclusion:
This genre analysis examined five astronomy articles published between 1999 and 2025 to understand how rhetorical strategies and different structure and format have evolved over time. A clear pattern emerged where discipline is moving from rigid, methodological reporting to more fluid, thematic structures. This shift suggests that with modern times the writing style has also changed. The rhetorical choices observed across these papers prove highly effective for their intended discourse community: by combining the objectivity of  passive voice in methods sections with careful claims in the discussions, the authors have successfully built credibility without overstating their findings.

	This analysis also demonstrates that scientific writing is not static, it changes based on the tools and evidence available. For students in university the main benefit of this work is realizing that to write effectively in astronomy as well as any other scientific topic is more than just following a template, it depends on the small details of rhetorical devices, different ways of supporting the claims and many more. However, there are limitations to the analysis, Since this analysis is only on the 5 papers and on a specific topic and genre, there might be more variations and nuances that might have been missed and can be learnt through different papers. Despite this, analyzing these papers provides a clearer roadmap to how to communicate with this specific audience and understand the basics of writing a scientific paper.
