Mini Lessons: The IKEA Effect in Writing: This concept explains why writers become emotionally attached to their work. Because they have invested significant 'labor' into a sentence or paragraph, they perceive it as having higher value than an outside reader would, leading to resistance during the editing phase.

Revision Self-Efficacy: Successful revision is not just about 'fixing' errors; it is tied to a writer's belief in their ability to improve a text. Using objective tools like rubrics and checklists can move a writer from 'gut-feeling' editing to strategic, effective revision.

Shared vs. Split Ownership: In collaborative writing, 'split ownership' (where each person writes a separate section) often leads to a disjointed final product and defensive behavior. 'Shared ownership' (where all members review and touch all parts of the paper) results in higher quality and more cohesive arguments.
data.essay_text:
1
Self-Editing Bias in Group Projects
Tiyana Freer
Faculty of Kinesiology, Sport, and Recreation, University of Alberta
WRS 101: Exploring Writing
Professor Dan Harvey
March 29, 2026
2
Self-Editing Bias in Group Projects
Imagine you put three hours into what you think is the perfect paragraph, the transitions
are smooth and every claim is airtight. Then you watch a group mate (attack) it with a ton of
redlined comments and section changes while defending their own writing. The group dynamic
is suddenly tense, there are suggestions all over, and that was supposed to be constructive, but is
now a battle of whose wording will remain. Why does this happen? Why do we hold every word
we have crafted dear but mercilessly criticize everyone else’s writing. This universal writing
experience has a name, it is self-editing bias, and it turns group projects into unexpected fields of
battle, where emotions scuffle with reader expectations. This reflective essay explores these
blind spots that make us overvalue our own work; It draws on peer reviewed research to explore
the strategies that transform defensive writers into group reviewers who prioritize clear writing
over ego.
When it comes to writing anything whether that be an essay or an article, there is a point
where you must edit the work that has been done. This can be as you work through paragraphs or
this can be at the end right before the final draft is turned in. No matter how you go about this it
is, in theory, faster and easier when you can do most of that editing yourself. For many, however,
this is extremely difficult because people cannot look at their writing as a reader and not the
writer. Lingard (Lingard, 2026) explains that readers are predictable, they expect main topics
early in the paper and look for new information in stress positions at the end of the sentence.
When these patterns are ignored, even if the idea is clear, the paper gets confusing. This
especially comes into play when in a group project that requires writing, in many group projects
the biggest issue is often not the topic, but each person’s refusal of changing their writing. This
3
can get very confusing; people will protect their paragraphs instead of focussing on what is best
for the project.
In a previous group project, a disagreement occurred, the disagreement was over how the
sentences and paragraphs would be written in the final draft. Each person was to write about a
specific type of organizational tool, and in the end, a person would go over it to make it sound
cohesive. The person, however, who decided to go over the paper, chose to rewrite the
introduction entirely and tried to rewrite most of another person’s section. The reviewer rejected
all the suggestions for their work, even though it would have improved grammar and
understandability. The correspondence shifted from a professional tone to something else, instead
of trying to figure out the best version for the reader. The suggestions turned into passive
aggressive comments, after suggestions for a new section, and blatantly aggressive comments,
after a small number of corrections, signalling frustration. The suggestions and gradually sharper
language show how quickly editing can lead to conflict (Guillaume Deffuant et al., 2024).
This dynamic, some sections improving with feedback, while others did not, illustrates
the self evaluation process. There is research that shows writers often overrate their drafts and
become less responsive to feedback. My sections became clearer with its words and sentences,
while the other stayed the same, though there were words that could have been removed and
grammar that could be better. A study by Dr. Valentina Sangeetha (Sangeetha, 2020) found ESL
students who were taught self-editing checklists, rather than gut instincts, improved their editing
drastically. Without these tools, revisions often do not feel like paper improvements but rather
(personal attacks).
This difference helped my understanding of the blind spots within my writing. The
reviewer and some classmates flagged issues with confusing sentencing, and I fixed these issues
4
before the final draft was due. The flaws for the reviewer, on the other hand, remained
unchanged because rewriting would have felt like admitting the original second draft was flawed.
Chen (Chen et al., 2021) explains this with revision self-efficacy, when there are no strategies
like planning and evaluating, writers doubt their ability to strengthen their papers. An experiment
reveals self graders scored 20 to 30% higher than other judges, bias being higher when identity
threat is present. There is the question of, “how will this be read” that contrasts with, “won’t they
understand my point.” These thoughts revealed mindset determines whether feedback ruins or
helps with collaboration.
Thinking back, had we consulted the rubric more, there would have been less
disagreements. The rubric, given by teachers, aids students in keeping the elements that increase
or decrease the end grade in mind. Cer (Cer, 2019) approves this metacognitive approach,
teaching students these elements produce significant writing improvements across the genres. We
debated the introduction with two rewrites from each person and had we paid attention to the
rubric, the elements that were needed would have become increasingly clear. The external
(authority) that the rubric (has) would have stopped the ego deadlock sooner than the due date
did.
There has been a study (Li & Zhang, 2021) that shows EFL students using goals, and
both instructor and peer feedback make more changes. Peer input tended to drive 2.5 times more
revision than just instructor feedback improving grammar and the paper overall. During this
project, I developed some personal self-editing techniques in order to create a better reader
experience. One of these techniques was reading aloud, it exposed flaws, such as confusing
phrases and wording that sounded bias. This technique also aided in my grammar and run-on
5
sentences, which leads me to another technique. I discovered that leaving your draft for an entire
day helps you forget what you wrote, therefore it aids you in reading your work objectively.
Though there were a good number of advances to the paper, there remained subtle forms
of biases. There were sentences that I favoured and hesitated to change, after some research I
discovered this is called the “IKEA effect.” This effect refers to one's tendency to value things
more when there is personal labour involved in its creation (Ioannidis et al., 2014). Research
reveals expert researchers often pay attention to information that supports their hypothesis or
existing beliefs, overlooking evidence that contradicts them. In other words, complete objectivity
does not exist, however, when you start using strategies for this exact purpose, the gap becomes
significantly smaller.
While research has proven that some of my instincts were correct, it has also widened my
perspective. I had emotional attachment to lots of my section, which led to a conflict, but I also
underestimated its rational factors. It has been revealed that self-editing is not a personal
weakness, but rather something predictable that requires strategies; those being rubrics, training,
and rest periods, among others. Strategy development proves to be teachable, that disproves my
earlier idea that editing objectively develops with experience (Karpen, 2017).
I believe this group experience has reshaped my future collaborations, because of the
initial view, towards group writing, was that of it being divided. For future projects I plan to
ensure everyone works together and that everyone writes, critiques, formats, and polishes the
paper. Folks who share all parts consistently outperform solo writers, in overall revision and final
quality. Split ownership – everyone doing one section – creates conflict, while shared
responsibility breeds excellence (Cer, 2019).
6
Overall, the group project proved to me that self-editing is about more than just fixing
grammar or creating sentences that sound better. Self-editing is also about learning to step back
and coming to terms with the fact that other people may find problems that I cannot see. At the
same time, I learned that groups work best when all members are willing to revise with the mind
of the reader rather than protecting each sentence as if it belongs only to them. The experience of
this project made me more cognitive of my own writing habits; it showed me that strong writing
comes from being able to adapt with the changes. In the future, I will try to focus more on
improving the paper as a whole and not focusing on defending my own writing.
7

Instead of just saying 'gaming helped me,' explain how the literacy practices in gaming (like reading complex wikis or collaborating in chats) might translate to academic writing skills.

Sentence Integrity: Avoid 'run-on' thoughts and 'fragments' by ensuring every sentence has a clear subject and verb. In reflective writing, there is a tendency to write as one speaks, which often leads to grammatical slips that undermine the author's authority.

data.essay_text:
The Impact of video games in the transition between high school and
Post-Secondary
The transition from high school to university has been the most turbulent step in my life.
This feeling of turbulence can be explained by a number of factors. One of which is my previous
experiences with transitions to high forms of education have been extremely underwhelming.
From the transition of elementary school to junior high and high school I had been told of the
difficulties the next stage entailed. Difficulties I had found to be grossly exaggerated. There had
certainly been increases in both freedom and struggle but never to the point of genuine shock I
had experienced during my first year attending post-secondary education. The trouble I found
myself in came not just from the difficulty jump but the freedom or more accurately the lack of
structure university had compared to high school and the changes in my social life. Sundqvist et
al. (2024) had found many individuals experienced feelings of loneliness and stress stemming
from increased academic demand and changes to their social networks. This aligned with my
experiences as I had relied on the structure of high school and my proximity to my friends for
social interaction. I found myself far more isolated as my schedule no longer aligned with my
friend’s schedules in a way that prevented me from reaching them physically.
Past views on video games were always focused on the potentially negative effects of
them, often neglecting the positive effects experienced by players (Granic et al., 2014). Video
games were one of the most crucial tools that had assisted me during this period. They acted as a
stress reliever that helped me relax after periods of intense study and work maintaining my
mental health, they acted as a connecting point for me and my friends to continue to interact and
help maintain my physical health. In this essay I will focus on four areas in which video games
have impacted my life. How they have positively impacted my physical, mental, and social
health and how they have negatively impacted my physical, mental, and social health.
Social help of gaming
A stereotype of them was that they were socially inept or that they lacked social skills
and connections. This view had always puzzled me because I viewed gaming as a deeply social
hobby. One that allowed me to maintain connections with friends even after our schedules no
longer aligned. I wasn’t the only one with an idea as Herodotou et al. (2014) aimed to correct this
misconception in their study finding that individuals that play games consistently had extensive
social networks and continued to play games partly due to those connections. This aligned with
my experiences with games. Whether it was action rpg games such as Warframe or games with
single player options like Minecraft, I found myself connecting with others through sharing
experiences with the game or helping each other obtain items.
Mental help of gaming
Mental health has been a major issue for young adults and especially university students.
Both international and domestic students face higher rates of depression, anxiety, and insomnia
as they go further in the year (King et al., 2023). These issues can result in academic decline only
further stressing students leading to a spiral downward at its worst. Therefore it is important to
curb stress.
For me video games have helped relieve stress and serve as a moment of peace during
periods of high academic demand such as midterms, finals, and important projects. Many game
genres have been proven to reduce stress even when not played for extended periods of time
(Pallavicini et al., 2021). This was especially important as usually free time wasn’t very abundant
during periods where I experienced high stress. They allowed me to reduce my stress quickly so
that I could continue to work.
Physical Help of gaming
With games like Dance Dance Revolution and Just Dance notable popularity, a growing
interest in the genre of video game academically known as exergames, have become the topic of
research in their potential academic and health benefits (Staiano et al., 2011). Exergames usually
use a system of incremental rewards which give them the ability to retain interest in them and
continue (Eisenberger et al,. 2009). This has allowed me who is often avoidant of physical
activity to maintain my physical health even in periods where I would never think to exercise.
Negative aspects of gaming
As with many things, video gaming can be a double edged sword. Halbrook et al. (2019)
discussed how moderation was key to success with handling the use of video games and I wasn’t
always the physical incarnation of balance, often I wasn't.
As discussed by Eisenberger et al.(2024) a system of incremental rewards can increase
interest in topics that would usually not attract it; An incremental reward system is present in
almost all games I play. This can cause me to spend excessive time procrastinating on work,this
assignment being late, rather than spending time on more important topics creating undue stress.
With the combination of schoolwork and the majority of my video games not needing
much movement besides wrist based activities I tend to negatively impact my health with
excessive sitting (Dunstan et al 2012).
In the same vein as what I have previously, my excessive video gaming could hurt my
social life causing me to not respond to my friends especially with the combination of video
games and university work taking up my time. This is a sentiment shared by many as found by
(Alshehri et al., 2025) in which they found that video gaming had negatively impacted their
social lives.
Conclusion
In conclusion, video games, which have been in my life for the vast majority, have
impacted my transition to post-secondary education socially, physically, and mentally in complex
ways both good and bad. This is mostly due to my own fault stemming from my lack of self
control in properly moderating my usage of video games however as with many things in life I
cannot say if they have been more positive or negative, only that they have had a great impact on
my transition.

Collaborative Learning in Group Writing: Benefits, Challenges, and What I Learned
Violet Chen












Collaborative learning is very common in group writing, especially in writing courses. Many teachers require students to complete group writing tasks because they believe students can learn from each other. In WRS 101, I also worked on several group writing assignments, which required us to share ideas and divide work cooperatively, and integrate all content into a final text. At first, I thought group cooperation was always helpful. However, after these experiences, I realized that collaborative writing was much more complex than I expected. Some parts of it supported my learning, but other parts made me feel stressed. Based on my experience and research, I believe that collaborative writing can help students learn, but only when the group operates effectively and when teachers provide sufficient guidance framework.

Collaborative writing has an important benefit. It can help students to learn from each other. Learning is not only an individual process; it also happens through interaction (Bruffee, 1999; Vygotsky, 1978). When students are working together, they can see different ways of thinking and writing. In my group, some students are better at organizing ideas, while others are stronger in academic language. By observing how they wrote, I learned a lot of new methods to improve my own work. For example, in one assignment, a group member suggested changing order of our ideas. This made the paragraph clearer, and the small change made a big difference. It also helped me to understand how to better structure my own writing in the future.

Research also shows that collaborative writing can improve writing process as well as final outcomes. Storch (2005) explains that when students work together, they can more easily notice errors and give feedback to each other, which I also experienced in the group. Sometimes, other students would point out unclear sentences or weak points in my writing. At first, I felt a bit uncomfortable, but later I realized that this feedback helped me improve. It made me more aware of my writing choices and encouraged me to revise more carefully. This supports the view that collaboration can make students become more careful and thoughtful writers.

Collaborative writing has another benefit, which is that it can improve critical thinking. During in group discussions, students need to explain their ideas and respond to others. This process forces them to think more carefully, with Johnson and Johnson (2009) and Slavin (2014) suggesting that group work can increase engagement and help students understand topics more deeply. In my experience, I often have to explain why I would choose certain specific idea or example, and sometimes my group members disagree with my viewpoint. This makes me to rethink my position. These moments help me view topics from different angles and improve my thinking ability.

However, my experience also shows that collaborative writing has obvious problems, and one of the biggest problems is unequal contribution. In theory, each person should complete their own part, but in reality, this does not always happen. Li and Zhu (2017) found that this problem is very common in group writing tasks, which I directly experienced. In one project, a group member did not complete their work on time. As a result, the rest of us had to quickly complete it. We were no longer improving our ideas, but only trying to finish the assignment before the deadline. This made the experience stressful but not very meaningful.

This experience made me question the view that collaborative writing is always helpful. In fact, when group work is unbalanced or unequal, it may reduce learning rather than improve it. McDonough et al. (2018) also pointed out that although collaborative writing can improve final outcome, not all students can benefit equally. In my case, when I actively participated in discussion, I learned more. In comparison, when I had to undertake additional work because of the little contribution of other people, I focused more on completing task rather than learning. It indicates that group writing does not always support individual learning.

Another challenge is communication, as work of group relies on clear communication, but this can be difficult. Students have different schedules and different working styles, which Dillenbourg (1999) explains that collaboration requires structure and shared understanding. In my group, communication was sometimes slow or unclear. Some people didn’t reply to messages quickly, and sometimes we were not sure about our plans. This made our process less efficient and also more frustrating. It also shows that collaboration does not happen automatically just because students are assigned to a group.

After reading research and thinking about my experiences, I now understand collaborative writing in a different way. In contrast, previously, I thought problem mainly lay with members of group. If someone did not complete their work, I viewed it as a personal problem. However, now I think problem is also related to way task is designed, as research shows that successful collaboration requires clear roles, shared responsibility, and guidance (Storch, 2013; Johnson & Johnson, 2009). It means that teachers play an important role, and students possibly don’t know how to collaborate effectively if there are no clear instructions or expectations.

This idea changed the way I viewed my own experience. It was not only about “good” or “bad” group members. It was also about course setup and whether it provided enough structure or not. For example, if the instructor set clear deadlines for each part, or checked the group’s progress, collaboration might proceed better. Without this support, students might struggle, even if they wanted to do well. This indicates that collaborative writing should not only be assigned, but also be carefully planned and supported.

Overall, I believe collaborative writing is both helpful and challenging. It can improve learning by allowing students to share ideas, give feedback, and think more deeply. At the same time, if participation is unequal or communication is poor, it may create stress. This means collaborative writing is not always effective, with its success depending on students and instructors. Thus, students need to participate actively and communicate clearly, while instructors need to provide structure and guidance.

In short, my experience in WRS 101 helped me understand collaborative writing in a more realistic way. It can be a valuable method, but only under suitable conditions. Research and my personal experience both show that group writing works best when there is equal participation, clear communication, and strong support from the instructor. However, without these conditions, collaborative writing may be quite stressful and ineffective. Therefore, collaborative writing is not automatically effective. It works well only when both students and instructors actively work together to support the process.













Reference List

Dillenbourg, P. (1999). What do you mean by collaborative learning? In P. Dillenbourg (Ed.), Collaborative-learning: Cognitive and computational approaches (pp. 1–19). Oxford: Elsevier

Understanding Why Students Struggle
with Academic Writing
Introduction
Academic writing is one of the most challenging parts of university life for many students. It is
not just about grammar or vocabulary, but also about understanding what the assignment is
asking, how to organize ideas, and how to approach the writing process. From my experience
and from what research shows, many students feel confused when starting assignments
because expectations are not always clearly explained. This can make writing stressful and
frustrating instead of a useful learning experience. Studies suggest that these difficulties come
from several factors, including unclear expectations, lack of planning strategies, limited
feedback, and even writing anxiety. Therefore, this paper argues that students struggle with
academic writing because they lack clear guidance, effective writing strategies, and supportive
learning environments, but these challenges can be improved through better instruction,
feedback, and active learning approaches (Starkowski, 2022; Teng et al., 2022).
Hidden Expectations in Academic Writing
One of the biggest reasons students struggle with writing assignments is that university writing
often comes with hidden expectations. These are things that instructors expect students to
know, but do not always clearly explain. For example, students are often told to “analyze,”
“critically evaluate,” or “develop an argument,” but they are rarely shown what these actually
look like in a real paper. Because of this, many students feel lost at the very beginning of an
assignment. Starkowski (2022) explains that first-year and underprepared students especially
struggle because they are not familiar with how academic writing works in university. What
makes this even more difficult is that professors may assume students already understand how
to break down a question, use sources properly, or structure their ideas in an academic way. In
reality, many students are still trying to figure these things out. This creates a situation where
students might spend hours working on an assignment but still miss the main expectation. So,
the issue is not always that students are not trying hard enough—it is that the “rules of
academic writing are not always clearly visible to them. When expectations remain hidden,
confusion becomes almost unavoidable.
Lack of Metacognitive Writing Strategies
Another important reason students struggle is that many of them do not yet have strong
metacognitive writing strategies. Metacognition basically means understanding how you learn
and being able to control your thinking process while working on a task. In writing, this includes
planning what you want to say, checking if your ideas make sense, organizing your arguments,
and reviewing your work carefully. However, many students jump straight intp writing without
doing much planning or reflection. Teng, Qin, and Wang (2022) show that students who use
strategies like planning, monitoring, and evaluating their writing tend to perform much better.
These students are able to stay on track and make improvements as they go. On the other
hand, students who do not use these strategies often end up with disorganized or unclear
writing. This idea is also suppoted by Wingate and Harper (2021), who found that stronger
students spend more time planning and reviewing their work, while weaker students focus
mainly on writing quickly without much direction. This shows that writing is not just about putting
words on paper—it is about thinking through the process step by step. Without that awareness,
even a capable student can struggle to produce a strong piece of writing.
Impact of Assignment Design and Prompts
The way assignments are designed also plays a big role in how students perform. Sometimes,
the problem is not the student, but the way the assignment is written. If a prompt is too vague,
too broad, or uses unclear language, students may not fully understand what they are supposed
to do. Liu and Stapleton (2018) explain that different types of prompts can lead to very different
writing outcomes. Some prompts guide students toward clear, structured answers while others
encourage deeper thinking but may be harder to interpret. This means that even before
students start writing, they may already be unsure about what is expected from them. For
example, a question that seems simple at first might actually require analysis, comparison, and
evaluation all at once. If students do not recognize this, they might respond in a basic way and
lose marks. In many cases, students spend more time trying to understand the assignment than
actually working on their ideas. This shows that writing difficulties are not only about writing
skills—they are also about understanding the task itself. When assignment instructions are not
clear enough, they can create unnecessary confusion and make the writing process much
harder than it needs to be.
Role of Feedback and Interaction
Feedback plays a very important role in helping students improve their writing. Writing is not
something that improves in one attempt; it requires revision and reflection. Paulus (1999) found
that feedback from teachers and peers helps students make deeper changes in their writing,
especially in terms of meaning and organization. Without feedback, students often focus only on
grammar instead of improving their ideas. In addition, Kaufhold (2025) explains that discussion
around writing, such as in writing groups, helps students understand academic expectations
better. When students talk about their writing with others, they can see different perspectives
and learn how to improve. This shows that writing is not only an individual activity but also a
social process.
Influence of Learning Environment and Practice
The learning environment also affects how students develop their writing skills. Traditional
classroom settings may not provide enough time for practice and feedback. Wihastyanang et al.
(2014) found that using online learning systems can improve writing because students can
practice more and receive feedback outside the classroom. This supports the idea that writing
needs time and repeated practice. Similarly, Hill, Khoo, and Hsieh (2020) show that writing skills
learned in one course can transfer to other subjects, which means that effective writing
instruction has long-term benefits. When students are given more opportunities to practice and
apply their skills, they are more likely to improve.
Writing Anxiety and Student Confidence
Another factor that affects writing is anxiety. Many students feel nervous or stressed when they
have to write, especially if they are not confident in their skills. Rohmah and Muslim (2021)
found that writing anxiety is linked to lower writing performance. Students who are afraid of
making mistakes or receiving negative feedback may avoid writing or rely on simple ideas. This
creates a cycle where lack of confidence leads to weaker writing, which then increases anxiety.
This shows that writing challenges are not only academic but also emotional.
Conclusion
In conclusion, students struggle with academic writing for several reasons, including hidden
expectations, lack of metacognitive strategies, unclear assignment design, limited feedback,
and writing anxiety. These factors make writing more difficult than it needs to be and can
negatively affect student performance. However, research shows that these challenges can be
improved when students receive clearer instructions, better feedback, and more opportunities to
practice and interact with others. Academic writing should not be seen as a skill that students
either have or do not have. Instead, it is something that can be learned and developed overr
time with the right support. By making expectations clearer and helping students understand the
writing process, universities can make writing a more manageable and meaningful part of
learning..

data.essay_text:
The confusion regarding nutrition information
It should not be this hard to figure out what to eat. Yet in my first year of university, the more I tried to
learn about nutrition, the more confused I became. One article blamed dietary fat, another warned about
refined carbohydrates, and social media only made things worse. A fitness influencer would confidently
promote cutting out entire food groups, while a registered dietitian would argue that doing so was
unnecessary or even harmful. What made it more frustrating was that all of these sources seemed credible.
They cited studies, experts, and statistics, yet their advice rarely matched.
At first, I assumed the problem was my own misunderstanding. However, the more I paid attention, the
more I realized this confusion was not random. It came from how nutrition information is produced,
simplified, and shared, especially online. Rather than reflecting unreliable science, much of the inconsistency
comes from how research is communicated to the public. Recognizing this does not eliminate the confusion
completely, but it does make it easier to understand why it exists.
The Complexity of Nutrition Research
One of the main reasons nutrition information appears inconsistent is because the research itself is difficult
to conduct and interpret. Unlike controlled laboratory experiments, nutrition studies involve real human
behavior over long periods of time. People eat combinations of foods, not just nutrients, and their habits are
influenced by factors such as stress, sleep, culture, and lifestyle. Because of this, research findings often come
with important conditions and limitations. However, when these findings are simplified for a broader
audience, those details are often removed. What remains is a more certain sounding conclusion than the
research actually supports. Nagler (2014) found that repeated exposure to conflicting nutrition messages can
reduce trust in health information, even when the differences reflect normal scientific progress.
Looking back, this explains my own reaction when I learned that recommendations about dietary fat had
changed over time. Instead of seeing it as an improvement in scientific understanding, I interpreted it as
evidence that no one really knew what they were talking about. This kind of response is common and can
lead people to move away from nutrition information altogether, rather than learning how to interpret it
more carefully.
How Information Gets Distorted
Another major factor contributing to confusion is how research is communicated beyond academic settings.
Studies rarely reach the public in their original form. Instead, they pass through several stages, including
press releases, news articles, and social media posts. At each stage, there is potential for exaggeration or
simplification.
Sumner et al. (2016) found that exaggeration in health related news often begins at the press release stage,
before journalists even report on the findings. As a result, small associations can be presented as strong
conclusions, and preliminary findings can appear more definitive than they actually are. By the time this
information reaches headlines, important details such as sample size, limitations, and context are often
missing.
Diekman and Manore (2023) describe this as a persistent issue in nutrition communication, where
misinformation becomes embedded in everyday decision making because it is presented in a way that
appears scientifically credible. This helps explain why conflicting advice is so common. It is not necessarily
that the research contradicts itself, but that the way it is presented exaggerates differences and removes
simplicity.
The Role of Social Media and Relatability
While traditional media contributes to the problem, social media intensifies it. Much of the conflicting
advice I encountered came from platforms like Instagram and TikTok, where content is designed to be brief
and engaging. In these formats, there is little room for explanation or qualification.
Mchiza et al. (2023) found that inaccurate nutrition information is particularly common on social media and
is difficult for audiences to recognize as inaccurate. This is partly because the content is often delivered with
confidence. Lissens et al. (2025) further showed that people are more likely to accept nutrition advice from
creators who seem relatable, regardless of their qualifications.
Regarding my own experience, I can see how this played out. Content created by individuals who appeared
similar to me felt more trustworthy than information from formal health organizations, even when that was
the more evidence based one. This suggests that credibility on social media is often shaped more by
relatability and presentation than by expertise.
Competing Dietary Narratives
Another source of confusion is the presence of multiple dietary approaches that are all presented as
effective. Diets such as low fat, low carbohydrate, plant based, and intermittent fasting are often promoted
as the best solution, even though they are based on different principles.
Freeman (2016) argues that when these approaches are presented as competing “answers,” the result is
confusion rather than informed choice. From my perspective, this created a sense of analysis paralysis. Each
approach seemed to have credible evidence behind it, yet they led to different outcomes about what people
should eat.
Vrinten et al. (2023) describes nutrition literacy as the ability to evaluate information critically, not just
access it. Their research suggests that many young adults lack this skill, even though they are frequently
exposed to nutritional content. This gap between exposure and evaluation helps explain why having more
information does not necessarily lead to better understanding.
Learning to Interpret Information Differently
What helped reduce this confusion for me was shifting my focus from quick summaries to the research itself.
Instead of relying on headlines or shortform content, I began looking at how studies were conducted and
what their findings actually meant.
For example, Johnston et al. (2014) compared several popular diets and found that differences in outcomes
were relatively small. What mattered more than the specific diet was whether individuals could maintain it
over time. This finding contrasts with how diets are often presented online, where each approach is
presented as uniquely effective.
This shift in perspective changed how I interpreted nutrition information. Rather than seeing conflicting
advice as evidence of unreliable science, I started to view it as a result of how information is communicated.
Schwitzer (2008) highlights that health journalism often fails to report the quality of evidence behind claims,
which reinforces this issue.
I became more aware that confidence in a claim does not reflect the strength of the evidence behind it. This
realization made it easier to approach nutrition information with a more critical mindset.
Conclusion
The confusion surrounding nutrition advice is real, but it is largely driven by communication rather than
scientific instability. Research in nutrition is complex, and when it is simplified, exaggerated, or presented
without context, it can appear contradictory. Social media further amplifies this problem by prioritizing
engagement and relatability over accuracy.
At the same time, this experience shows that understanding nutrition requires more than just access to
information. It requires the ability to evaluate sources, interpret evidence, and recognize how information is
being presented. Before university, I did not have these skills, which made the volume of information feel
overwhelming.
Once I began to approach nutrition information more critically, the confusion became more manageable.
The core recommendations remained relatively consistent, while the surrounding noise became easier to
identify. This shift did not eliminate uncertainty, but it changed how I responded to it, making it possible to
engage with nutrition information in a more informed and confident way.

Contents
1. Tiyana Freer — Self-Editing Bias in Group Projects
2. The Confusion Regarding Nutrition Information (no author)

Essay 1 — Tiyana Freer: Self-Editing Bias in Group Projects
1. Revision placeholders left in the final draft
You write "you watch a group mate (attack) it with a ton of redlined comments" and later "revisions
often do not feel like paper improvements but rather (personal attacks)". In both cases the word in
parentheses is the word you actually mean — just write it without the brackets. As it stands a reader
pauses and wonders if those parentheses are doing something intentional, which they are not.
Rubric: Writing quality and proofreading
2. Citation redundancy and a date error on the Lingard source
On page 2 you write "Lingard (Lingard, 2026) explains that readers are predictable" — the author's
name appears twice, which is not APA style. More importantly the in-text citation says 2026 but the
reference list shows 2022, and a 2026 publication date is impossible for a paper submitted in March
2026. Correct both the in-text citation and the reference entry to the actual publication year.
Rubric: APA documentation
3. The Ioannidis source does not support the IKEA effect claim
You cite Ioannidis et al. (2014) to support the idea that people overvalue things they have built, but
that paper is about publication bias in cognitive sciences — it does not discuss the IKEA effect. The
IKEA effect comes from Norton, Mochon, and Ariely (2012), which is the source that actually
supports your claim. Using a source that says something different from your claim is a research
integration problem the rubric directly targets.
Rubric: Research integration
4. 'Works Cited' heading used with APA formatting
Your reference page is titled "Works Cited", which is MLA terminology, but all your in-text citations
and reference entries follow APA style. This inconsistency signals that the final format was not fully
checked before submission. Rename the page "References" to match the APA style you are using
throughout.
Rubric: APA documentation
5. Wrong word in the conclusion
The last paragraph reads "The experience of this project made me more cognitive of my own
writing habits." The word you want is cognizant (meaning aware), not cognitive (which describes
mental processes in general). Reading your draft aloud — the exact strategy you recommend in the
essay — would catch this immediately.
Rubric: Writing quality
Essay 2 — The Confusion Regarding Nutrition Information (no author
listed)
1. No title page or author identification
This essay has no title page — there is no student name, faculty, course section, or date visible
anywhere in the document. APA format requires a title page, and without one a reader has no way
to know who submitted the work. Add a proper title page before submitting the final version.
Rubric: APA formatting
2. Personal reflection is too thin for the genre
The reflective moments here are mostly one-liners like "Looking back, this explains my own
reaction when I learned that recommendations about dietary fat had changed over time." That is an
entry point into a reflection, not the reflection itself — what did you actually do, eat, avoid, or stop
trusting? The rubric asks for genuine personal insight tied to specific moments, and right now the
research is doing all the work while the personal voice barely appears.
Rubric: Personal reflection
3. The thesis is an observation, not an argument
The closest thing to a thesis reads "Recognizing this does not eliminate the confusion completely,
but it does make it easier to understand why it exists." That is a reasonable takeaway but it does
not make a claim someone could disagree with. A stronger thesis would name the specific
mechanism driving the confusion and argue something about it, the way Diekman and Manore
(2023) do when they argue that misinformation embeds itself through its scientifically credible
presentation.
Rubric: Thesis clarity
4. The bold section headers impose a research-paper structure
Organizing the essay around sub-topics like "The Complexity of Nutrition Research" and
"Competing Dietary Narratives" gives it the feel of a literature review rather than a reflective essay.
The personal voice ends up feeling inserted into a research scaffold rather than driving it. Try
organizing the sections around how your thinking evolved, not around categories of the topic.
Rubric: Organization and genre
5. Johnston et al. reference links to a third-party site
The Johnston et al. (2014) entry lists a URL pointing to practitioner.macklinmethod.com rather than
the journal or a DOI. APA 7 requires you to link to the primary source, and using a third-party host
raises questions about whether the original article was actually accessed. Find and use the direct
DOI from the JAMA publication.
Rubric: APA documentation
Essay 3 — Understanding Why Students Struggle with Academic
Writing (Rehman)
1. Personal experience almost entirely absent
The introduction promises "From my experience and from what research shows, many students feel
confused" but after that sentence the writer almost completely disappears from the essay. There is
no specific memory, no concrete moment of confusion or struggle, no scene the reader can picture.
The rubric expects personal experience to drive the essay, not just appear as a disclaimer in the
first sentence.
Rubric: Personal reflection
2. Reference list has category headers that do not belong
The reference list is broken up with bold headers like "Metacognition Paper" and "Peer & Teacher
Feedback (VERY IMPORTANT)" — these are working-bibliography notes, not part of a formatted
reference list. In APA format the reference page is a single alphabetically ordered list with no labels,
numbers, or category headings. Clean up the reference section so it follows standard APA
formatting.
Rubric: APA documentation
3. Typos suggest the draft was not proofread
In the body you write "many students jump straight intp writing" and "This idea is also suppoted by
Wingate and Harper (2021)", and the conclusion has "developed overr time." Three typos in a
submitted draft suggest minimal proofreading; running spellcheck would fix all three in seconds.
Rubric: Writing quality
4. The strongest claim appears only in the conclusion
The conclusion states "Academic writing should not be seen as a skill that students either have or
do not have." That is actually the most interesting idea in the essay, but it appears for the first time
at the very end with no development. If that is the argument, it should be the thesis — move it to the
introduction and build the whole essay around it.
Rubric: Thesis and organization
5. Sources are cited but not explained or engaged with
Each body paragraph follows the same pattern: name a problem, drop a citation, move on. For
example, "Liu and Stapleton (2018) explain that different types of prompts can lead to very different
writing outcomes" — but what types? What outcomes? The rubric expects you to explain what the
source actually found, not just use it as a stamp of authority.
Rubric: Research integration
Essay 4 — The Impact of Video Games in the Transition to
Post-Secondary (no author listed)
1. No author or title page
There is no title page listing the student's name, faculty, course section, or date. APA format
requires this, and without it the reader has no way to identify who submitted the work.
Rubric: APA formatting
2. Introduction takes too long to reach the actual topic
The first paragraph spends four sentences on previous school transitions before university is
mentioned, and video games only appear in the second paragraph. The reader needs to know
within the first two sentences what the essay is about. Consider opening directly with the university
transition and the role games played in it.
Rubric: Organization and introduction
3. Pronoun reference problem in the social section
The social section opens with "A stereotype of them was that they were socially inept or that they
lacked social skills" — "them" and "they" have no clear antecedent in the preceding paragraph. The
reader has to guess that you mean gamers, which should never be something a reader has to
guess. Name the group directly in the first sentence of the section.
Rubric: Writing clarity
4. Eisenberger citation date does not match the reference list
In the negative aspects section you cite Eisenberger et al. (2024), but the reference list shows the
same authors with the year 2009 — the dates cannot both be right, and a reader who tries to locate
the source will fail. Also, the 2009 entry lists only two authors, so APA 7 requires you to list both
names rather than using 'et al.'
Rubric: APA documentation
5. The conclusion avoids making a claim
The essay ends with "I cannot say if they have been more positive or negative, only that they have
had a great impact on my transition." The body sections actually do build a case — social
connection, stress relief, physical activity — so refusing to conclude feels like a missed opportunity
rather than genuine nuance. What would you do differently, or what did this experience teach you
about moderation?
Rubric: Argumentative closure
Essay 5 — Violet Chen: Collaborative Learning in Group Writing
1. Vygotsky in-text citation does not match the reference list
You cite "Vygotsky, 1978" in the text as a primary source, but the reference list entry reads
"Yengoyan. (1980). L.S. Vygotsky: Mind in Society... Language in Society, 9, 249" — that is a
review article written by Yengoyan, not the original Vygotsky text. If you read Yengoyan's review,
cite that; if you read the original, fix the reference entry to list Vygotsky as the author.
Rubric: APA documentation and source integrity
2. Personal reflection goes generic in the middle sections
The most effective moment in the essay is "a group member suggested changing order of our
ideas. This made the paragraph clearer" — that is specific and memorable. But then you often
revert to observations like "some students are better at organizing ideas, while others are stronger
in academic language", which could describe any group anywhere. The rubric values moments that
only you could have written, so push the specific details further.
Rubric: Personal reflection
3. Several sentences have grammatical errors that break the flow
"This makes me to rethink my position" should be "makes me rethink" — "makes" does not take an
infinitive with "to" here. And "In contrast, previously, I thought problem mainly lay with members of
group" is missing two articles ("the problem," "the members of the group") and the opening phrase
creates an awkward pause. Reading the essay aloud would catch both of these.
Rubric: Writing quality
4. The conclusion restates the introduction without adding new insight
The final two paragraphs essentially repeat the thesis: collaborative writing needs equal
participation, clear communication, and instructor support. The most interesting moment of genuine
growth — the realization that the problem is "also related to way task is designed" — appears
buried in the body and never gets the emphasis it deserves. Bring that insight forward into the
conclusion; that is where your thinking actually changed.
Rubric: Organization and conclusion
5. McDonough et al. is cited without explaining what the study found
You use McDonough et al. (2018) to note that "not all students can benefit equally" from
collaborative writing, but you never say what the study found about why. Was it unequal
participation, task design, proficiency differences? Without that detail the citation functions as a
vague authority nod rather than actual evidence — explain what the study shows before using it to
support your point.
Rubric: Research integration
Peer feedback — WRS 101 Module 2, April 2026

Mini Lessons: The 'Grade Shock' Concept: This paper effectively uses the term 'grade shock' to anchor the research. In academic writing, adopting or defining a specific phenomenon helps create a cohesive narrative throughout the report.

Transitioning from Research to KT: A Knowledge Translation (KT) document should not just repeat the essay; it should adapt the tone for a specific audience. While this script does that, it must be accompanied by visual elements (as per the rubric) to effectively 'translate' knowledge to a non-specialist audience.

Punctuation for Lists: Remember that a colon (:) is used to introduce a list, while a semicolon (;) is used to connect two independent clauses. Using a semicolon to introduce 'inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity' is a common grammatical error.
data.essay_text:
How ADHD Plays a Role in the Highschool–Post-Secondary Transition
Alex Patrickson and Olivia Beaver-Whyte
WRS 101 SEM X50 - Winter 2026 - EXPLORING WRITING
Dan Harvey
Introduction
Studies have shown that on average, grades drop 10% in the first year of post-secondary
education (Kljajic et al., 2023; Gaudreau et al., 2023; Mayers et al., 2017; Badal et al., 2025).
This is because the transition from high school to university can be taxing on many students for
several different reasons, however this transition is especially taxing on students diagnosed with
ADHD. This research report will focus on the common issues students face when transitioning
from high school to post-secondary, and how students with ADHD experience the struggles of
this transition to a greater extent.
Issues When Transitioning From Highschool to Post-Secondary
Many students who enter post-secondary programs from high school face the challenge
of their grades decreasing during their first year. According to Badal (2025), 90% of students
will notice their grades decrease during their first year of university. Further research shows that
grades drop 10% in the first year of post-secondary compared to the last year of high school
(Kljajic et al., 2023; Gaudreau et al., 2023; Mayers et al., 2017; Badal et al., 2025). Gaudreau
(2023) calls this phenomenon of a decreasing GPA during the transition from high-school to
post-secondary a “grade shock”. Many studies have been conducted as to why grade shock
happens, as it seems to be a primary reason affecting student’s mental health.
Students who experience grade shock can often fall into a positive feedback loop of poor
academic performance, causing psychological distress. Kljajic (2023) proposed that
procrastination was the main cause of a decrease in student's GPAs. Another study by Gaudreau
(2023) found that students higher on their proposed perfectionism scale were more likely to
experience a greater decrease in their grades, and subsequently, negative effects on their mental
health. Badal (2025) discovered that symptoms alone of anxiety or depression can negatively
influence a student's GPA. Achieving a high GPA is becoming increasingly more important for
students in today's world, so this grade shock not only affects students academically, but
psychologically (Gaudreau et al., 2023). With the findings from Badal (2025)–that anxiety and
depression are significantly correlated with a decrease in GPA–and the findings from Kljajic
(2023)–that voluntary procrastination is correlated to cause anxiety and depression–it is easy to
see how susceptible first year students are to grade shock. All of the added stress to succeed can
affect not only the learning experience of students, but also their self-concept (Gaudreau et al.,
2023). If a student holds themselves to a high standard or has higher levels of perfectionism
(Gaudreau et al., 2023), receiving a lower grade can lead to depression as the student thinks less
of themselves. This depression then feeds the positive feedback loop of poor academic
performance, and therefore a lower self-concept, and so on until the student is crushed by the
weight of their stress and the situation. These negative mental health symptoms become
amplified due to the fear of academic failure, but they begin from the drastic change in lifestyle
students face.
Factors of ADHD Contributing to the Struggle
For most students, the transition from high school to post-secondary is stressful, but for
students with ADHD, it can be unbearable. ADHD is primarily characterized by 3 symptoms;
inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity (Henning et al., 2022; Howard et al., 2016; LaCount et
al., 2018; Mayo Clinic, 2023). Since hyperactivity and impulsivity decrease with age (Mayo
Clinic, 2023), studies found that inattention seems to be the main symptomology that makes the
transition especially difficult. (Henning et al., 2022; Howard et al., 2016). Since starting out with
low attention makes it more likely to continue throughout their academic career, they are more
likely to become discouraged at their inability to learn, leading to higher drop-out rates (Henning
et al., 2023; LaCount et al., 2018). It's not only about how inattention impacts their ability to
learn, it is also about how their inattention results in poor planning, organization, and time
management skills (Centre for ADHD Awareness, Canada, n.d.).
Academically, adolescents are used to having most everything planned or specifically laid
out for them. Within the first few weeks of post-secondary, the workload increases significantly,
and how you manage it is completely in your hands. Being coordinated and organized is
considered essential, but for students with ADHD, staying organized is especially difficult
(LaCount et al., 2018; Mayo Clinic, 2023). In individuals with ADHD, the cognitive abilities that
allow us to be co-ordinated are impaired, resulting in executive dysfunction (Southon, 2022).
Executive dysfunction affects time management and organization, as well as working memory
and focus. The abrupt shift to this unstructured environment intensifies these issues and can lead
to chronic procrastination, grade shock, and ultimately academic failure (Southon, 2022;
Gaudreau et al., 2023). The feeling of failure from and poor planning and inattention is also
likely to trigger more stress and panic in the student (Centre for ADHD Awareness, Canada,
n.d.).
For students with ADHD, it can be difficult to navigate new lifestyle changes, thus
making students more likely to become overwhelmed. ADHD students are at substantial risk of
stress and anxiety as the new lifestyle brings with it unique challenges. They face executive
dysfunction and emotional dysregulation, making test taking and studying considerably more
daunting (Prevatt et al., 2015). Other disorders like anxiety and depression are often associated
with ADHD and make students with ADHD more likely to experience mood swings, which can
worsen when frustrations in academia arise (Mayo Clinic, 2023). Though the odds are stacked
against students with ADHD, there are resources meant specifically to overcome these struggles.
Common Solutions for Post-Secondary Students with ADHD
For students with ADHD, the transition begins 1-2 years prior to the first day of
post-secondary. This gives time for the student to learn their learning strengths and weaknesses,
develop necessary adult skills like budgeting and cooking, and familiarize themselves with
schools and programs they’re applying to (Centre for ADHD Awareness, Canada, n.d.). The
increased time given for planning and preparing helps relieve the overwhelming stress and
uncertainty they’re likely to face when taking that first step. In order to effectively transition,
students have to consider what they are giving up.
Students entering post-secondary should anticipate changes like losing their ADHD
support. By meeting with counselors and the special needs department–or even developing peer
groups by joining clubs–the student can set up a new network for themselves (Centre for ADHD
Awareness, Canada, n.d.). Students with increased home, teacher, and peer support show
significantly greater positive academic engagement and decreased inattention than those without
support (Chen et al., 2023), so developing this foundation early on is key. Not only do students
have to develop new networks, they must cope with the loss of structure they have been given by
their parents.
For adolescents with ADHD, going from a very structured home life provided by your
parents to a non-structured life can be daunting (Howard et al., 2016). Throughout the transition,
students should keep multiple organizational tools at hand like physical and digital calendars,
note taking apps, study groups and tutors, and even self care routines to avoid the academic
stress so many ADHD peers face (Roncon, 2023). Setting up a structured environment decreases
students’ risk of missed classes, the potential for procrastination, and the feeling of being
overwhelmed (Centre for ADHD Awareness, Canada, n.d.). As discussed, this transition from
structured to non-structured can result in grade shock, a phenomenon that has proved to be
difficult to combat
Studies show that students going through this transition in isolation are more likely to
experience grade shock. Mayers (2017) found that students who engage in campus life or
recreation feel less negative mental health impacts due to grade shock. Experiencing campus life
and recreation, such as joining clubs, utilizing campus resources, and other social aspects,
improves retention rates. Students who participate in campus life are more efficient at balancing
the academic and social aspects of post-secondary programs, and are more likely to do better
academically (Mayers et al., 2017). Support systems for both non-ADHD and ADHD students
are considered to be significantly important, proving that students should refrain from isolation.
Conclusions
All new post-secondary students face challenges adapting to the new lifestyle school
brings, it’s inevitable. Though difficult, what the typical student faces during this transition is
nowhere near as mentally tasking as it is for individuals with ADHD. A considerable amount of
work–like maintaining multiple calendars, planning out every step of the process, transferring
over healthcare plans–must be taken on just to keep up in academia.
Knowledge Translation Script
(Will be an interview-style video, asking students around campus to answer the following
questions. Hopefully asking specifically ADHD students, starting briefly discussing their
experience in transitioning from high school to post-secondary. Plus free candy!!!)
General introduction questions
Q: Are you a student with ADHD or that struggles with inattention and poor organization?
Q: What year and program are you in?
Q: What if I told you that many students, 90% even, go through hard times during their first year,
so you're not the only one. What do you think are the three biggest factors that make the
transition from high school to post-secondary so difficult?
A: losing structure and social aspects, increasing workload and time demands, new lifestyle
Q: What struggles did you face in your first year?
Questions specific to our research
Q: Among some of these struggles during the transition from high-school to post-secondary is
grade shock. Grade shock is the decrease in grades that students face in their first year. By what
percent do you think they decrease, and what do you think leads to this grade shock?
A: They decrease by 10%
A: Procrastination, that's a very popular one, very common, I've done it a lot myself. But this
procrastination can actually cause a lot of stress as deadlines approach, and this stress can lead to
anxiety and depression. Studies show that even just showing symptoms of these mental disorders
can lead to a drop in your GPA. Perfectionism also leads to grade shock because if you receive a
bad grade as a perfectionist or if you hold yourself to too high of a standard, then the bad grade
could make you feel less of yourself which could lead to anxiety or depression and that feeds
right back into the same cycle from before.
Q: So as we said, students in their first year experience loss of structure, increasing workloads,
and new lifestyle changes. How do you think these struggles differ for students with ADHD?
A: Students with ADHD go through the same thing, but significantly amplified. Stress and
emotional dysregulation are considerably higher, so failing in one aspect for them can destroy
their mental health. It is more difficult for them to adjust, and developing a support system is
incredibly important.
Q: How much more likely do you think students with ADHD are to drop out than their
non-ADHD counterparts?
A: According to the Children and Adults with ADHD centre, only 15% of students with ADHD
complete their 4 year degrees compared to the 48%. They also have 25% lower average GPAs.
Solutions
Q: Research has shown that some effective strategies to avoid these struggles include; preparing
1-2 years prior, developing peer groups and other forms of support (like counseling, tutoring etc),
and keeping multiple organizational tools at hand. Do you agree? What is your experience
dealing with inattention and such, and what advice would you give to your ADHD peers?
Q: Do you think that going out and participating in and experiencing campus life and recreation
helps or hinders your GPA?
A: It helps. It's a delicate balance between the academic and the social parts of post-secondary
but taking a step back and going out to socialize can actually improve retention rates in the brain.
This is anywhere from joining one of the campus clubs to using the campus gym. Exercise and
socialization are very beneficial to the body and the brain and essential to having a support
system if you're struggling.

Mini Lessons: **The 'Which' Trap (Sentence Fragments):** A sentence fragment occurs when a group of words is punctuated as a sentence but lacks an independent clause. In this essay, several sentences start with 'Which' or 'Particularly'. These are usually dependent clauses that belong to the previous sentence. Think of a dependent clause like a sidecar on a motorcycle; it can't go anywhere on its own! To fix this, simply replace the period before the 'Which' with a comma and change the 'W' to lowercase.

**Balancing the Personal and the Academic:** In many university writing courses, personal reflection is encouraged. However, in a formal research-based essay, the 'I' voice can sometimes weaken your authority. Imagine you are a lawyer presenting a case: you wouldn't just say 'I feel the defendant is guilty'; you would say 'The evidence suggests the defendant is guilty.' Try to frame your personal experiences as examples of the broader trends found in your research. Instead of 'I find it hard to focus,' try 'Consistent with the findings of Kolhar et al. (2021), many students—including myself—experience significant difficulty focusing on non-digital tasks.'

**Subject-Verb Agreement with Compound Subjects:** When you have two or more subjects joined by 'and', you almost always need a plural verb. In the phrase 'Brain fog and fatigue has become,' the subjects are 'fog' and 'fatigue.' Since there are two things, the verb must be 'have.' An easy way to check this is to replace the subjects with the pronoun 'They.' You wouldn't say 'They has become'; you would say 'They have become.' Always double-check your 'and' phrases to ensure the verb matches the plural nature of the subject.
data.essay_text:
The Negative Impacts of Social Media
Leanne Cote
WRS 101: Exploring Writing, Winter Semester
March 29th, 2026
Professor Dan Harvey
Social media has become extremely popular over the past few decades. It can be accessed
almost anywhere in the world and by almost anyone of any age. Development of social media
began in the 1970s and 1980s and proceeded to really take off in the 1990s and early 2000s and
has now evolved into what we know today, with apps like Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.
These platforms were initially formed to be able to communicate with others and create
communities over great distances. It is a great place to stay connected with friends and family,
however, this constant accessible stream of information can become overstimulating and
addicting, particularly for young minds. Social media negatively impacts academic performance,
as well as the health and wellness of university students.
Scrolling on social media has become a daily activity for me and often becomes
problematic. I say I’m just going to scroll for a few minutes and before I know it, hours have
passed and I’ve done nothing productive for my academic work or in my personal life. Which is
exactly what social media apps are designed to do (Yousef et al., 2025). The continual scrolling
is what they want to promote so they purposefully capture our interest with weird, funny or
interesting information. Yousef et al. (2025) also explained that this addictive cycle is stimulated
by the hormone dopamine which provides a rush sensation when scrolling through videos which
increases the desire to scroll to a greater extent. This process makes it challenging to discontinue
the usage of these apps which makes it easy to maintain these overindulgent habits. This
feedback loop specifically targets younger people and 90% of those who are between the ages of
18 and 29 engage in these platforms which is much higher compared to any other age group (Cai
et al., 2026; Yousef et al., 2025).
In my experience with doomscrolling, I find that it escalates my procrastination even
worse. I always leave things until the last minute because I find it hard to just sit down and do
the work when I could be engaging with people online or watching funny videos instead of using
my brain power to perform the tasks I need to. In a study done on Thai university students, a
relationship was found between internet addiction and school related procrastination (Nadarajan
et al., 2023). Students would rather go online and thereby put-off their academic work. The
authors also explained that those who procrastinate are more likely to have worse self control,
time management and negative repetitive thought patterns. According to Nadarajan et al. (2023)
these are all said to reflect internet addiction characteristics. Since students tend to use the
internet excessively, addiction and procrastination problems can arise at the same time. This
uncontrolled use of social media and the internet can be due to the fact students want to escape
reality. It is so much easier for me to ignore all the responsibilities I have to do when I’m
1
distracted with social media. Then because I haven’t started the work, everything always seems
so intimidating and overwhelming that I don’t want to start and would rather resort to something
that takes less effort, like scrolling.
A study also showed that those who have increased time on social media, have worse
performance in their academic programs (Kolhar et al., 2021). This hasn’t necessarily been the
case for me. Social media hasn’t had a great impact on my overall grades but I can recall a few
assignments that I could’ve done better if I had put the effort in. Kolhar et al. (2021) reported
that over 50% of students said they were addicted to social media and that it has severely
impacted their ability to learn. The authors also expressed that many students were more
interested in social media than their studies. This statement is particularly relatable for me. Brain
fog and fatigue has become more apparent in my daily life over the past few years, making it
difficult for me to want to learn and understand the materials in my classes. My memory and
learning skills don’t feel as strong as they used to be. This could be affected because the constant
usage of social media can cause sensory overload which impacts these skills (Kolhar et al.,
2021). When the brain is constantly receiving new information, it can cause chronic fatigue
because it is just trying to understand and process all of it (Yousef et al., 2025). Additionally,
memory tends to worsen because the manner in which the brain retrieves information is
interrupted with too much use of social media and mindless scrolling.
There are lots of times when trying to study or work on assignments, I feel the need to go
back on my phone because the tasks I am doing are often too boring for my brain, which is
habituated to overstimulation. Due to the immense satisfaction I get from scrolling, caused by the
dopamine reward system in my brain as described by Yousef et al. (2025), I crave to engage with
these platforms. Even though I am cognizant that this problem decreases my concentration and
mental clarity, thereby decreasing my productivity and intellectual abilities, I still continue
regardless which has become normal for many students (Yousef et al., 2025). This causes
unnecessary delay on my assignments when I could have finished them much earlier if I had put
my full effort and undivided attention into them which leads to higher stress on my part.
Particularly, when this affects all of my other assignments and the studying I need to do. In
addition, I find it hard to focus in class and on topics that don’t immediately capture my
attention. Many youth are more likely to struggle with focusing on their tasks or chores, and in
one study, more females had increased trouble concentrating than males across multiple age
groups (Schimmele et al., 2021). Also, it was shown that 19.6% of Canadian post-secondary
students were overwhelmed with all their responsibilities (Nowrouzi-Kia et al., 2021). These
feelings are common with the over-consumption of social media. I also lack the motivation to do
the smallest chores such as making my bed or emptying the dishwasher due to being
overwhelmed and tired. These symptoms also fall hand in hand with depression.
Mental health issues like depression and anxiety are greatly associated with the utilization
of social media (Kolhar et al., 2021). Depression is not something I struggle with but I find when
I excessively use social media, I get many depression symptoms. Putting aside schoolwork
2
makes me even more stressed and anxious. When I don’t perform as well because of these habits,
I feel more disappointed in myself, knowing I could do better. There is an intent of doing better
but the measures are never fully taken to succeed due to the lack of self-discipline (Anwar et al.,
2022). Anwar et al. (2022) states that this causes problems in the future because of wanting to be
carefree and content in the present, which is what happens with procrastinators. These issues
exacerbate the feelings of anxiousness and sadness when it is time to face the consequences.
When I do have free time from school and work, I feel that I’m never fully rested because
all I do is scroll in my free time. My body may be resting but my brain is receiving non-stop
information. Yousef et al. (2025) says that because of this sensory overload, it can lead to
unhappiness and misery, particularly when we receive this narrative about how our lives are
supposed to be. Since I only scroll in my freetime, I don’t feel the will to do anything. I lose my
creativity and motivation for my hobbies. The term that designates using social media just to
detach from the real world and to scroll without a goal or intention is zombie scrolling (Yousef et
al., 2025). This mind numbing use of social media and the internet increases fatigue and a sense
of emotional disengagement from life.
Additionally, I fall asleep later at night because I stay up late on my phone to text or
watch reels which impacts my mood, my attention, focus and performance at school. Gong et al.
(2025) state that educational burnout and conditions that involve trouble sleeping are commonly
linked with scrolling on social media instead of going to sleep. The authors also discuss that this
further decreases student’s energy levels and incentive to work, thereby resulting in worse
academic involvement and marks. Kolhar et al. (2021) explains that hyperarousal happens while
scrolling through social media before going to bed, which causes more difficulty when trying to
fall asleep. It is also said that a person becomes more irritable and has less mental acuity when
lacking sleep. Their study showed that 39-45% of students used social media late into the night
and therefore slept less than the recommended amount (Kolhar et al., 2021). The lack of sleep
and rest also has a big impact on my physical wellbeing.
Since I procrastinate on my schoolwork and personal tasks, I end up putting aside
important things like taking care of my body. Working out and proper nutrition sometimes fall to
the back burner because of this behaviour. According to Kolhar et al. (2021), there is a higher
chance of the onset of a chronic disease like hypertension, diabetes and obesity due to an inactive
lifestyle when all free time is spent on social media. Most adults go above the recommended 2
hours of leisure screen time a day and don’t follow the Canadian movement recommendations
(Weatherson et al., 2021). A large portion of adults are sedentary and I find myself falling into
that category, particularly during the school year. This causes a serious danger because it has
been shown that every hour increase in inactive, stationary time can cause a higher mortality rate
(Kolhar et al., 2021). However, because frequent social media users prioritize short-term joy
instead of long term accomplishments, sedentary people lack the motivation to make a change
(Anwar et al., 2022).
3
Social media causes many unfavourable effects for university students such as
substandard academic performance along with decreased mental and physical health.
Procrastination and getting stuck in dopamine fueled cycles with social media platforms can
reduce motivation and multiple other cognitive functions that students need to succeed. In
addition to that, uncontrolled usage of social media can worsen mental health challenges,
decrease the amount and quality of sleep as well as the amount of physical activity.
The implications of this increased popularity in social media means that students are
sacrificing their overall wellbeing for temporary relief which can have huge effects on their long
term health and their work ethic in their future profession. It is difficult to escape this never
ending loop, but action must be taken to strengthen intellectual capabilities so that students don’t
become mindless, mentally drained individuals.
4
References
