criteria.name: Appropriate Structure
criteria.feedback: The essay connects study and experience effectively and includes the required 8 sources. However, it fails the length requirement (approx. 950 words vs. the 1200-1500 required). It also misses a direct address to writing scholars or curriculum developers, focusing more on general psychology than writing pedagogy.

criteria.name: Course Strategies and Execution
criteria.feedback: The topic is highly focused and specific. You identified three clear aspects: habit architecture, passion types, and the aMCC. Sources are integrated seamlessly into the narrative, and APA documentation is largely correct.

criteria.name: Compelling Structure and Organization
criteria.feedback: The organization is a major strength. The introduction is engaging, the research question is clear, and the conclusion effectively synthesizes the reflective process. Paragraphs flow logically with strong transitions.

criteria.name: Clarity, Conciseness, and Writing Quality
criteria.feedback: The prose is active and compelling. However, there are significant technical issues with spacing (e.g., 'HarderthanI’veeverfought') throughout the text which hinder readability. There is also a typo in the university name ('Alebrta').

criteria.name: Peer Comments Integration
criteria.feedback: There is no explicit evidence or mention of how peer comments were incorporated into this draft. This is a neutral score based on the lack of provided data for this specific rubric item.

suggestions: Expand the essay by at least 250 words to meet the minimum length requirement. Focus this expansion on the 'writing' aspect of the prompt.
Explicitly address writing scholars or curriculum developers by discussing how these neurological concepts could change how writing is taught in universities.
Perform a thorough proofreading pass to fix the pervasive spacing errors and the typo in the header ('University of Alebrta').
Ensure all mentioned studies, such as the 'Fortune/Michigan study,' are included in the final References list with full APA details.

Mini Lessons: Meeting Word Count through Audience Expansion: When an essay is short, the best way to expand is to look at your 'Audience' requirement. The rubric asks you to write for writing scholars and curriculum developers. You can add 300 words by discussing how a writing teacher might use the 'aMCC' research to help students who are struggling with writer's block or failure. By applying your neuroscience research to the specific field of writing education, you satisfy the audience requirement and the length requirement simultaneously.

The Importance of Visual Polish: In professional and academic writing, formatting is as important as content. The spacing issues in your text (words running together) act like 'noise' that distracts the reader from your 'signal' (your ideas). Think of it like a radio station with static; even if the music is great, people will turn it off if the static is too loud. Always do a final 'Print Preview' or read your work aloud to catch these technical glitches before submission.

Synthesizing Research and Reflection: You do an excellent job of 'braiding' your personal story with scientific facts. This is called synthesis. A good way to push this even further is to use the research to 're-interpret' your past. Instead of just saying 'I felt bad,' you said 'My aMCC was underdeveloped.' This transition from emotional language to analytical language is exactly what professors look for in high-level reflective writing.

What the Grade Didn’t Teach Me
Prem
University of Alberta
April 2026
So I fight. Harder than I’ve ever fought for anything academic. I pull apart every requirement, follow every step, leave nothing to chance. For once, I feel like I’ve actually done everything right, and I mean everything. I let myself believe it might actually work.
Then I open my results.
The grade stares back at me: a flat-out fail. Not a near-miss, not a “you almost had it”, just a number that doesn’t move no matter how long I sit there. I close the laptop. Open it again. Still there. That heavy, hollow silence where your brain hasn’t caught up to what your eyes are reading.
I’d put everything I had into that paper. Everything.
The assignment was a reflective essay for a first-year writing course — a genre I had never seriously attempted, in a class I had underestimated from week one. I spent more time on it than anything else that semester. I pulled apart the rubric, addressed every requirement, revised more than I normally would. The confidence I felt submitting it wasn’t arrogance. It was the specific, quiet certainty of someone who genuinely believes they finally figured something out.
But here’s the thing — this isn’t really a story about a grade. It’s about the specific shock of realizing that effort and correctness are not the same thing. That working hard and working right are not interchangeable. Most of us, in school, in work, in the quiet private goals we tell almost no one, have been confusing the two for years without ever noticing. The question I couldn’t stop asking after that failure wasn’t what went wrong. It was: why did my brain let me believe I had already figured it out?
Part 1: The Brain’s Hidden Limits
The answer, I’ve come to understand, begins in the brain — and not in the way we’re usually taught. Every behavior we repeat enough times gets quietly promoted by the basal ganglia, the brain’s efficiency system, which converts repeated actions into automatic habits that require no conscious effort (Balleine & O’Doherty, 2010). This isn’t weakness. It’s optimization. But it means that what we call the “comfort zone” is not a character flaw — it’s a neurological default, the brain’s way of conserving energy by staying with what’s already mapped.
The limits go further than habit. Tim Noakes’ Central Governor Model proposes that the brain applies a conservative cap on both physical and mental output — not because we’re genuinely exhausted, but because it is protecting a biological reserve it calculates it might need later (Noakes, 2011). The wall we hit mid-workout, mid-essay, mid-difficult-conversation — that’s not a true limit. It’s a neurological estimate of where “safe” ends. When I think back to that paper — the one I failed — I had hit that estimate without ever knowing it existed. I thought I’d reached my limit. I’d actually reached my brain’s first guess.
What’s significant for students and writers specifically is that this governor doesn’t distinguish between a 10K run and a difficult draft. Cognitive load research confirms that the brain treats sustained effortful thinking as a resource-depleting task (Kahneman, 2011), which means the same protective withdrawal that stops a runner at kilometre eight can stop a writer at paragraph three. The experience of “hitting a wall” in a writing assignment is not a sign of insufficient effort. It is the governor deciding it has done enough.
Part 2: Running on the Wrong Kind of Passion
Biology is only half the problem. The other half is direction — and most of us have never been fully honest about it.
A 2023 survey by Deloitte found that 86% of Gen Z respondents identified purpose as central to their work, yet most reported remaining in environments that provided none of it (Deloitte, 2023). A Pew Research Center study on job satisfaction found that roughly half of U.S. workers described themselves as not highly satisfied with their current roles — not because they lacked skills, but because the work didn’t connect to anything they actually cared about (Pew Research Center, 2023). These are not career statistics. They are direction statistics — the fingerprint of people who know, vaguely, what they want and still haven’t moved toward it.
Psychologist Robert Vallerand (2008) offers one explanation for why this gap persists. Through decades of research, he identified two structurally different kinds of passion. Harmonious passion is self-determined: it grows from genuine identity, and it predicts resilience, wellbeing, and sustained engagement over time. Obsessive passion, by contrast, is pressure-driven — it comes from what looks impressive, what is expected, or what we have decided we should want. The discomfort of working right, as opposed to just working hard, often reveals which kind of passion you’re actually running on. Obsessive passion can generate enormous short-term effort; it rarely generates the kind of flexible problem-solving that improves under pressure. I didn’t know which kind I had. I just knew the one I had wasn’t working.
Part 3: What Resistance Actually Builds
After the failure, I had no choice but to move — not out of discipline, but out of desperation. I went to my teacher. I sat with concepts I didn’t understand and asked questions that made me feel like someone who didn’t know the basics. That shame was real. I put it aside and focused on the goal. Eight hours a day, sometimes more — not because I was motivated, but because I had run out of excuses to stop.
What was happening neurologically during those weeks is something I can now name. The anterior midcingulate cortex (aMCC) is a brain region that activates specifically during tasks we find aversive or effortful. It does not fire during comfort. It fires during resistance. Critically, it grows denser with repeated activation — each instance of pushing through unwanted difficulty is literally building the architecture of persistence (Parvizi et al., 2013; Touroutoglou et al., 2020). Studies show this region is measurably larger in elite athletes and in individuals with longer lifespans; it is measurably smaller in those who chronically avoid discomfort. But it is not fixed. It responds to use.
David Goggins describes this as “callousing the mind.” Neuroscientists call it aMCC hypertrophy (Touroutoglou et al., 2020). Both are describing the same process: the brain rewiring itself not despite discomfort, but because of it. The discomfort I felt drafting and redrafting essays I didn’t understand was not a warning signal. It was construction.
Part 4: When the Work Becomes Its Own Reward
Somewhere in those weeks, something changed that I had not expected. The weight of writing for a grade became lighter. I started drafting personal essays and practice pieces outside of class — not for marks, not for anyone. Just because the momentum was there.
Inzlicht et al. (2025) demonstrated that when effortful activity is consistently paired with meaningful outcomes over repeated trials, the brain begins generating genuine reward signals during the effortful task itself — not just after. The doing becomes its own return. This is not motivation in the conventional sense. It is a structural change in how the brain has categorized the activity.
Vallerand (2008) would call this a passion transition. I had entered the course running on obsessive passion — grade-dependent, fear-adjacent, externally pressured. I came out the other side with harmonious passion: freely chosen, integrated into my sense of self, no longer requiring the threat of consequences to sustain it. This is the difference between working hard and working right. Working hard can be sustained by fear. Working right requires that the activity has become, in some genuine sense, yours.
This transition doesn’t happen automatically, and it doesn’t happen quickly. It requires staying past the point where the Central Governor is still pulling back, past the aMCC’s initial resistance, into the territory where the effort itself starts to feel like the point. Most people stop before that threshold. I almost did.
I think back to that moment — the grade on the screen, the laptop open, the silence that sat heavier than any noise. I remember thinking something was fundamentally wrong with me. That I had done everything right and still failed, which could only mean the problem was me.
It wasn’t. The basal ganglia had been quietly filing the unfamiliar under “unsafe” long before I opened that assignment. The Central Governor had already set a conservative output cap. The aMCC, the region that builds persistence through discomfort, was underdeveloped — not because I was incapable, but because I had never been pushed past the point where it needed to grow. That failure wasn’t a verdict. It was a starting condition.
For students and writers navigating the gap between effort and result, the research points to something clarifying: the brain is not a fixed instrument. The habit architecture of the basal ganglia can be interrupted. The Central Governor’s estimate can be revised. The aMCC can be grown. None of these changes happen through harder effort alone — they happen through different effort, effort aimed at the right direction, sustained past the point of initial resistance.
The ceiling I kept hitting was never mine. I just had to stay in the room long enough — and work in the right direction long enough — to find that out.

What the Grade Didn’t Teach Me
Prem
University of Alberta
April 2026
So I fight. Harder than I’ve ever fought for anything academic. I pull apart every requirement, follow every step, leave nothing to chance. For once, I feel like I’ve actually done everything right, and I mean everything. I let myself believe it might actually work.
Then I open my results.
The grade stares back at me: a flat-out fail. Not a near-miss, not a “you almost had it”, just a number that doesn’t move no matter how long I sit there. I close the laptop. Open it again. Still there. That heavy, hollow silence where your brain hasn’t caught up to what your eyes are reading.
I’d put everything I had into that paper. Everything.
The assignment was a reflective essay for a first-year writing course — a genre I had never seriously attempted, in a class I had underestimated from week one. I spent more time on it than anything else that semester. I pulled apart the rubric, addressed every requirement, revised more than I normally would. The confidence I felt submitting it wasn’t arrogance. It was the specific, quiet certainty of someone who genuinely believes they finally figured something out.
But here’s the thing — this isn’t really a story about a grade. It’s about the specific shock of realizing that effort and correctness are not the same thing. That working hard and working right are not interchangeable. Most of us, in school, in work, in the quiet private goals we tell almost no one, have been confusing the two for years without ever noticing. The question I couldn’t stop asking after that failure wasn’t what went wrong. It was: why did my brain let me believe I had already figured it out?
Part 1: The Brain’s Hidden Limits
The answer, I’ve come to understand, begins in the brain — and not in the way we’re usually taught. Every behavior we repeat enough times gets quietly promoted by the basal ganglia, the brain’s efficiency system, which converts repeated actions into automatic habits that require no conscious effort (Balleine & O’Doherty, 2010). This isn’t weakness. It’s optimization. But it means that what we call the “comfort zone” is not a character flaw — it’s a neurological default, the brain’s way of conserving energy by staying with what’s already mapped.
The limits go further than habit. Tim Noakes’ Central Governor Model proposes that the brain applies a conservative cap on both physical and mental output — not because we’re genuinely exhausted, but because it is protecting a biological reserve it calculates it might need later (Noakes, 2011). The wall we hit mid-workout, mid-essay, mid-difficult-conversation — that’s not a true limit. It’s a neurological estimate of where “safe” ends. When I think back to that paper — the one I failed — I had hit that estimate without ever knowing it existed. I thought I’d reached my limit. I’d actually reached my brain’s first guess.
What’s significant for students and writers specifically is that this governor doesn’t distinguish between a 10K run and a difficult draft. Cognitive load research confirms that the brain treats sustained effortful thinking as a resource-depleting task (Kahneman, 2011), which means the same protective withdrawal that stops a runner at kilometre eight can stop a writer at paragraph three. The experience of “hitting a wall” in a writing assignment is not a sign of insufficient effort. It is the governor deciding it has done enough.
Part 2: Running on the Wrong Kind of Passion
Biology is only half the problem. The other half is direction — and most of us have never been fully honest about it.
A 2023 survey by Deloitte found that 86% of Gen Z respondents identified purpose as central to their work, yet most reported remaining in environments that provided none of it (Deloitte, 2023). A Pew Research Center study on job satisfaction found that roughly half of U.S. workers described themselves as not highly satisfied with their current roles — not because they lacked skills, but because the work didn’t connect to anything they actually cared about (Pew Research Center, 2023). These are not career statistics. They are direction statistics — the fingerprint of people who know, vaguely, what they want and still haven’t moved toward it.
Psychologist Robert Vallerand (2008) offers one explanation for why this gap persists. Through decades of research, he identified two structurally different kinds of passion. Harmonious passion is self-determined: it grows from genuine identity, and it predicts resilience, wellbeing, and sustained engagement over time. Obsessive passion, by contrast, is pressure-driven — it comes from what looks impressive, what is expected, or what we have decided we should want. The discomfort of working right, as opposed to just working hard, often reveals which kind of passion you’re actually running on. Obsessive passion can generate enormous short-term effort; it rarely generates the kind of flexible problem-solving that improves under pressure. I didn’t know which kind I had. I just knew the one I had wasn’t working.
Part 3: What Resistance Actually Builds
After the failure, I had no choice but to move — not out of discipline, but out of desperation. I went to my teacher. I sat with concepts I didn’t understand and asked questions that made me feel like someone who didn’t know the basics. That shame was real. I put it aside and focused on the goal. Eight hours a day, sometimes more — not because I was motivated, but because I had run out of excuses to stop.
What was happening neurologically during those weeks is something I can now name. The anterior midcingulate cortex (aMCC) is a brain region that activates specifically during tasks we find aversive or effortful. It does not fire during comfort. It fires during resistance. Critically, it grows denser with repeated activation — each instance of pushing through unwanted difficulty is literally building the architecture of persistence (Parvizi et al., 2013; Touroutoglou et al., 2020). Studies show this region is measurably larger in elite athletes and in individuals with longer lifespans; it is measurably smaller in those who chronically avoid discomfort. But it is not fixed. It responds to use.
David Goggins describes this as “callousing the mind.” Neuroscientists call it aMCC hypertrophy (Touroutoglou et al., 2020). Both are describing the same process: the brain rewiring itself not despite discomfort, but because of it. The discomfort I felt drafting and redrafting essays I didn’t understand was not a warning signal. It was construction.
Part 4: When the Work Becomes Its Own Reward
Somewhere in those weeks, something changed that I had not expected. The weight of writing for a grade became lighter. I started drafting personal essays and practice pieces outside of class — not for marks, not for anyone. Just because the momentum was there.
Inzlicht et al. (2025) demonstrated that when effortful activity is consistently paired with meaningful outcomes over repeated trials, the brain begins generating genuine reward signals during the effortful task itself — not just after. The doing becomes its own return. This is not motivation in the conventional sense. It is a structural change in how the brain has categorized the activity.
Vallerand (2008) would call this a passion transition. I had entered the course running on obsessive passion — grade-dependent, fear-adjacent, externally pressured. I came out the other side with harmonious passion: freely chosen, integrated into my sense of self, no longer requiring the threat of consequences to sustain it. This is the difference between working hard and working right. Working hard can be sustained by fear. Working right requires that the activity has become, in some genuine sense, yours.
This transition doesn’t happen automatically, and it doesn’t happen quickly. It requires staying past the point where the Central Governor is still pulling back, past the aMCC’s initial resistance, into the territory where the effort itself starts to feel like the point. Most people stop before that threshold. I almost did.
I think back to that moment — the grade on the screen, the laptop open, the silence that sat heavier than any noise. I remember thinking something was fundamentally wrong with me. That I had done everything right and still failed, which could only mean the problem was me.
It wasn’t. The basal ganglia had been quietly filing the unfamiliar under “unsafe” long before I opened that assignment. The Central Governor had already set a conservative output cap. The aMCC, the region that builds persistence through discomfort, was underdeveloped — not because I was incapable, but because I had never been pushed past the point where it needed to grow. That failure wasn’t a verdict. It was a starting condition.
For students and writers navigating the gap between effort and result, the research points to something clarifying: the brain is not a fixed instrument. The habit architecture of the basal ganglia can be interrupted. The Central Governor’s estimate can be revised. The aMCC can be grown. None of these changes happen through harder effort alone — they happen through different effort, effort aimed at the right direction, sustained past the point of initial resistance.
The ceiling I kept hitting was never mine. I just had to stay in the room long enough — and work in the right direction long enough — to find that out.
